CHAPTER I 
RECOMMENDATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT 
OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF THE DEMANDS FOR GRANTS (2025-26) OF THE MINISTRY 
OF WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT (M/o WCD) 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee observes that Ministry has been allocated Rs. 26,889.69 crores under BE 2025-26 
which is 0.53% of the total budget allocation of the Government of India. Further, allocation at BE 
2025-26 is 3.05% more than BE 2024-25 and 15.98% more than RE 2024-25. The Committee notes that 
Ministry of Women and Child Development caters to 67% population of the country as per the Census 
2011, however, allocation of only 0.53% of the total budget allocation for FY 2025-26, is very meagre 
amount to facilitate implementation of various schemes and plans. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends the Ministry to seek more funds from Ministry of Finance at the RE stage so that the 
schemes/plans do not shift due to shortage of funds.      
                      (Para 2.4 ibid) 
 
Reply 
The Ministry acknowledges the observations of the Committee regarding the budgetary allocation for 
the financial year 2025–26 and submits that it is committed for effective implementation of its schemes 
and programmes.  However, it may be appreciated that Ministry of WCD is one of the several 
Ministries which are involved in the area of work related to development of women and children.   
Health, Education, Rural Development, Food and Public Distribution, Social Justice and Empowerment, 
Tribal Affairs, Agriculture, etc., are other key Ministries which are involved in this job.  Moreover, the 
expenditure in this Ministry is demand driven and the budget of the Ministry is fixed taking this into 
account.  However, the Ministry will approach Ministry of Finance at the suitable stage for enhancing 
the allocations so that the schemes are not affected due to financial constraints. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee notes that Ministry was allocated Rs. 26,092.19 crores at BE 2024- 25 which was 
reduced by 11.14% to Rs. 23,182.98 crores at RE 2024-25, which is Rs. 1835.48 crores less than the 
Actual utilization by the Ministry during 2023-24. Moreover, the Actual utilization during 2024-25 as 
on 17.02.2025 is only 18,497.21 crores which is 70.89% of BE 2024-25 and 79.79% of the RE 2024-
25.The Committee feels that in view of the inflationary trends in the country, the allocation and Actual 
utilization should increase at least 8% to 10% over the allocation/utilization during previous year to 
accommodate the inflation and to maintain the existing standards for expenditure by Ministry and to 
avoid further decline in actual allocation/expenditure. Further, the Ministry of Finance should be taken 
into confidence so that substantial reduction in allocations at RE stage is avoided in order to make the 
schemes efficacious.           
(Para 2.5 ibid) 
Reply 
The Ministry takes note of the Committee’s observations regarding the reduction in allocation at the 
Revised Estimates (RE) stage. All out efforts were made by the Ministry to enhance the allocation. 
Consequently, MoF allocated an additional fund of Rs.1405.32 crore in RE 2024-25 due to which total 
RE became to Rs.24588.30 crore against which an amount of Rs.24529.48 crore was incurred by the 
Ministry i.e 99.76% of Final RE.  Further, the Ministry will also engage proactively with the Ministry 
of Finance to avoid substantial reductions at the RE stage in future and seek adequate funds in 
alignment with schemes' requirements and inflation-adjusted needs.  Efforts will be made to get 
sufficient budget outlay for the schemes of the Ministry during the forthcoming 16th Finance 
Commission. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee notes that Actual utilization by the Ministry over allocation at RE and BE had been 
89.22% and 62.47%, respectively during 2020-21, 91.73% and 87.10%, respectively during 2021-22, 
98.32% and 93.40%, respectively during 2022-23 and 98.31% and 98.31% during 2023-24. However, 
Actual utilization as on 17th February, 2025 over RE and BE 2024-25 has been 79.79% and 70.89%, 
respectively. In this regard, the Committee would like to refer to Rule 56(3) of General Financial Rules 

3 
 
(GFR), which states that rush to expenditure particularly in the closing months of financial year should 
be avoided in future. As per the guidelines, the last quarter expenditure must be limited to actual 
procurement of goods and services and reimbursement of expenditure already occurred. Ministry of 
Finance's instructions seeks to restrict last quarter expenditure to 33% ceiling and last month (March) 
expenditure to 15% ceiling only.  
In backdrop of the Actual Expenditure by Ministry of Women and Child Development during 2024-25 
and Rule 56(3) of General Financial Rules (GFR), the Committee recommends that the Ministry should 
adhere to Rule 56(3) of GFR, streamline its expenditure during 2025-26 to optimize the utilization of 
funds allocated to it and to avoid piling up of expenditure in the last quarter of the financial year. 
          (Para 2.6 ibid) 
Reply 
During the F.Y 2024-25, an amount of Rs.26092.19 crore was allocated by Ministry of Finance which 
was reduced to Rs.23182.98 crore at RE stage. An amount of Rs.3308.20 crore was sought from 
Ministry of Finance during 2nd Supplementary Demands however, at that time funds were not 
provided.  However, keeping in view good expenditure trend and further efforts made by the Ministry, 
an additional amount of Rs.1405.32 crore was allocated by MoF during the last month of Financial 
Year.  Accordingly, final RE of the Ministry was enhanced to Rs.24588.30 crore against which an 
amount of Rs24529.48 crore was incurred by the Ministry i.e. 99.76% of Final RE 2024-25 and 94.01% 
of BE 2024-25. It is also to be mentioned that necessary relaxation was obtained from MoF for 
incurring more than 33% and 15% of Budget Estimates during last quarter and last month respectively. 
However, it is stated that necessary measures will be undertaken during F.Y 2025-26 onwards to 
streamline the planning and execution of schemes and programmes to avoid any such rush of 
expenditure in the last quarter. 
  
Recommendation 
From perusal of Table 3 & 4, it is evident that there are huge variations of allocations such as (-) 
45.63% under Anganwadi Services, (-)23.44 under Mission Vatsalya earlier Child Protection Services, 
(-)33.33 under Nari Adalat, (-)28.83% under Shakti Sadan and Home for Widows earlier Swadhar 
Greeh/Ujjawala, (-)16.67% under Palna/ National Creche Scheme and (-)31.82% under Gender 
Budgeting in BE 2025-26 over projections made by the Ministry of Women and Child Development to 
Ministry of Finance. Further, there are huge variations of (-) 35.71% under National Institute of Public 
Cooperation and Child Development NIPCCD/SPNIWCD, (-) 26.44% under National Commission for 
Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) and (-) 11.70% under National Commission for Women over 
projections made by the Ministry to Ministry of Finance. Similarly, there is overall variation of (-) 
40.37% and (-) 25.58% in scheme-wise and Organization/ Institution/Bodies-wise in BE 2025-26, 
respectively over projections made by the Ministry to Ministry of Finance. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that review of the Projections made to Ministry of Finance and actual allocations made in 
respect of each scheme should be undertaken by the Ministry of Women and Child Development 
wherein there is gap between projections and allocations to make implementation of schemes/plans 
more realistic. The Committee also recommends the Ministry to monitor the physical and financial 
progress of the schemes, so that these schemes do not suffer due to reduced allocations. Such an 
objective review will help the Ministry to seek additional funds at RE stage for the schemes/plans.  
The Committee further recommends the Ministry of Finance to allocate funds to the Ministry of 
Women and Child Development liberally against the projections in view of the fact that the Ministry 
caters more than half of the population of the country and runs many crucial schemes for their well-
being and development. 
          (Para 2.8 ibid) 
Reply 
The Ministry of Women and Child Development acknowledge the recommendations of the Committee. 
The Ministry has reviewed the projections made to the Ministry of Finance and the actual allocations 
received under each scheme. This exercise will aid in aligning future projections with realistic 
implementation needs. Further, the Ministry is also making efforts to strengthen its monitoring 
mechanisms to track both physical and financial progress of schemes to ensure their effective 
implementation of the schemes. 
Further, it is mentioned that significant gap between projection made by this Ministry to MoF 
and actual allocation of fund provided to this Ministry by MoF is mainly under the scheme Saksham 

4 
 
Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0 as MoF provided the fund under this scheme considering the total outlay 
approved for this scheme during the 15th Finance Commission. However, efforts are being made by the 
Ministry to get the outlay of the scheme increased during 2025-26 with the approval of the Competent 
Authority. 
 Further, as regards to cut imposed by MoF in other schemes, it was due to availability of 
unspent balance in SNA accounts with States/UTs.  To resolve this issue, regular VCs are being made 
and regular advisories to the states are also being issued. The Ministry is hopeful that the measures 
being taken will reduce the unspent balance with the states significantly resulting in expenditure of fund 
as per approved Quarterly Expenditure Plan.   
Variation in projection made by the Ministry and allocation by MoF in respect of 
NIPCCD/SPNIWCD, NCPCR and NCW was due to the fact that distribution of fund in Autonomous 
Bodies and Secretariat was to be done within available fund under non-scheme.  However, efforts will 
be made get more fund for the aforesaid Bodies during RE or supplementary grant stage. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee observes that the Ministry acts as the nodal Ministry which runs important programmes 
like Saksham Anganwadi, Poshan 2.0 for children, Mission Vatsalya and Mission Shakti for the 
development of women and children and many of the programmes run by the Ministry play a 
complementary role to developmental programmes in the sectors of health, education, rural 
development, and safety of women and children. However, the Committee notes that the total unutilized 
funds with respect to BE 2023-24 is Rs. 1622.32 crores while it is Rs. 804.21 crores with respect to RE 
2023-24 under Mission Shakti against allocation of Rs. 3143.96 crores and Rs. 2325.85 crores at BE 
and RE 2023-24, respectively. The total unutilized fund during 2023-24 under 
 
SAMARTHYA Scheme is Rs. 1416.83 crores and Rs. 698.72 crores against BE & RE 
allocations of Rs. 2581.96 crores and Rs. 1863.85 crores, respectively which is not satisfactory. 
Similarly, the total unutilized fund during 2023-24 under SAMBAL Scheme is Rs. 205.49 crores and Rs. 
105.49 crores against BE & RE allocations of Rs. 562.00 crores and Rs. 462.00 crores, respectively 
which is also not very satisfactory.         
(Para 2.11 ibid) 
Reply 
Ministry acknowledges the observation made by the Committee. Further, it is stated that the less 
expenditure was incurred in Mission Shakti scheme during the FY 2023-24 mainly due to incomplete 
proposal received from the States and unspent balance lying in the SNA account of the States under the 
various components of sub schemes of Sambal and Samarthya under Mission Shakti. In so far as 
PMMVY which is the largest constituent of Samarthya sub-scheme, is concerned, the major reasons for 
the funds not being released to several States/UTs were the non-compliance of mandatory SNA norms 
(formulated by Department of Expenditure) by those States, regarding requirement of deposit of Central 
share of Interest accrued in the bank account, deficit in the transfer of funds from State Treasury to 
SNA bank accounts of the respective schemes, etc. Under PMMVY, the transition to new software 
which is Paper-less and Aadhaar authentication and NPCI seeding enabling, also led to slow 
implementation by the States/ UTs. The transition to new software is now complete (except in cases of 
Tamil Nadu and Odisha, where the scheme is being implemented in co- branded manner with the 
corresponding state schemes). Accordingly, the fund release and utilization should now improve 
significantly. Also, the pending applications from the old software have now been migrated into the 
new software through a separate module. As a result, the process of payment to beneficiaries should 
now be expedited. 
Recommendation 
The Committee further observes that during 2024-25, the unutilized funds as on 31st January, 2025 
under Saksham Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0 with respect to BE and RE is Rs. 5661.17 crores and Rs. 
4532.07 crores against BE and RE allocations of Rs. 21200.00 crores and Rs. 20070.90 crores, 
respectively. Under Mission Vatsalya, unutilized funds as on 31st January, 2025, with respect to BE 
and RE are Rs. 568.80 crores and Rs. 487.63 crores against BE and RE 2024-25 allocations of 
Rs.1472.17 crores and Rs. 1391.00 crores, respectively. Under SAMBAL scheme unutilized funds as on 
31st January, 2025, with respect to BE and RE are Rs. 472.58 crores and Rs. 265.94 crores against BE 
and RE 2024-25 allocations of Rs. 629.00 crores and Rs. 422.36 crores, respectively. Under 

5 
 
SAMARTHYA scheme unutilized funds as on 31st January, 2025, with respect to BE and RE are Rs. 
1823.28 crores and Rs. 335.05 crores against BE and RE 2024-25 of Rs.2516.97 crores and Rs. 
1028.74 crores, respectively. Under Mission Shakti unutilized funds as on 31st January, 2025, with 
respect to BE and RE are Rs. 2295.86 crores and Rs. 600.99 crores against BE and RE 2024-25 of 
Rs.3145.97 crores and Rs. 1451.10 crores, respectively.  
The Committee notes that increased BE is allocated which is reduced at RE stage in general, 
and up to 30-40% in case of schemes like Mission Shakti in particular. The Actual utilization is again 
very less vis-à-vis BE and RE allocations during 2023-24 and 2024-25. The Committee therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry should adhere to Rule 56(3) of GFR and streamline its expenditure 
during 2025-26 to optimize the utilization of funds allocated to it and to avoid piling up of expenditure 
in the last quarter of the financial year. Further, trend of substantial reduction in allocations at RE 
stage under various schemes of the Ministry should be taken care of and avoided as far as possible. 
          (Para 2.12 ibid) 
Reply 
This Ministry acknowledges the recommendation made by the Committee. Further, it is to mention that 
during the F.Y 2024-25, an amount of Rs.26092.19 crore was allocated by MoF which was reduced to 
Rs.23182.98 crore at RE stage. But with the efforts made by the Ministry, an additional amount of 
Rs.1405.32 crore was allocated by MoF under all three Missions of this Ministry due to which Final RE 
came to Rs.24588.30 crore against which an amount of Rs.24529.48 crore was incurred by the Ministry 
i.e. 99.76% of Final RE 2024-25 and 94.01% of BE 2024-25. 
Moreover, it is also stated that the schemes viz Mission Vatsalya, Mission Shakti and Saksham 
Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0 are mostly demand driven schemes and the release of funds also depends on 
receipt of the proposals complete in all respects, as per the schematic norms and duly recommended by 
the State Governments/UTs. Sometimes the proposals are received at the fag end of the FY resulting in 
more release during the last quarter of FY.  However, it is stated that necessary measures will be 
undertaken during F.Y 2025-26 to streamline the planning and execution of schemes and programmes 
to avoid any rush of expenditure in the last quarter. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee notes that the unspent balances in States’ SNA accounts are substantial and that they 
are part of the reason the Ministry is unable to secure a larger budget. The Committee was provided 
state-wise details of the same, which are attached in Annexure 1. The Committee recommends that the 
Department work more closely with State Governments to understand the constraints, if any, in 
spending the outstanding SNA balance and the steps that can be undertaken to accelerate the utilization 
of these funds.     
(Para 2.13 ibid) 
Reply 
For resolving the issue of SNA balance, regular follow up meetings, both physical and through VCs, are 
being held with the States /UTs since last 2 years.  The Ministry is hopeful that with the regular efforts 
being made, the availability of unspent balance with the states will reduce significantly.  Here, it is also 
stated that with the Mission Shakti scheme of the Ministry getting onboarded on SNA SPARSH module 
from SNA module, the issue of unspent balance will not be there and expenditure will be made on real 
time basis. 
 
SCHEMES/MISSIONS OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN & CHILD DEVELOPMENT 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee notes that the Ministry was allocated for Centrally Sponsored Schemes like Saksham 
Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0, Mission Vatsalya, Mission SHAKTI and Other Schemes Funded from 
Nirbhaya Fund, a total of Rs. 25848.14 crores under BE 2024-25 which was reduced to Rs. 22943.00 
crores at RE stage. Out of the said allocation Ministry has been able to spend Rs. 18,284.24 crores only 
as on 17th February, 2025 under these flagship schemes which pegs at 70.73% & 79.69% of the BE & 
RE 2024-25, respectively. The Committee expresses its concern over the poor fiscal management and 
under utilization of allocated funds under various flagship schemes of the Ministry like Saksham 
Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0, Mission Vatsalya, Mission SHAKTI and Other Schemes Funded from 
Nirbhaya Fund. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should take effective

Reply 
Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0 is a Centrally Sponsored scheme. The Central 
Government is responsible for policy and planning and the State Governments are responsible for day-
to-day program implementation of this scheme.   
  Anganwadi Workers (AWWs) and Anganwadi Helpers (AWHs) are “honorary workers” from 
the local community who voluntarily come forward to render their services in the area of child care and 
development to help the community. Being honorary and voluntary workers, they are paid a monthly 
honorarium as decided by Government from time to time. Currently, an Anganwadi Worker is paid 
honorarium @Rs.4,500/- per month and Anganwadi Helper is paid honorarium @Rs.2,250/- per month 
on cost sharing basis between the Centre and State/UT along with performance linked incentive of 
Rs.250/- per month for AWHs and Rs.500/- to AWWs. In addition, States/UTs are also paying 
additional monetary incentives/honorarium to these functionaries from their own resources which vary 
from State to State.  
  As per Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0 Guidelines issued by the Ministry, promotional 
opportunities for Anganwadi Workers have been enhanced. 50% posts of Anganwadi Workers shall be 
filled by promotion of Anganwadi Helpers and 50% posts of Supervisors shall be filled by promotion of 
Anganwadi Workers subject to fulfilment of other criteria. States/ UTs have been requested to adopt a 
uniform retirement date i.e 30th April of each year with respect to Anganwadi Workers and Helpers to 
ensure proper human resource planning. 
        Keeping in view the importance of their contribution towards society, insurance benefits have been 
provided to Anganwadi Workers and Helpers under Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana 
(PMJJBY) for life cover of Rs.2.00 lakh (covers life risk, death due to any reason) to AWWs/AWHs in 
the age group of 18 to 50 years and Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana for accidental cover of 
Rs.2.00 Lakh (accidental death and permanent full disability)/Rs.1.00 Lakh (partial but permanent 
disability) to AWWs and AWHs in the age group of 18-59 years. Insurance cover under PMJJBY and 
PMSBY is provided to AWWs/AWHs through their bank accounts and the funds towards premium 
payment are released to the States/UTs on the prescribed cost sharing ratio under Anganwadi Services 
Scheme. 
MWCD has also requested State Governments/UT Administrations to encourage eligible 
AWWs/AWHs to enrol themselves under Pradhan Mantri Shram Yogi Mandhan (PM-SYM) Pension 
Scheme on voluntary basis to get an assured monthly pension on attaining the age of 60 years. 
Under the Budget announcement 2024-25, healthcare cover under the Ayushman Bharat scheme has 
been extended to all AWW/AWHs. Apart from the above, other facilities are also being extended to 
AWWs/AWHs, including leave for 20 days per year, paid absence on abortion/ miscarriage once for 45 

11 
 
days and paid maternity absence of 180 days. There is a provision for set of two uniforms (saree/suit per 
annum) to AWW/AWHs.  
  Further, Mission Poshan 2.0 empowers the frontline functionaries i.e. Anganwadi workers by 
providing them with smart phones.  The ‘Poshan Tracker’ application was rolled out on 1st March 2021 
as an important governance tool to strengthen and bring about transparency in nutrition delivery support 
systems at the Anganwadi centres. Poshan Tracker facilitates monitoring and tracking of all Anganwadi 
Centres, Anganwadi workers (AWWs) and beneficiaries on defined indicators.  
  The introduction of Poshan Tracker has significantly streamlined the operations of AWWs, 
reducing the time-consuming and cumbersome tasks they previously undertook. Prior to Poshan 
Tracker, AWWs were burdened with maintaining physical records of growth monitoring, carrying 
bulky IEC materials, manually scheduling home visits and updating 9 registers on regular basis. The 
physical records of Growth Monitoring have been replaced by auto-generated monthly reports in 
Poshan Tracker. These reports can be downloaded and used in the review meetings by the supervisors. 
All the home visits are now auto-scheduled in Poshan Tracker for which the Anganwadi Worker also 
receives reminders. Report on completed and pending Home Visits is available in Poshan Tracker. 
WHO standard growth charts are auto-generated for each child on the basis of height and weight 
entered by AWWs in Poshan Tracker. With “Poshan Tracker”, real time data on malnutrition indicators 
is available every month. Aadharshila "ECCE-Learning" module has also been incorporated in Poshan 
Tracker Application which provides daily learning prompts in the form of videos and voice notes for all 
Anganwadi Workers (AWWs). 
Poshan Tracker application and dashboard has not only eliminated the need to keep physical 
registers, it has reduced drudgery from the daily work routine of the AWW and has increased her 
capacity for more direct engagement with beneficiaries and quality improvement in service delivery 
which helps in making better decisions and monitoring each beneficiary every day. 
 State/UTs have time and again been requested not to involve AWWs/AWHs in non-scheme 
related work as it burdens the AWWs/AWHs and affects the implementation of the scheme. 
  Further, Government has issued orders for upgradation of all mini-AWC to regular AWCs. This 
would add an Anganwadi Helper in these Mini Anganwadi Centres across the country to share the 
burden of Anganwadi Worker so that the component of Early Childhood Care and Education can be 
strengthened. 
 Since the implementation of the Scheme is done by the State Government/UT Administration, 
therefore, no specific guidelines have been laid by the Government of India with respect to recruitment, 
retirement benefits, and payment of Gratuity for Anganwadi Workers and Anganwadi Helpers. Only a 
broad framework has been designed to allow the States/UTs to have the required flexibility in 
implementation of the Scheme so as to achieve maximum efficacy as per their local requirements. 
Whenever the matter of irregular payment of Honorarium or non-payment of Honorarium 
arises, the matter is taken up with the concerned State/UT for taking action.

During the 15th Finance Commission cycle, 2 lakh Anganwadi Centres (AWCs) located in Government 
buildings @ 40,000 AWCs per year are sanctioned to be strengthened and upgraded as Saksham 
Anganwadis for improved nutrition delivery and for Early Childhood Care and Education under 
Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0. Saksham Anganwadis are to be provided with better 
infrastructure than the conventional Anganwadi Centres including LED screens; water 
purifier/installation of RO Machine, Poshan Vatika, ECCE related books and learning material etc. 
AWCs with the following pre-requisite will be upgraded into Saksham Anganwadi: 
1. AWCs should be in Government owned building 
2. Availability of Electricity/power supply 
3. Drinking Water Facility  
4. Functional Toilet  
5. Functional Kitchen  
 
Mission Saksham Anganwadi & Poshan 2.0 is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme, where the 
responsibility of implementation of the Scheme falls under the ambit of State Government/UT 
administration.  
Under the supplementary nutrition program of Mission Saksham Anganwadi & Poshan 2.0, all 
beneficiaries including children (06 months to 6 years), pregnant women and lactating mothers 
(PW&LM) and Adolescent Girls (14 to 18 years in Aspirational Districts and North East Region) are 
provided supplementary nutrition for minimum of 300 days in a year  in the form of Hot Cooked Meals 
and Take Home Ration through Anganwadi centres to bridge the gap between the Recommended 
Dietary Allowance and the Average Daily Intake (ADI).  
The same is provided as per nutrition norms specified in Schedule-II of the National Food 
Security Act, 2013.  In order to address the challenge of malnutrition more effectively, these nutrition 
norms have been revised and notified on 25.01.2023 to make them more comprehensive in terms of 
both quantity and quality of supplementary nutrition based on the principles of diet diversity that 
provides quality protein, healthy fats and 7 essential micronutrients. The approvals of revised cost 
norms are being followed. 

13 
 
As per the guidelines of Mission Poshan 2.0, Take-Home Ration (not raw ration) and Hot 
Cooked Meals (HCM) and Morning snacks (MS) shall be tested from FSSAI recognized 
laboratories/NABL accredited laboratories. 
Ministry of Women & Child Development and Ministry of Health & Family Welfare have 
jointly released the protocol on 10th October, 2023 for Community Management of Malnutrition 
(CMAM) providing detailed steps for identification and management of malnourished children at the 
Anganwadi level, including decision-making for referral, nutritional management and follow-up care. 
Poshan Tracker application helps AWWs in measuring children’s height and weight, following 
the CMAM (Community-Based Management of Acute Malnutrition) protocol for enabling early 
detection and intervention for malnourished children

Recommendation 
The Committee observes that percentage of stunted children were 38.4 % during 202526, 35.5% during 
2019-21 as per the NFHS 4 & 5 respectively. However, as per the Poshan Tracker data of January, 
2025, it has increased to 39.61% among children of 0-5 years. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
the Ministry should take initiatives on the following:  
(i) Breakfast Inclusion: A national breakfast program should be introduced to combat morning hunger 
and enhance cognitive performance, particularly in rural and economically weaker sections.  
(ii) Decentralized Procurement & Localized Meal Planning: Community-led food sourcing, integrating 
locally grown grains, vegetables, and dairy should be promoted to improve nutrition while 
supporting local farmers as well.  
(iii) Third-Party Quality Audits: Quarterly meal quality, hygiene, and taste of the meal checks should be 
conducted through independent agencies, ensuring compliance with dietary standards and 
addressing reported issues in real time.  
(iv)  Nutritional Fortification: Iron and protein fortification in meals under Poshan 2.0 should be 
implemented to tackle widespread deficiencies in children. Provision of a glass of milk daily should 
also be ensured in view of the fact that around 40% children in the country are stunted.  
(v) Revision of Nutritional Norms: The nutritional norms should be revised for the meals under 
POSHAN 2.0 on the line of recommendations by the ICMR.  
(vi) The Committee notes that combating malnutrition and anaemia among children below the age of 5 
and pregnant and lactating women requires coordinated action across Departments. Poor 
performance on these two 96 critical indicators has hurt India’s HDI rankings globally. 
Accordingly, the Ministry should take the lead in setting up a National Mission to eradicate both 
malnutrition and anaemia, which brings together stakeholders from across the Ministries of WCD, 
Health, Education, and Finance with the goal of a malnutrition and anaemia free India by 2032. 
               (Para 3.4.38 ibid) 
Reply 
As per the data available in Poshan Tracker For  as on April 2025, the percentage of stunted children 0-
6 years stands at 36.00%. During NFHS 4 & 5 the sample size was limited whereas the sample size for 
April 2025 8.8 crore beneficiaries from 0-6 years. 
i. As per the existing guidelines of the Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0, Children (3-6 
Years) are currently being provided supplementary nutrition in two servings i.e. Morning Snacks and 
Hot Cooked meal. 
ii.   Streamlining Guidelines have been issued by the Ministry on 13.01.2021 for all the States and UTs. 
This Guidelines cover Quality Assurance, Roles and Responsibilities of Duty Holders such as 
DMs/DCs, procedure for procurement, integrating AYUSH concepts and Data Management and 
Monitoring through Poshan Tracker for transparency, efficiency and accountability in delivery of 
Supplementary Nutrition. As per the streamlining guidelines dated 13.01.2021, State/UT must introduce 
transparent processes for procurement of supplementary nutrition as per GFR and vigilance guidelines 
and ensure that THR procured conforms to technical and nutritional standards set by MOWCD. Local 
dietary inputs and fresh produce (green vegetables, fruits, medicinal plants and herbs), fortified rice and 
millets, nuts and oilseeds like groundnut and sesame seeds are actively incorporated in meals which are 
served to different categories of beneficiaries under the Scheme to promote health, wellness and 
immunity and to manage Anaemia. The food items for Take Home Ration (not raw ration) and Hot 
Cooked Meals (HCM) are specific to the States and include locally grown/available wholesome fruits 
and vegetables. 
iii.    As per the existing guidelines of the Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0, States/UTs 
share ensure the quality of Supplementary Nutrition-THR and HCM. Supplementary nutrition must 
conform to prescribed standards laid down under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and 
regulations made there under to ensure consistent quality and nutritive value per serving.  Quality 
testing shall be done through Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) owned or 
authorized laboratories.  State Governments and UTs shall carry out periodic checks and get 

15 
 
supplementary nutrition tested through the FSSAI owned/registered/empanelled/accredited laboratories 
in accordance with streamlining guidelines dated 13.01.2001. The District Nutrition Committee under 
the DM shall ensure period testing of THR in randomly selected AWCs. In case of Hot Cooked Meal, it 
should be ensured that it is prepared in proper kitchen sheds having adequate sanitation and safe 
drinking water so as to maintain hygienic conditions. 
iv.   In pursuance of the Hon'ble Prime Minister's Address on 75th Independence Day, Fortified Rice is 
being provided under Wheat Based Nutrition Programme (WBNP) and Scheme for Adolescent Girls 
(SAG) since 2021-22 in lieu of normal rice. This helps in fighting malnutrition and Anaemia in women 
and children arising due to deficiency of micro nutrients like Iron, Folic Acid and Vitamin B-12. 
v.  The ICMR guidelines talks about intake of all the essential nutrients through a balanced diet to 
maintain good health. Poshan 2.0 guidelines also mentions about intake of balanced diet and diet 
Diversity for addressing malnutrition. Further, the nutritional norms were reviewed and revised by an 
Inter-Ministerial Committee constituted by the Department of Food and Public Distribution (DoFPD) 
under the co-chairpersonship of Secretary (DoFPD) and Secretary (MoWCD). The Commission 
consisted of members from line ministries, National Institute of Nutrition and technical experts. The 
revised nutrition norms were notified on 25th January, 2023 based on the recommendations contained 
in the report submitted by National Institute of Nutrition (NIN) after detailed deliberations by the 
committee. Poshan 2.0 Guidelines follows the revised nutrition norms mentioned in Schedule 2 of 
NFSA (National Food Security Act). 
vi.  Nutrition goes beyond mere eating of food; it requires proper digestion, absorption, and metabolism 
which are influenced by factors like sanitation, education and access to safe drinking water. As 
malnutrition requires a multi-sectoral approach involving dimensions of food, health, water, sanitation 
and education, it is crucial to effectively address the issue of malnutrition in a convergent manner. It is 
being addressed under Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0 by establishing cross cutting 
convergence amongst 18 Ministries/Departments. Under Mission 2.0 a new strategy has been made for 
reduction in malnutrition and for improved health, wellness and immunity through activities like 
community engagement, outreach, behavioral change, and advocacy. It focuses on Maternal Nutrition, 
Infant and Young Child Feeding Norms, treatment of Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM)/ Moderate 
Acute Malnutrition (MAM) and wellness through AYUSH practices to reduce prevalence of wasting, 
stunting, anaemia and being underweight. Fortified rice is being supplied to AWCs to meet the 
requirement of micro-nutrients and to control anaemia among women and children. Ministries of 
Women and Child Development and Health and Family Welfare have jointly released the protocol for 
Community Management of Malnutrition (CMAM) to prevent and treat severely acute malnutrition in 
children and for reducing associated morbidity and mortality. The Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare is implementing Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child, Adolescent Health and Nutrition 
(RMNCAH+N) strategy in a life cycle approach under National Health Mission (NHM), which includes 
interventions to address malnutrition and anemia across all States/UTs in the country. One of the 
interventions is Anaemia Mukt Bharat. Anaemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) a flagship programme of 
Government of India under Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoH&FW), launched in 2018, 
aims to reduce the prevalence of anemia through 6x6x6 strategy implemented among the six target 
beneficiaries-children 6-59 months, children 5-9 years, adolescents 10-19 years, women of reproductive 
age group, pregnant women and lactating mothers.

Reply 
As malnutrition requires a multi-sectoral approach involving dimensions of food, health, water, 
sanitation and education, it is crucial to effectively address the issue of malnutrition in a convergent 
manner. It is being addressed under Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0 by establishing cross 
cutting convergence amongst 18 Ministries/Departments. Under this mission, Supplementary Nutrition 
is provided to Children (6 months to 6 years), Pregnant Women, Lactating Mothers and Adolescent 
Girls to beat the intergenerational cycle of malnutrition by adopting a life cycle approach. 
Supplementary nutrition is provided in accordance with the nutrition norms contained in Schedule-II of 
the National Food Security Act. These norms have been revised in January 2023. The old norms were 
largely calorie-specific; however, the revised norms are more comprehensive and balanced in terms of 
both quantity and quality of supplementary nutrition based on the principles of diet diversity that 
provides for quality protein, healthy fats and micronutrients. 
Fortified rice is being supplied to AWCs to meet the requirement of micro-nutrients and to 
control Anaemia among women and children. Greater emphasis is being laid on the use of millets at 
least once a week for preparation of Hot Cooked Meal and Take Home Ration at Anganwadi centers. 
 Ministry of WCD has signed an MoU with M/o Ayush for use of evidence-based Ayurveda 
interventions to prevent anemia and improve the nutritional status among Adolescent girls (14-18 years) 
in Mission Utkarsh Districts. The intervention is planned to be rolled out in the Districts of Dhubri 
(Assam), Bastar (Chhattisgarh), Paschimi Singhbhum (Jharkhand), Gadchiroli (Maharashtra), and 
Dhoulpur (Rajasthan) 
Anaemia and its prevalence amongst adolescent girls falls under the purview of Ministry of 
Health and Family Welfare. However, the Ministry of Women and Child Development, supports the 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare through convergence at various levels and make sure that the 
nutrition being provided to the beneficiaries helps in reducing it.

Reply 
Mission Poshan 2.0 is a Centrally Sponsored mission, where the responsibility for implementation of 
various activities lies with the States and UTs. This mission is a universal self-selecting scheme where 
there are no entry barriers for any beneficiary to register and receive services. It is being implemented 
across the country with the beneficiaries including children between 0-6 years, pregnant women, 
lactating women and adolescent girls. 

18 
 
The data being collected through the Poshan Tracker application is collected for all categories 
including SCs, STs and others with no barriers whatsoever is also available on Poshan Tracker. The 
Anganwadi Centers across the country are divided into Urban, Rural, Tribal and Non-tribal centers. 
Through the data collected on Poshan Tracker application, malnutrition hotspots are monitored using 
the heat maps created on the application for future strategies to improve upon the prevalence of 
malnutrition. This data is collected based on the geographical location of the Anganwadi center. This 
helps take data driven decisions at local or district level based on the availability of the resources 
locally. 
Under Mission Poshan 2.0 a new strategy has been made for reduction in malnutrition and for 
improved health, wellness and immunity through activities like community engagement, outreach, 
behavioral change, and advocacy. It focuses on Maternal Nutrition, Infant and Young Child Feeding 
Norms, treatment of Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM)/ Moderate Acute Malnutrition (MAM) and 
wellness through AYUSH practices to reduce prevalence of wasting, stunting, Anaemia and being 
underweight. 
  The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare takes the focused approach towards incidents of 
Anaemia. Additionally, the Anaemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) programme being implemented by Ministry 
of Health & Family Welfare with a 6x6x6 strategy to reduce anemia across various age groups, 
including children and pregnant women. Since, dealing with the prevalence of anaemia requires a multi-
sectoral approach a convergence the Ministry of Women and Child Development and its departments 
supports the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare through convergence at various levels to achieve 
the vision of AMB.  
Existing data from sources like the National Family Health Survey (NFHS) consistently reveal 
significant disparities in health and nutritional outcomes across different social groups and geographical 
regions. Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST), along with populations in certain 
underdeveloped districts, disproportionately bear the burden of malnutrition and anemia among children 
and pregnant women.

Recommendation 
The Committee observed that there are wide fluctuations in POSHAN Tracker data, and that the data 
doesn’t correspond easily with the National Family Health Survey data –  
 i.   The Committee flagged that the NFHS data showed higher rates of malnutrition among children 
than POSHAN Tracker. It was noted that this may be partly due to the fact that NFHS is static and a 
few years whereas POSHAN Tracker is a dynamic survey updated regularly.  
ii. The Committee recommends that the Ministry leverage the expertise of NIPCCD/SPNIWCD and 
other experts to set up a data monitoring team for POSHAN Tracker. This team can identify gaps in

(Para 3.4.60 ibid) 
Reply 
The rollout of the Poshan Tracker by the Government of India represents the largest mobile phone 
nutrition monitoring system in the history of global health. Within three years of the inception of the 
Poshan Tracker, there has been a universal uptake with nearly 13 lakh Anganwadi workers downloaded 
the app across all States/UTs and are using it every day for monitoring Anganwadi services. The 
beneficiary base is approximately 10 crore per month – details of more than 10.08 crore beneficiaries 
(Pregnant women, Lactating mother, children (0–6years) and adolescent girls) are being captured on the 
platform. Due to the large base of beneficiaries and the constant change in the collected data and 
fluctuation may appear in real-time, though the reliability of the data being entered at source is void of 
any changes made otherwise. 
(i) With “Poshan Tracker”, real time data on malnutrition indicators is available every month. As 
compared to NFHS (sample size of approx 6.1 lakh households), Poshan Tracker consistently measures 
approx. 7-8 crore children each month revealing the real time nutritional status of beneficiaries. 
(ii) National e-Governance Division (NeGD) under MeitY provides user support for login, data 
entry, and other technical issues. The Supportive Supervision module, developed by NeGD, is designed 
to facilitate timely correction of incorrect data entered by Anganwadi Workers (AWWs). It enables 
supervisors to identify, validate, and rectify data errors at the source, ensuring improved data accuracy 
and accountability. In addition, Central Programme Management Unit (CPMU), at Central Ministry, 
assists in identifying data gaps, verifying entries, and analyzing implementation trends. The checks and 
balances placed by NeGD help assure the credibility of data. Any data, put into the Poshan tracker 
application cannot be changed without the intervention of the supervisor. To address the monitoring of 
data an MoU with IIT Bombay has been signed under Centre for Technology Alternatives for Rural 
Areas (CTARA). Based on the observations of the CPMU and CTARA teams, States/UTs are informed 
of any deviations or irregular entries found during meetings and APIP. The officers of the Ministry 
conduct regular visits to AWCs to make sure adherence to parameters. Trainings at regular intervals are 
provided to all AWWs through curriculum prepared by NIPCCD/SPNIWCD under the Poshan Bhi 

21 
 
Padhai Bhi program to ensure correctness of data being entered on the Poshan Tracker application. To 
support Anganwadi Workers (AWWs) in effective use of the Poshan Tracker application NeGD has 
stationed its coordinators in each State and the Ministry has placed its block coordinators. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee observes that universal ECCE, as envisioned in the National Education Policy (NEP), is 
critical to securing lifelong thinking and reasoning capabilities for all of India’s children. In its Report 
363 for School Education and Literacy Department, the Committee emphasized that ECCE includes 
early childhood care and education – and since care is an integral part of what must be available to 
children, Anganwadi workers are integral to the achievement of universal ECCE. The Committee also 
noted the challenges in bringing geographic and operational convergence between the Anganwadis and 
Bal Vatikas.    
(Para 3.4.61 ibid) 
Reply 
The Ministry of Women and Child Development (MWCD) concurs with the Committee’s observation 
that universal Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) is foundational for lifelong learning and 
development. MWCD acknowledges the dual components of care and education within ECCE, as 
articulated in the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, and recognizes Anganwadi Workers (AWWs) 
as central pillars for delivering this integrated package to children under 6 years. 
 Under Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0, MWCD has initiated key reforms to 
strengthen ECCE delivery through Anganwadi Centres (AWCs), including rollout of the “Poshan Bhi 
Padhai Bhi” initiative in May 2023, focusing on capacity building of Anganwadi Workers through a 3-
day training workshop, equipping them with skills and resources to transform Anganwadis into high-
quality learning centers with improved infrastructure and play-based learning tools; development of 
standardized national ECCE curriculum MWCD has developed two national curriculum frameworks:

The Committee notes that regardless of which department runs the ECCE program, children need to be

i. Samagra Shiksha Abhiyan’s financial norms provide Rs 500 per child per annum for Teaching 
Learning Material (TLM) for pre-primary classes, whereas the SA&P 2.0 guidelines provide only Rs 
1,000 per Anganwadi per annum for TLM, which is a lot lesser. To bridge this gap between pre-primary 
classes and Anganwadis, additional funds should be provided to increase availability of TLMs in

The point-wise reply is as follows: 
Under the Poshan Bhi Padhai Bhi(PBPB) initiative, the Ministry increased the budget allocation for

This increase ensures the availability of adequate Teaching-Learning Materials (TLM), which include

PBPB Programme was launched with an objective to improve the quality of education in the 
Anganwadi centres along with the focus on nutrition. This national initiative aims to provide all 13.9 
lakh Anganwadi Workers (AWWs) with a 5 day in person training - 3 days in Round 1 (2023-25) and 2

The Committee has discussed that the prevalence of child marriage is the highest in rural areas, and is 
more prevalent among communities belonging to the Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, Other 

25 
 
Backward Classes, and/or religious minorities. The issue of child marriage is rooted in the socio-
economic deprivation of the families and individuals in question, and any policy action taken on child 
marriage must be cognizant of the same. In its discussion on child marriage during its study visit in

                  (Para 3.5.13 ibid) 
Reply 
It is respectfully submitted that the issue of prevalence of child marriage is not uniform across States / 
UTs. As per NFHS V some of the States have higher burden of child marriages as compared to others. 
To address this, the Ministry has launched the “Bal Vivah Mukt Bharat” (BVMB) campaign which is 
focused on spreading awareness for the prevention of child marriages, greater involvement of parents, 
communities, CSOs for the cause, strengthening the role of Child marriage Prohibition Officers 
(CMPO) in the prevention of child marriages. Further, focus is also on skill development and capacity 
building of girls and identifying and assisting the adolescent girls who are drop outs or who have 
abruptly stopped coming to school to ensure their education. Early reporting can lead to timely action 
and significantly prevent the solemnization of child marriages. Therefore, focus is also on encouraging 
citizens to report the cases of child marriages through enhanced awareness and sensitization 
programmes, so that such incidents may be prevented.  
The Ministry also launched a ‘Bal Vivah Mukt Bharat’ portal, a digital platform designed to facilitate 
the effective reporting of such incidents. The portal serves as a publicly accessible, centralized 
repository of information on CMPOs across the country, providing an efficient reporting mechanism for 
child marriage cases. Moreover, the portal not only facilitates preventive actions but also provides the 
facility to link a girl child with various government schemes and policies aimed at encouraging girl 
education and preventing child marriage, and maintains data on these efforts. It also features the 
capability to maintain data/records on awareness programs and training sessions conducted by CMPOs. 
Till date, the campaign has already seen active participation of over 15 lakh citizens. Further, the detail 
of more than 36,000 CMPOs across the country is available in public domain on portal. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee notes that the state is responsible for the provision of basic socio-economic rights to all 
children from the moment of birth to the age of 18. In its discussions, the Committee invariably focus on 
the need for convergence in Government action to protect children, since there is currently a 
multiplicity of rights and policies of varying degrees of enforcement, across various agencies, and 
without a coherent vision that centers child and adolescent welfare and agency. For instance, the 
Committee notes that while the NEP calls for universal secondary school education, the Child Labour 
Act allows children of 15 to 18 years to discontinue education and enter the workforce. Meanwhile, the 
NEP does not engage with ‘child labour’ or ‘child marriage’ as factors impeding a child’s education. 
The issue of convergence between Bal Vatikas and Anganwadis is another instance of the same. 
Therefore, as the nodal Ministry for children, the WCD must work with the Ministry of Home Affairs, 
Finance, Education, and Health to craft a comprehensive National Framework for Children to provide 
an integrated view of the rights of children and adolescents, the responsibilities of the state to them, and 
the pathways to ensuring that these efforts are coordinated across agencies and across levels of 
Government.  Some key provisions of such a framework may include 
 Provision for a nationwide creche program  
 Uniform guidelines for children’s right to food, across Bal Vatikas and Anganwadis  
 Operational convergence in ECCE  
 Inclusion of modules on child trafficking, child sexual abuse, domestic violence, and child 
marriage in school curriculum  
 Reconciliation of child labour laws and secondary school education 
          (Para 3.5.14  ibid) 
 
Reply 
The Ministry of women and Child Development has introduced Palna Scheme under the Samarthya 
Vertical of Umbrella Mission Shakti for all States and UTs w.e.f. 01 April 2022, to provide day care 
facilities and protection to children.  

26 
 
   Lack of proper day-care services is, often, a deterrent for women to go out and work. Hence, 
there is an urgent need for improved quality and reach of day care services/crèches for working women 
amongst all socio-economic groups both in the organized and unorganized sectors. To address these 
difficulties faced by the working mothers in giving due child care and protection to their children, day-
care crèche facilities are being provided through Palna Scheme. This will also enable more mothers, 
who will be free from unpaid child-care responsibilities, to take up gainful employment. 
          Anganwadi centres are the world's largest childcare institutions dedicated to providing essential 
care and support to children ensuring delivery of care facilities till the last mile. In a first of its kind 
approach, Ministry has extended the services of childcare through Anganwadi cum Crèche (AWCC). 
This will ensure whole day childcare support ensuring their well-being in a safe and secure 
environment. Anganwadi cum Crèche initiative aims to increase ‘women work force participation’ in 
the economy. The objective of Palna Scheme is to provide quality crèche facility in safe and secure 
environment for children (from ages 6 months – 6 years), nutritional support, health and cognitive 
development of children, growth monitoring & immunization. Crèche facilities under Palna are 
provided to all mothers, irrespective of their employment status.  
During the 15th Finance Cycle i.e. up to FY 2025-26, a total of 17,000 Anganwadi-cum-
Creches (AWCCs) have been envisioned for establishment under the Palna Scheme. Proposals for 
establishment of AWCCs are received from the respective State Governments/UT Administrations who 
also contribute their corresponding share for the implementation of the Scheme. Till date, a total of 
14,599 AWCCs have been approved by the Ministry as per proposals received from various States/UTs 
and out of which, 2605 (As on 10.10.2025) have been made operational by States/UTs.

co-branded manner with the corresponding state schemes). Accordingly, the funds release and 

29 
 
utilization should now improve significantly. Also, the pending applications from the old software have 
now been migrated into the new software through a separate module.  
As a result, the process of payment to beneficiaries have been expedited which is evident from the fact 
that actual expenditure has increased from Rs. 569.11 crores (as on 31.01.2025) to Rs. 1448.01 Crores 
(as on 31.03.2025). 
 One of the major reasons, as to why funds are not released to the States/ UTs in a timely manner under 
SNA module is that mandatory compliances are required from the States regarding requirement of 
deposit of Central share of Interest accrued in the bank account and Deficit in the transfer of funds from 
State Treasury to SNA bank accounts of the respective schemes. 
 However, the suggestion of the Committee has been noted for compliance. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee observes that under PMMVY, 4.29 crores beneficiaries have been enrolled, however, 
3.79 crores have been benefitted, so far. The Committee, therefore, recommends that steps should be 
taken to cover and extend the benefits to all the enrolled beneficiaries under the scheme in mission 
mode.                 (Para 3.6.23 ibid) 
 
Reply 
As per the information available on the PMMVY Portal (as on 17.06.2025), a total of 4.45 crore 
beneficiaries have been enrolled and a total of 4.03 crore beneficiaries have been benefitted under the 
PMMVY Scheme so far. Some of the beneficiaries during scrutiny are also found ineligible and 
therefore rejected. As on 17.06.2025, around 0.15 Crore applications have been rejected. Further, the 
transition to new software which is Paper-less and Aadhaar authentication and NPCI seeding enabled, 
led to slow implementation by the States/ UTs. The transition to new software is now complete (except 
in cases of Tamil Nadu and Odisha, where the scheme is being implemented in co-branded manner with 
the corresponding state schemes). Accordingly, the funds release and utilization should now improve 
significantly. Also, the pending applications from the old software have now been migrated into the 
new software through a separate module. 
 As a result, the process of payment to beneficiaries have been expedited which is evident from the fact 
that percentage of beneficiaries paid to total enrolled has increased from 88.2% (as on 31.01.2025) to 
90.6% (as on 17.06.2025). 
  Additionally, following facilitative steps have been taken towards payment of benefits to all the 
enrolled beneficiaries: 
a. Search and Track Status for all enrolled beneficiaries to check the approval and payment status 
of their applications. 
b. Grievance Lodging and status module for all citizens to lodge any PMMVY related grievance. 
The Module directly sends the grievance to the implementing authorities thus saving time and leads to 
swifter resolution. 
c. PMMVY toll-free and multi lingual helpline (14408) is available for PMMVY related enquiries 
and grievances. 
d. For transparency purposes, the Applicants/beneficiaries receive SMS in one of the 10 languages 
at different stages such as registration of application, rejection of registration, payment etc. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee appreciates the objectives of the scheme which aims at payment of maternity benefits of 
₹5,000/- in beneficiary’s bank/post office account linked to her Aadhaar Number in Direct Benefit 
Transfer (DBT) mode in three instalments. However, the Committee notes that wide publicity of the 
scheme is required and recommends the Ministry to take necessary steps to publicize the benefits of the 
schemes through print, electronic and digital media, so that, none of the eligible beneficiaries are left 
out.           (Para 3.6.24)  
 
Reply 
The Ministry conducts various awareness programs including those on Maternity Benefits through 
SANKALP-Hub for Empowerment of Women (HEW) scheme for all States/UTs. It includes various 
Information, Education and Communication (IEC) and Behavior Change Communication (BCC) 
activities such as Prabhat Pheri, Nukkad Natak, Newspaper Advertisements, Airing Radio Jingles, 

30 
 
Selfie Campaign, Door to Door Campaign, Community Programmes which are conducted at field 
functionary levels. Further, the Ministry is also running special campaign for registration of eligible 
beneficiaries in all the States and UTs under PMMVY on a periodic basis. 
  During the recent Programme Approval Board (PAB) Meetings of Mission Shakti for the Financial 
Year 2025-26, the States/UTs were directed to prepare the State Action Plan and District Action Plans 
for creating awareness and publicity on the schemes of the Mission Shakti. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee was informed that the Ministry did not conduct any study of how Aadhar Based 
Payment Systems [ABPS] and online registration may have impacted the ability of eligible beneficiaries 
to access PMMVY. However, the Ministry noted that the “transition to new software which is paper-
less and Aadhaar authentication and NPCI seeding enabled, led to slow implementation [of PMMVY] 
by the States/UTs.” Thus, ABPS may have had an impact on the ability of eligible beneficiaries to 
benefit from PMMVY. The Committee recommends that all technological tools and interventions used 
by the Ministry must be evaluated by the Ministry, in-house or through a third party, to ensure that the 
technology integrates smoothly with the scheme’s programmes. 
          (Para 3.6.25 ibid) 
Reply 
Before the deployment of the technological tools and interventions, all required checks such as User 
Acceptance Testing (UAT) and security audit are conducted by the NIC. After the tools are deployed, 
adequate training and handholding of the field functionaries and all the other stakeholders is also 
conducted.  
  The field functionaries and other stakeholders are now well-versed with the Aadhaar Based 
Payment System which is evident from the expedited pace of payments to the beneficiaries. However, 
the suggestion of the Committee has been noted. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee notes that the PMMVY is currently only available to all woman aged 18-55 years for 
their first child, and to women who have a second child only if the child is a girl. The Committee was 
informed that the PMMVY Rules, 2022 were notified under sub-section 3 of section 39 of the National 
Food Security Act, 2013 on 22nd December, 2022. The NFSA says that “every pregnant woman and 
lactating mother shall be entitled to…maternity benefit of not less than rupees six thousand, in such 
instalments as may be prescribed by the Central Government.” The Act is therefore unequivocal that 
the maternity benefit is due to every pregnant woman and not only to those pregnant with their first 
child and/or second girl child. The Committee recommends that the Department extend the benefits 
provided under PMMVY to all eligible pregnant and lactating women, not just those with their first 
child and/or a second a girl child, particularly of women from BPL families.   
                (Para 3.6.26  ibid) 
 
The Committee notes the NFSA stipulates that the maternity benefit due to pregnant and women is Rs. 
6,000 whereas the amount due under PMMVY is only Rs 5,000. The Committee was informed by the 
Department that eligible women may be receiving another Rs 1,000 through the JSY after institutional 
delivery, which would bring the composite amount to Rs. 6,000. The Committee notes that the NFSA 
was brought with the intention to ensure food security for pregnant and lactating women, and that it 
must not be linked to the JSY which is focused on institutionalization of childbirth. Hence, the PMMVY 
amount must be increased to Rs. 6,000. Further, periodic increase in the PMMVY amount must be 
undertaken, indexed to food price inflation.       
                 (Para 3.6.27 ibid) 
Reply 
The National Food Security Act, 2013 (NFSA) provides that subject to such schemes as may be framed 
by the Central Government, every Pregnant Women & Lactating Mother (PW&LM), except those who 
are in regular employment with the Central Government or State Government or Public Sector 
Undertaking or those who are in receipt of similar benefits under any law for the time being in force, 
shall be entitled to maternity benefit of not less than rupees six thousand, in such instalments as may be 
prescribed by the Central Government. 

31 
 
The Ministry of Women and Child Development has notified Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana 
Yojana Rules, 2022 (PMMVY Rules) under sub-section 3 of Section 39 of NFSA on 22nd December, 
2022. The PMMVY Rules were also laid on the Table of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha on 3rd February, 
2023 and 8th February, 2023 respectively. 
Under Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana (PMMVY), maternal benefit of ₹5,000/- is 
provided to eligible Pregnant Women & lactating Mothers (PW&LM) during the period of pregnancy 
and lactation. The eligible beneficiary also receives the remaining cash incentive as per approved norms 
towards maternity benefit under Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) after institutional delivery so that on an 
average, a woman gets ₹6,000/-. 
Normally, the first pregnancy of a woman exposes her to new kinds of challenges and stress 
factors. Hence, the scheme provides support to the mother for safe delivery and immunization of her 
first child. Under Mission Shakti, w.e.f. 01.04.2022, to promote positive behavioural change towards 
girl child, the maternity benefits of ₹6000 is also provided to beneficiaries for second child subject to 
condition that the second child is a girl. 
Every pregnant women & lactating mother is entitled to meal, free of charge, during pregnancy 
and six months after child birth through the Anganwadi, so as to meet the nutritional standards specified 
in schedule of NFSA Act. These foodgrains are being allocated to the states through the Wheat Based 
Nutritional Programme (WBNP) wherein foodgrains (Wheat/Rice/Coarse grains (Millets)) are allocated 
to the States/UTs through the Department of Food & Public Distribution for use as Supplementary 
Nutrition at NFSA rates.However, the suggestion of the Committee has been noted for further 
consideration. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee was provided the data of the beneficiaries enrolled, beneficiaries paid, and total amount 
disbursed under this scheme for each year between 2019-20 and 2024-25 [Annexure-IV]. The 
Committee notes that the number of beneficiaries paid varies widely across the years. Since the pool of 
eligible beneficiaries (i.e., pregnant and lactating women aged 18-55 years) cannot vary to such a large 
degree, it follows that the Ministry and the implementing departments of the State Government are not 
able to consistently reach all the eligible beneficiaries’ year-on-year. Accordingly, the Committee 
recommends the Department look into the reasons for the same and proposes that suitable 
modifications to the scheme must be conducted accordingly.     
                 (Para 3.6.28  ibid) 
Reply 
The Scheme is implemented through a paperless app and portal and enrollment is at the door step level 
through Anganwadi Workers and ASHA. The ease of enrolment and its reach till the village level is 
ensured in order to make it accessible to all willing and eligible beneficiaries.  
Further, the transition to new software which is Paper-less and Aadhaar authentication and NPCI 
seeding enabled, led to slow implementation by the States/ UTs leading to fall in payment numbers in 
2023-24. However, the same has been completed and in the financial year 2024-25 80.48 lakhs 
beneficiaries were paid. 
 
Further, there exists a well- structured mechanism for effective implementation of the 
Scheme. Regular monitoring of the pendency clearances is being done through Video Conferences, 
wherein pendency clearance at different stages of application process is monitored. The Ministry has 
also introduced ‘Track Application Status’ module and ‘Integrated Grievance Redressal’ module on the 
PFMS portal, which would lead to increased accountability and expedited payments.

SANKLAP-HEW 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee notes that Rs. 210.00 crores were allocated at BE 2023-24 which was reduced to Rs. 
150.00 crores at RE stage under SANKALP: HEW while the Actual utilization is Rs 102.52 crores 
which is 48.81 % of BE and 68.34% of RE 2023-24, respectively. Similarly, Rs. 210.00 crores were 
again allocated at BE 2024-25 which was reduced to Rs. 100.00 crores at RE stage while the Actual 
utilization is Rs 37.13 crores as on 31st January, 2025 which is 17.68 % of BE 2024-25 and 37.13% of 
RE  2024-25. The Committee expresses its concerns over reduction of allocation at RE stage and 
underutilization of RE allocation under SANKALP: HEW scheme which aims to facilitate intersectoral 
convergence by acting as a single-window coordination platform, integrating resources and services 
from various ministries and departments to address women's empowerment needs comprehensively. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry to adhere to Rule 56(3) of GFR of Ministry of Finance 
and streamline its expenditure during 2025-26 to optimize the utilization of funds allocated to it under 
the scheme.           
(Para 3.6.32 ibid) 
Reply 
Reduction of allocation under the Scheme is due to slow pace of its operationalisation by the States/ 
UTs, which has impacted fund utilisation.  
The recruitment of functionaries to act as Project Management Units (PMUs) at the State and 
District level HEWs has been delayed, further constraining the operational capacity of HEWs. Non-
compliance by States and Union Territories with the Single Nodal Agency (SNA) norms earlier 
required for the release of funds under the Scheme has contributed to the overall utilisation of fund. 
Further, on introduction of SNA SPARSH model for release of funds, the implementation of SNA 
SPARSH by the States has also contributed to release of funds and its utilisation. However, the 
suggestion of the Committee has been noted for compliance. 
 
PALNA 
Recommendation 
The Committee notes that of the 17,000 AWCCs targeted under the 15th Finance Commission, only 
11,395 were approved. Of those, only 1,350 (less than 10% of the target) are currently operational – 
with many districts and states having zero functioning AWCCs. The Ministry in its response to the oral 
questions of the MPs has also noted that the operationalisation of crèches by States/UTs has been going 
at a slow pace. The Ministry must investigate the reasons for the same and take action to expedite the 
same if possible. Moreover, the Committee also recommends the Ministry to seek more funds from 
Ministry of Finance under the scheme in view of its recommendation above for universal childcare.
     
(Para 3.6.39 ibid) 
Reply 
Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) has allowed to set up 17,000 Anganwadi cum Crèches 
(AWCCs) under Palna during 15th Finance Commission Cycle.  As on 24.10.2025, Ministry has 
approved 14,599 AWCCs for operationalisation and out of which 2605 AWCCs have been made 
operational by States/UTs. Funds are being released to States/UT with Legislature under SNA Sparsh 
guidelines while funds are being released to UTs as per SNA guidelines issued by Ministry of Finance 
and provision under GFR Rule 2017. 
SNA Sparsh Model have been introduced by Ministry of Finance for release of funds as ‘Just-
in-time’ and the same is being implemented for Palna Scheme. All States/UTs with Legislature to be 
covered under SNA Sparsh Model for Palna Scheme in phase manner. Till 24.10.2025, 27 States/UTs 
with Legislature have been onboarded on SNA Sparsh platform which will facilitate the States to 

33 
 
submit their demand as and when required. Centre will release central share funds as ‘just-in-time’ basis 
under SNA Sparsh guidelines.     
Palna scheme has been allocated Rs. 125 Cr (central share) under BE for Financial Year 2025-
2026 for operationalization/running the crèches. Ministry will seek more funds on the basis of 
utilization made by the States/UT. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee also observes that Ministry should take efforts to identify children with challenges like 
autism and related issues and with low learning abilities in their early childhood and recommends the 
Ministry to evolve a system in place that could identify these children and facilitate them to overcome 
these challenges through Palna scheme.   
(Para 3.6.40 ibid) 
Reply 
Anganwadi cum Creches (AWCCs) under Palna scheme is being implemented with intra scheme 
convergence with Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0 scheme of the Ministry. There is a component 
called Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) under both the scheme i.e. (Palna of Mission 
Shakti and Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0 scheme). The children (06 months – 06 years) 
including PwDs of mothers irrespective of their employment status are entitled to crèche facilities under 
Palna.  
 The Ministry has launched specific protocols under Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0 
aimed at identifying and supporting children with developmental challenges. The Anganwadi Protocol 
for Management of Malnutrition at the Community Level (CMAM Protocol) was launched on 10th 
October 2023, providing detailed steps for identification and management of malnourished children at 
the Anganwadi level, including decision-making for referral, nutritional management, and follow-up 
care. 
Further, the Anganwadi Protocol for Divyang Children was launched on 28th November 2023 
to enable Anganwadi Workers to screen and refer children with disabilities for detailed assessment by 
PHC/RBSK teams. Under the Poshan Bhi Padhai Bhi programme of the Ministry, field functionaries of 
Anganwadi Services—including DPOs, CDPOs, Supervisors, and Anganwadi Workers—are being 
trained in the screening, referral, and inclusion of Divyang children as per the protocol. So far, over 
40,000 state-level master trainers and 5.5 lakh AWWs have been trained. Additionally, a checklist has 
been developed as part of the Home Visit Module for Anganwadi Workers to help identify children 
with potential developmental delays so that they may then be referred for further assessment. Presently, 
data is captured on Poshan Tracker for children with Movement, Mental, Visual, Hearing and Speaking 
disabilities.
