Recommendation 
The Committee notes that that in the construction mode of the Sakhi Niwas scheme, each hostel had an 
average capacity of 100 beds. However, in the present rental mode, each hostel has an average 
capacity of 50 beds. The Committee observes that to compensate for the fall in the beds per hostel, the 
number of hostels must be increased considerably. Moreover, the Committee observes that a number of 
states lack functional Sakhi Niwas which aims to promote availability of safe and conveniently located 
accommodation for working women and for those women who are pursuing higher education/training, 
with Day care facility for children in urban, semi urban, and even rural areas where employment 
opportunity for women exist. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should ensure 
that each State have a reasonable number of Sakhi Niwas.     
          (Para 3.6.44 ibid) 
 
Reply 
Sakhi Niwas Scheme (Working Women Hostel) under the overarching Mission Shakti, is a demand 
driven Centrally Sponsored Scheme where States and UTs forward proposals on the basis of their local 
need and requirement which are discussed with States and UTs and approved by Programme Approval 
Board (PAB) under Mission Shakti. Under the Scheme, financial assistance is provided for running of 
Sakhi Niwas in rented premises and the component of new construction has been discontinued.   
Further, all States and UTs have also been encouraged to assess the demands of setting up new Sakhi 
Niwas from time to time and submit more proposals to the Ministry.   
During Financial Year 2024-25, 1st installment of Rs.2.65 crore has been released to the States 
and UTs for setting up of 82 new Sakhi Niwas on rental mode.    
 The funds to the States and UTs under Sakhi Niwas Scheme released based upon the receipt of 
Statement of Expenditure (SoE) and Utilization Certificate (UC).  In order to avoid the delay in the 
release of funds to the States and UTs, this Ministry has developed a dedicated portal for uploading of 
SoE and UC by the States and UTs. It is submitted that as on 31.03.2025, actual release of Rs.8.14 crore 
has been made against RE of Rs.8.13 crore which is 100.12% during Financial Year 2024-25. 
Further, as per Department of Expenditure (DoE), Ministry of Finance guidelines, funds are 
now released through SNA SPARSH instead of SNA.  The SNA SPARSH was notified by DoE on 13th 
July, 2023 to bring in more efficiency in cash management and to achieve the goal of “Just in time” 
funds flow from both Centre and State Consolidated funds through an integrated network of State 
IFMIS, e-kuber of RBI and PFMS.  The SPARSH system has been designed in a way that these issues 
will no longer exist, and flow of funds will happen in a smoother manner. 
 Additional steps for setting up Sakhi Niwas (Working Women Hostel) 
          The Government of India has also provided financial assistance to Central Universities and 
States/ UTs for construction of WWH for accommodating working women and female students who are 
pursuing higher education/ training away from their native place under Nirbhaya Fund, where the 
Universities/ State Government provide land and take the responsibility to manage and operate the 
Hostels.  Under Nirbhaya Fund, 21 hostels have been appraised.   Under Nirbhaya Fund, Rs.12.60 crore 
to Nagaland, Rs.3.77 crore to Punjab and Rs.10.76 crore to Tamil Nadu and Rs.11.49 crore to 
Uttarakhand has been released by MWCD. 
Ministry of Finance (MoF), Department of Expenditure (DoE) vide O.M. No.44(1)/PF-S/2024-
25 (CAPEX) dated 09.08.2024 has also allocated Rs.5,000/- crores to 28 States under Part (X) 
(Construction of Working Women Hostels) of Special Assistance to States for Capital Investment 

36 
 
(SASCI) Scheme for construction of working women hostel.  Under SASCI Scheme, DoE has approved 
construction of 254 working women hostel with total capacity of 53336 beds in 28 States at a total 
approved cost of Rs.4,826.31 crore and out of this 1st installment of Rs.3,148.28 crore has been 
released to the States during 2024-25. Based on the demands assessment, the States will construct 
hostels in the vicinity of industrial area, economic centres and some of the States will also construct 
hostels within the industrial areas, adjacent to premier industries for accommodation for working 
women. 
 
SHAKTI SADAN 
Recommendation 
The Committee takes note of Shakti Sadan in various States and observes that many States either do not 
have any Shakti Sadan or the number of functional Shakti Sadans is very less in comparison to their 
population. The scheme aims at Integrated Relief and Rehabilitation Home for women in distressful 
situations including trafficked women and victims of domestic violence. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends the Ministry to encourage the States for provision of adequate Shakti Sadans in their 
respective States, so that, women in distress could be rescued and rehabilitated. 
          (Para 3.6.49 ibid) 
 
The Committee notes that the number of beneficiaries in the Shakti Sadan scheme have fallen from 
32,113 to 24,753 between 2022-23 and 2023-24. The Committee was also informed that 11 Shakti 
Sadans functional in the state of Uttar Pradesh were shut down by the State Government. The 
Committee also noted that various States either do not have any Shakti Sadans or that the number of 
functional Shakti Sadans in these states is not adequate in comparison to their population. The scheme 
aims at Integrated Relief and Rehabilitation Home for women in distressful situations including 
trafficked women and victims of domestic violence. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry 
to encourage the States for provision of adequate Shakti Sadans in their respective States, so that; 
women in distress could be rescued and rehabilitated.      
             (Para 3.6.50 ibid) 
 
Reply 
Shakti Sadan is a demand driven Centrally Sponsored Scheme where States/UTs forward proposals on 
the basis of their local need and requirement which are discussed with States and UTs and approved by 
Programme Approval Board (PAB) under Mission Shakti. Under the Scheme, financial assistance is 
provided for running of Shakti Sadan in rented premises.  Further, all States and UTs have been 
encouraged to assess the demands of setting up new Shakti Sadans from time to time and submit more 
proposals to the Ministry.  In this regard, this Ministry has also issued a letter dated 16.05.2025 to all 
States and UTs for setting up new Shakti Sadan on rental mode under the capacity of State and UT as 
per Mission Shakti Guidelines. 
It is informed that during FY 2024-25, 1st instalment of Rs.9.71 Cr. has been released to the 
States and UTs for setting up of 78 New Shakti Sadans on rental mode which includes 10 in the State of 
Uttar Pradesh. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee observes that the condition of Shakti Sadans at many places is not up to the mark. These 
Shakti Sadans lack infrastructure facilities and the salaries provided to the employees deployed there 
are not being paid on regular basis. The Committee, therefore, recommends that infrastructure facilities 
be upgraded in these Shakti Sadans and Ministry should take efforts in coordination with the State 
Governments to ensure that regular salaries to employees deployed there is disbursed. The Committee 
also recommends the Ministry to start skill development programme in Shakti Sadans to train and equip 
these women with skills required for enhancing their employment opportunities and rehabilitation.
                 (Para 3.6.51 ibid) 
Reply 
The funds to the States and UTs under Shakti Sadan Scheme released based upon the receipt of 
Statement of Expenditure (SoE) and Utilization Certificate (UC).  In order to avoid the delay in the 
release of funds to the States and UTs, this Ministry has developed a dedicated portal for uploading of 
SoE and UC by the States and UTs.  Further, as per Department of Expenditure (DoE), Ministry of 

37 
 
Finance guidelines, funds are now released to the States and UTs through SNA SPARSH instead of 
SNA.  The SNA SPARSH was notified by DoE on 13th July, 2023 to bring in more efficiency in cash 
management and to achieve the goal of “Just in time” funds flow from both Centre and State 
Consolidated funds through an integrated network of State IFMIS, e-kuber of RBI and PFMS.  The 
SPARSH system has been designed in a way that these issues will no longer exist, and flow of funds 
will happen in a smoother manner.    On account of these measures, funds are released in lesser time 
helping States and UTs in further disbursing regular salaries to the employees deployed in the Shakti 
Sadan. 
As per Mission Shakti Guidelines, arrangement is to be made by the implementing organization 
for providing vocational training/ skill development classes to the women through the Vocational 
Training Institutes recognized by the Directorate General of Employment and Training under the 
Ministry of Labour and Employment/ Training Partners of National Skill Development Council 
(NSDC). Training and examination fee, if not provided under any other scheme/ programmes of the 
Central/ State Government, would be reimbursed on submission of the certificate issued by the 
vocational training institute on successful completion of training. For the purpose of monitoring of 
Shakti Sadans, this Ministry has developed a dedicated Mission Shakti Dashboard for capturing details 
like staff deployed, beneficiaries, location details (Latitude and Longitude), physical infrastructure, ICT 
infrastructure, activities conducted, facilities provided to beneficiaries, etc. 
 
Recommendation 
The Ministry has noted that it does collect geo-tagged data of its implementing offices and officials but 
that this is not done at a Ministry-wide level and to the level of granularity desired. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry develop a Samiksha Kendra, along the lines of the Rashtriya Vidya 
Samiksha Kendra built by the Department of School Education and Literacy. This Samiksha Kendra 
may include –   
i. A live, national-level database of all Govt employees and contractual workers working on 
women and child related issues - include AWWs, AWHs, CMPOs, CPOs, CWCs, JJBs, CDPO, DCPUs, 
SCPS, SARAs etc - right down to the habitation-level.  
ii.  Updated tracking of the trainings undertaken by each worker and official with 
NIPCCD/SPNIWCD or other organizations  
iii. A geo-tagged, navigable nationwide registry of facilities for the support of women and children 
– including Anganwadis, Shakti Sadans, VatsalyaSadan, Sakhi Niwas, One-Stop Centers, etc, as well as 
the staff attached to each   
iv.        Live monitoring of the financial transactions relating to each worker and facility to track the 
availability of funds with them, any delays in the receipt of the same, and the necessity for remedial 
action.              (Para 3.6.52 ibid) 
 
Reply 
(i).Mission Poshan 2.0 empowers the frontline functionaries i.e. Anganwadi workers and Lady

Recommendation 
The Committee takes note of the Projects of Ministry of Women and Child Development being 
funded/appraised under "other schemes funded from Nirbhaya Fund" as mentioned at Para 3.7.2 and 
recommends that the Ministry should take initiatives to construct working women hostels in capital 
cities of each States/UTs and at places of educational centres to facilitate working women in the 
country.         
(Para 3.7.3 ibid)

Recommendation 
The Committee notes that BE and RE 2024-25 under the head 'Other Schemes Funded from Nirbhaya 
Fund' is Rs. 30.00 crores. However, the Actual utilization as on 17.02.2025 is Nil. BE 2025-26 for the 
said head is again Rs. 30.00 crores. The Committee expresses its concerns regarding Nil utilization of 
fund allocated under the head 'Other Schemes Funded from Nirbhaya Fund' and recommends the 
Ministry to ensure optimum utilization of allocated funds during the FY 2025-26.   
                   (Para 3.7.7 ibid) 
Reply 
Since the projects under Nirbhaya Fund are demand driven, every year, the Ministry keeps

(iii)       Public Awareness and Accountability: Ministry should introduce a real-time online dashboard

The Committee was informed that under the Ministry's Research, Publication and Monitoring Scheme,

(Para 3.7.11 ibid)

NATIONAL INSTITUTION OF PUBLIC COOPERATION AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT 
(NIPCCD/SPNIWCD) 
Recommendation 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry to work with the Ministry of Law and Justice and 
NIPCCD/SPNIWCD to develop training modules for the judiciary to sensitize them to the issues of 
women and children. 
          (Para 3.7.12 ibid) 
Reply 
The recommendation of the Committee has been noted.  It is further respectfully submitted that on the 
SHe box portal, Ministry has uploaded the handbook on SH Act, training module and is also imparting 
training to the functionaries of States/ UTs through various means including through 
NIPCCD/SPNIWCD. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee observes that NIPCCD/SPNIWCD has been allocated Rs. 90.00 crores under BE 2025-
26. The Committee also notes that Rs. 88.87 crores were allocated under BE 2024-25. However, it was 
reduced to Rs. 79.50 crores and Actual utilization as on 17thFebruray, 2025 is Rs. 69.58 crores. The 
actual utilization during 2023-24 is Rs. 63.04 crores. The Committee, therefore, recommends the 
Ministry to ensure full utilization of allocated funds during FY 2025-26 and reduction of allocation at 
RE stage should be avoided for institutions like NIPCCD/SPNIWCD which is crucial for training in 
research of AWWs/AWHs and overall domain of women and child development. 
         (Para 4.1.3  ibid) 
Reply 
Although the RE 2024-25 was reduced to 79.50 Crore, additional grant of Rs. 4.00 Crore was sought 
from the Ministry. The actual expenditure for the year 2024-25 was Rs. 81.17 Crore. 
NIPCCD/SPNIWCD has been allocated Rs. 90.00 Crore under BE 2025-26. However, we will need 
more fund due to various additional initiatives like opening up Regional Centre at Ranchi, 
Jharkhand, Complete renovation of NIPCCD/SPNIWCD Hostel and part renovation of staff quarter and 
administrative block of NIPCCD/SPNIWCD Headquarters etc. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee takes note of the reasons provided for under utilization of funds and recommends the 
Ministry to ensure recruitment of staffs and faculty members on direct recruitment basis at the earliest. 
The Committee also recommends the Ministry to redress the inadequate infrastructures, dilapidated 
conditions of hostels and ongoing renovation of hostel, etc. at the earliest and ensure optimum 
utilization of allocated funds.     
(Para 4.1.5 ibid) 
Reply 
The process of recruitment of staffs and faculty members on direct recruitment basis is in progress. 
Structural Assessment of NIPCCD/SPNIWCD Headquarters was done by IIT Delhi. In its 
recommendations which structural retrofitting was suggested for addressing the issues of dilapidated 
conditions of buildings. Renovation process presently under process including Hostel and others. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee notes that out of total 287 sanctioned posts during 2024 which has been reduced from 
total sanctioned strength of 338 in 2023, 124 posts are lying vacant in NIPCCD/SPNIWCD which is 

43 
 
43.21% of the reduced total sanctioned strength. The Committee also notes that 9 posts under SC quota, 
11 posts under ST quota, 16 posts under OBC quota and 5 posts under EWS quota are lying vacant. 
Further, the Ministry has informed that only one Group ‘C’ staff (Staff Car Driver) was appointed on 
regular basis since 2019 till 31st December, 2024 which shows that regular recruitment has been 
stopped in NIPCCD/SPNIWCD. The Committee recommends the Ministry to start recruitment on 
regular/permanent basis against the vacancies including the reserved category vacancies of SC, ST, 
OBC, EWS etc. and ensure its time-bound completion in view of the crucial role assigned to 
NIPCCD/SPNIWCD in the domain of women and child. 
(Para 4.1.9 ibid) 
Reply 
The Institute is in process for filling up of all vacant posts on regular basis through direct recruitment 
basis and promotions basis, failing which on deputation basis as per the Recruitment Rules of the 
Institute. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee notes that 73 contractual appointments were made during 2019 out of total sanctioned 
strength of 338, 66 contractual appointments during 2020, 60 contractual appointments during 2021, 
86 contractual appointments during 2022, 84 contractual appointments during 2023 and 103 
contractual appointments were made during 2024 out of total sanctioned strength of 287 which is 
35.88% of the total sanctioned strength. The Committee expresses its concerns over increasing number 
of contractual appointments that undermines the Constitutional provision of reservation in Government 
jobs to SC, ST, OBC, EWS etc. and recommends that Ministry should stop contractual appointments 
and ensure appointments on regular/permanent basis in NIPCCD/SPNIWCD.   
                (Para 4.1.10 ibid) 
 
Reply 
The filling up of all vacant posts on regular basis as per the Recruitment Rules of the Institute is under 
process. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee observes that NIPCCD/SPNIWCD is critical for training professionals in child 
development and women’s welfare, yet its outreach remains limited, and its programmes lack real-
world applicability. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry of Women and Child 
Development/SPNIWCD as under:  
(i) Launch an Online Training Platform for Anganwadi Workers: NIPCCD/SPNIWCD should 
provide AI-driven personalized training modules accessible on mobile devices;  
(ii) Create Regional Centers of Excellence: Ministry should establish satellite NIPCCD/SPNIWCD 
centers to ensure nationwide training coverage; and  
(iii) Introduce a Training Certification System: Ministry/SPNIWCD should introduce mandatory 
training certification for all professionals working in child and women welfare services. 
          (Para 4.1.12 ibid) 
 
Reply 
i. Under Poshan Bhi Padhai Bhi (PBPB), five days in person training of AWWs is being 
undertaken in the States/UTs. YouTube Live Streaming Sessions for officials of Anganwadi Services 
Scheme including AWWs is being carried out by NIPCCD/SPNIWCD for sensitization with regard to 
ECCE: Aadharshila and Navchetana. Further, Online Training Programmes are being planned.  
ii.  NIPCCD/SPNIWCD at present is functioning through its Headquarters at New Delhi and its 
Five Regional Centres and a new Centre at Ranchi, Jharkhand (likely to start soon).  
The main vision of NIPCCD/SPNIWCD is to become National Centre of Excellence by enhancing the 
capacity of its Regional Centres as well as HQ to ensure nationwide training coverage.  
iii.  Ministry NIPCCD/SPNIWCD is in process of introducing training certification for 
programmes. Efforts have been initiated with the National Council of Vocational Education and 
Training (NCVET), the National Skills Regulator, with the Ministry of Skill Development and 
Entrepreneurship. 
 

44 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee notes that most states are served by a NIPCCD/SPNIWCD regional centre, but that 
Odisha, West Bengal, and Andaman and Nicobar Islands are served by the NPCCD Headquarters in 
Delhi. The Committee recommends that the Department investigate the feasibility of a regional centre 
to better support Ministry activities in these states. 
(Para 4.1.13 ibid) 
Reply 
NIPCCD/SPNIWCD with its Headquarters at New Delhi and anchored in its five Regional Centres 
namely Regional Centres at Guwahati, Bengaluru, Indore, Lucknow, Mohali and new centre at Ranchi 
(likely to start soon). Jurisdiction of States under headquarters and Regional Centres is being reworked 
keeping in view, the feasibility of logistics issues    for supporting the Ministry through various 
activities across the States. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee notes that there is no uniform policy for the provision of TA/DA for training of officials 
in NIPCCD/SPNIWCD. The hostel facilities at NIPCCD/SPNIWCD’s regional centers, such as the one 
in Bengaluru, may also need upgradation to facilitate the training of officials from outstation. Current 
norms for honorarium of resource persons contracted for NIPCCD/SPNIWCD trainings may also need 
to be raised to accommodate the labour costs of larger cities. The Committee also recommends that 
NIPCCD/SPNIWCD faculty be sent on exposure visits to the field for capacity building and better 
formulation of training programs. Funds must also be made available to them for course development 
and building of teaching-learning materials.        
(Para 4.1.15 ibid) 
Reply 
i. NIPCCD/SPNIWCD pays TA/DA to Government Officials attending training under Mission 
Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan as per 7th CPC and as per their entitlement. Participants from NGO 
are given AC-III tier Fare. 
ii. As NIPCCD/SPNIWCD is relying on 100% Grants-in-Aid, it is undertaking up-gradation of 
hostel facilities in a phase manner. Modernizations of hostel of Headquarters and Regional Centre 
Guwahati have been taken in 1st phase. 
iii. The Honorarium to outside Resource Persons will be reviewed to at par with other Training 
Institute. 
iv. NIPCCD/SPNIWCD have been deputing faculty to training and other exposure visit to other 
organizations within the county and abroad. Institute has deputed faculty members in four batches for 
training at NIMHANS.  However, no faculty has been deputed to other country after COVID 19. 
Further, NIPCCD/SPNIWCD also deputed its administrative staff and officers for training in related 
field to institute like ISTM, etc. 
v. Fund for the same is allocated as per budget allocated by the Ministry. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee notes that NIPCCD/SPNIWCD also has a research function which is of critical 
importance. The Committee recommends that the Ministry to work with NIPCCD/SPNIWCD to develop 
a national-level research plan to provide direction to its faculty members in conducting research 
projects.          
(Para 4.1.16 ibid) 
Reply 
NIPCCD/SPNIWCD in the FY 2025-26, is undertaking various National Level Research Studies 
monitored by NIPCCD/SPNIWCD Research Advisory Committee (RAC). 
 
NATIONAL COMMISSION FOR WOMEN (NCW) 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee observes that NCW has been entrusted with duties of providing constitutional and legal 
safeguards for women, to review the existing legislations and suggest amendments, wherever necessary, 
to look into the complaints and take suo-motu notice of the cases involving deprivation of the rights of 
women in order to provide support, legal or otherwise, to helpless women. The Committee, therefore, 

45 
 
recommends that Ministry should ensure following at the earliest to enhance the efficiency of the 
Commission: (i) Strengthening and popularising 24X7 Helpline developed by NCW; 
(ii)  Providing more focus to public awareness on women’s rights through seminars, workshops and 
consultations; 
(iii) Frequent meetings with State Women Commissions to ensure effective functioning in collaboration 
with NCW;   
(iv) Filling up of vacant posts in the Commission and State Women Commissions; and     
(v) Ministry should proactively take up with Ministry of External Affairs for Mutual Legal Assistant 
Treaty with the remaining countries for safeguarding the interest of women in respect of NRI 
marriages. 
                   (Para 4.2.8 ibid) 
Reply 
Recommendations of the committee have been noted.It may be mentioned that Women Commissions in 
the States/UTs are established by the statutes of the respective States/UTs. NCW has no jurisdiction 
over the Women Commissions in the States/UTs however, NCW will endeavour to work more closely 
with state Women Commissions. 
As regards filling up of vacant posts in NCW is concerned, action regarding framing of   
Recruitment Rules (RRs) for various posts has been initiated and further action will be undertaken as 
per the extant guidelines of Department of Personnel & Training (DoPT). 
Regarding recommendation No.(v), India has entered into Mutual Legal Assistant Treaty (MLAT) with 
42 countries which facilitates redressal of grievances of Indian Women distressed in NRI marriages or 
deserted by their NRI/OCI spouses. The directions of the Committee on the subject are noted. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee takes note of the contractual appointments and appointments on daily wages basis in 
NCW and observes that a number of persons are working on contractual and daily wages basis in the 
Commission for more than 20 years. The Committee, therefore, recommends that contractual 
appointments and appointments on daily wages should be stopped and the Ministry should consider to 
regularize those who are working there for more than 10 years on contractual and daily wages basis 
and all facilities associated with permanent appointees should be extended to them.   
(Para 4.2.13 ibid) 
 
Reply 
The Commission has not made any appointment on daily wages since 2002. However, the 
recommendation of the committee have been noted subject to extant rules and instructions of the 
Government. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee observes that NCW plays a pivotal role in advocating women’s rights, but it faces gaps 
in legal outreach, enforcement, and awareness campaigns. The Committee, therefore, recommends the 
Ministry/NCW as under:  
 
(i) Expand Legal Aid Networks: Ministry/NCW should establish dedicated legal aid cells in each 
district to assist women facing gender-based violence;  
(ii) Create a National Gender Justice Index: Ministry/NCW should develop a ranking system for 
states based on gender equity and women’s rights enforcement;  
(iii)Strengthen Corporate Engagement: Ministry/NCW should collaborate with private companies for 
workplace gender sensitization and equal pay audits; and 
(iv) Increase Digital Outreach: Ministry/NCW should launch AI-powered chatbots to guide women on 
their legal rights and available support mechanisms.  
(Para 4.2.14 ibid) 
Reply 
The Commission on the occasion of Women’s Day has launched a Scheme of empanelment for the 
Advocates and Psychologists on pro bono basis, where it is proposed to utilize the services of these 
empanelled professionals for legal and psychological aide to the women all across the country. This 
would enhance the legal reach of the Commission to women in need and would provide immediate 

46 
 
support to women in distress. Through this initiative, the Commission aims to empanel at least one 
advocate and one psychologist in each district of the country. 
The Commission has informed that they are already in the process of strengthening its 
engagement with corporate workplace gender sensitization and awareness of PoSH. 
 The Commission has recently revamped its website and has plans for launching AI-powered 
chatbots to guide women on their legal rights and available support mechanisms. Further, the 
Commission has a dedicated App “Her Legal Guide”. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee acknowledges the Reports of the National Commission on Women from its enquiry visits 
to Manipur.  The reports note that women are the worst affected in a crisis, and many instances of 
violence against women are not being reported due to the fear of social stigma. Further, the NCW 
Report shares that in a meeting with women   associations and student federations, “they narrated their 
loss of faith and confidence in the system. In such a situation, the Committee recommends that the NCW 
stay apprised of issues relating to law and order in Manipur and proactively ensure that the concerns of 
women are registered and acted upon by the relevant authorities. 
        (Para 4.2.15 ibid) 
Reply 
The Commission keeps itself updated of the issues in Manipur through its regular communication with 
Manipur State Women Commission. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee notes that the Reports of the NCW from its consultations in Manipur consistently 
emphasized the need for a women-led peace building and cooperation effort. The Committee notes that 
the NCW Northeast Cell’s activities has largely been focused on other states in the Northeast during the 
last two years, but that its resources can be leveraged to support peace building and conflict resolution 
between local communities in Manipur.  
(Para 4.2.16 ibid) 
 
Reply 
NCW is in the process of taking up two projects for empowering Internally Displaced Women in 
Kakchling District and Bishnupur through Sustainable Livelihood in collaboration with NGOs. The

in New Delhi, Bhopal, Mumbai, Ranchi, and Guwahati, along with another major event in Varanasi.

Council (NDMC) raised an arrear rent demand due to retrospective reassessment of the space occupied

For the year 2023-24, NCPCR conducted 116 benches/camps where 40,843

Recommendation 
The Committee observes that the NCPCR is responsible for monitoring child rights and ensuring the 
effective implementation of child protection laws. However, gaps in outreach, inadequate tracking of 
complaints and limited enforcement capacity reduce its effectiveness. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends as under:  
(i) Establish a National Child Rights Dashboard: Ministry/NCPCR should establish a real-time 
digital platform for tracking cases of child rights violations, with geo-tagging of complaints and AI-
driven case prioritization;  
(ii) Strengthen Child Protection Committees: Ministry/NCPCR should ensure every district has an 
active committee that conducts quarterly reviews of child rights cases; 
(iii) Increase Legal Aid for Child Rights Cases: Ministry/NCPCR should partner with legal aid 
groups to provide pro bono services for cases of abuse and exploitation;   and  

48 
 
(iv) Mandatory Child Impact Assessments: Ministry/NCPCR should ensure that all policy decisions 
impacting children undergo an NCPCR-led impact assessment before implementation. 
          (Para 4.3.6 ibid) 
 
Reply 
(i) NCPCR has already digitized its complaint redressal mechanism through the introduction of the e-
BaalNidan portal in the year 2015. Through this platform, any individual may register a complaint and 
obtain a complaint registration number, enabling them to monitor the progress of their complaint’s 
redressal. Also, POCSO Tracking Portal of the Commission has been in operation to enable monitoring 
of cases pertaining to victims of child sexual abuse. The portal facilitates the services such as victim 
compensation, rehabilitation, and other support mechanisms for the care and protection of the child. 
Further, POCSO e-Box is an online interface developed to enable children to report incidents of sexual 
offences in a simple, confidential, and direct manner, thereby ensuring prompt action.  
With respect to geo-tagging of complaints and AI-driven case prioritization, the Commission will 
undertake the study for implementation of the same. 
(ii) Child Protection Committees (CPCs) do not fall within the monitoring mandate of NCPCR under 
Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015. 
CPCs are part of Mission Vatsalya Scheme of Ministry of Women and Child Development (MWCD). 
Ministry may take action for strengthening of CPCs. 
(iii) NCPCR established under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005, is vested 
with specific functions as enumerated under the said Act. Accordingly, the Commission does not enter 
into partnerships with legal aid groups for the purpose of rendering pro bono legal services to children. 
However, the Ministry of Women and Child Development (MWCD), in collaboration with the National 
Legal Services Authority (NALSA), may consider facilitating legal aid services for cases involving 
child abuse and exploitation, as NALSA is the competent authority established under law for the 
provision of free legal services, including, to children, before appropriate judicial forums. 
(iv) Ministry, which is making law that impacts children, normally undertakes the inter-ministerial 
consultations with MWCD. Therefore, the views of the MWCD are taken into account.

Recommendation 
The Committee notes that Manipur has been reeling under an extraordinary crisis for 21 months, with 
hundreds of lives lost and fifty to sixty thousand individuals internally displaced. A significant portion 
of those affected are women and children, who have been rendered homeless, deprived of basic 
necessities, and left in extreme distress. Their access to nutrition, education, and healthcare has been 
severely disrupted. These children, pregnant women, lactating mothers, and elderly women are facing 
immense hardship, leading to grave psychological and social consequences. The absence of economic 
opportunities has further deepened the despair. The Committee notes that the Government has taken 
many steps to support the victims but that more needs to be done. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends that the Ministry of Women and Child Development establish a dedicated special 
committee with a targeted and separate program/policy/scheme for these internally displaced women 
and children. This initiative should ensure direct monitoring and transparent delivery of assistance to 
prevent misuse and guarantee the well- being of affected individuals. Special provisions must be made 
for the education of displaced children, healthcare for lactating mothers, and employment alternatives 
for affected women to rebuild their lives. Steps must be taken to safeguard women and children in relief 
camps from sexual violence.         
(Para 3.4.35 ibid) 
Reply 
Ministry of Women and Child Development is implementing a Centrally Sponsored Scheme namely 
‘Mission Vatsalya’, through the State/ UT Governments on pre-defined cost sharing basis to deliver 
various services for children in difficult circumstances, which include both institutional care and non-
institutional care services. The scheme provides services to the Children in Need of Care and Protection 
(CNCP) as well as Children in Conflict with Law (CCL) for their rehabilitation and social re-integration 
into the mainstream of the society. The Child Care Institutions (CCIs) established under the Mission 
Vatsalya scheme support, inter-alia, age-appropriate education, access to vocational training, recreation, 
health care, counselling etc. Support under non-institutional care is provided by way of sponsorship, 
foster care and after care to children in need of care and protection. Under Non-Institutional Care, 
Rs.4000/- per child is provided. In Manipur, 78 number of CCIs were approved for the State. Child 
Welfare Committees under Sections 27-30 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) 
Act, 2015, are empowered to take decisions with regard to the children in need of care and protection, 
keeping their best interest in mind. They are also mandated to monitor the functioning of the CCIs. The 
JJ Act, 2015 (Section 109) provides for the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights at 
national level and State Commission for Protection of Child Rights at State level respectively to 
monitor the implementation of the Act. Mission Shakti and Mission Poshan 2.0 provide support for 
women and children. Mission Vatsalya envisages State and district level committees for field level 
implementation of the schemes. 
In view of above there may not be requirement to establish a dedicated special committee with 
a targeted and separate program/policy/scheme for these internally displaced women and children.  
The Central Government gives the highest priority to ensuring the safety, security, and empowerment of 
women and has taken several initiatives specially for help and support to the women and children in 
need. Ministry of Women and Child Development (MWCD), under the 15th Finance Commission 
(from FY 2022–23), is implementing three major Centrally Sponsored Schemes for the welfare of 
women and children: 
(i).        Mission Shakti aims at the safety, security, and empowerment of women. 
 It comprises of two verticals: 
a. Sambal vertical focuses on women’s safety and security through components like One Stop 
Centres (OSCs), which provide temporary shelter, medical and police assistance, legal aid, and 
counseling services under one roof, the Women Helpline (181) provides a 24x7 toll-free service to 

52 
 
women seeking support and information. Till 30 June 2025, Manipur had 16 operational OSCs, which 
have assisted 2,059 women and the Women Helpline in the state received 37,882 calls and provided 
assistance to 1,415 women. 
b. Samarthya vertical focuses on women's empowerment. It includes Sakhi Niwas (Working 
Women Hostels) to provide safe and conveniently located accommodation for working women, Shakti 
Sadan is an Integrated Relief and Rehabilitation Home for women in distress situations and difficult 
circumstances, including victims of trafficking, the Hub for Empowerment of Women (HEW) to bridge 
information gaps on women's schemes, and the Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana (PMMVY), 
which provides maternity benefit through Direct Benefit Transfer for the first child (and second child if 
a girl). As on 30.06.2025, 43 Shakti Sadans and 18 Sakhi Niwas are functional in the State of Manipur. 
(ii).        Saksham Anganwadi & Poshan 2.0 aims to improve the nutritional and health status of 
children, pregnant women, and lactating mothers, and also provides early childhood care and education. 
(iii).      Mission Vatsalya focuses on the protection and welfare of children in difficult circumstances, 
including those in need of care and protection and those in conflict with the law. 
In addition to these schemes, several other Ministries of the Central Government are 
implementing welfare programmes that contribute to the overall well-being of women. These include 
Samagra Shiksha, Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya, Babu jagjeevan Ram Chhatravas Yojana and 
Eklavya Model Residential Schools for improving access to education; Ayushman Bharat for free 
healthcare services, including 141 women-specific medical packages; Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya 
Janaushadhi Kendras for affordable medicines and sanitary products; Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana – 
Gramin and Urban for providing pucca houses; Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY) for 
skill and vocational training; PM Jan Dhan Yojana (PM-JDY) for financial inclusion; Stand-Up India 
and MUDRA Yojana for access to credit and promotion of women entrepreneurship; and Mahatma 
Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS), Start-up India, and Pradhan 
Mantri Street Vendors AtmaNirbhar Nidhi (PM SVANidhi) for employment and livelihood support. 
Schemes such as Atal Pension Yojana (APY), Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY), and 
Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (PMJJBY) provide insurance and social security benefits. 
Further, under Swachh Bharat Mission, Ujjwala Yojana, and Jal Jeevan Mission, access to toilets, clean 
cooking fuel, and potable tap water has been significantly expanded, contributing to improved living 
standards for women, particularly in rural areas. It is respectfully submitted that the aforesaid schemes 
are implemented by various Ministries and Departments of the Central Government. The Ministry of 
Women and Child Development does not maintain data regarding these schemes, and if desired, the 
Committee may consider seeking the relevant information from the concerned Ministries/ Departments. 
The Government, through institutions like the National Commission for Women (NCW), 
National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) and their counterparts in States have 
been spreading awareness through seminars, workshops, audio- visual, print and electronic media etc. to 
sensitize the people about the safety and security of women and children and also about various 
provisions of legislation and policies, etc.

CHILD ADOPTION RESOURCE AUTHORITY (CARA) 
Recommendation 
The Committee was informed that there are two systems of adoption prevalent in the country - one 
through CARA, and the other through the Hindu Adoption and 118 Maintenance Act (HAMA). The 
Committee was notified that currently, it takes about 3.5 years for a prospective parent to adopt a child. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry/CARA as under:  
(i)The Committee recommends a revisiting of current protocols for family placement of OAS children, 
as well as a review of the existing dual system of adoption laws to plug any loopholes in the same; 
(ii) Fast-Track Special Needs Adoptions: Ministry/CARA should provide financial and legal support for 
parents adopting children with disabilities or health challenges  
(iii)Expand Post-Adoption Support Services: Ministry/CARA should introduce mental health 
counseling, peer support groups, and legal assistance for adoptive families; 
(iv)Streamline Inter-Country Adoptions: Ministry/CARA should reduce red tape and align with 
international best practices to increase the number of successful adoptions; and  
 (v)Awareness amongst public on legal adoption: Ministry/CARA should leverage social media to 
spread awareness and extensive training and outreach activities with respect to adoption. 
          (Para 4.4.6 ibid) 
 
Reply 
(i)  The present protocols were revisited. In order to address the issue of the 3.5-year waiting period 
faced by prospective adoptive parents, CARA conducted a detailed analysis and identified key issues 
such as low registration rates and delays in declaring OAS children as LFA. Accordingly, letters were 
issued to all States/ UTs to conduct stakeholder sensitization through regular training sessions and to 
monitor the functioning of CWCs at the district level, among other measures. Identification Cell has 
been constituted under CARA to: 
i)   To ensure registration of all children less than 18 years of age in CCIs who are falling in five 
categories i.e. Orphan, Abandoned, Surrendered, No Visitation, Unfit Guardians/ Parents on CARINGS. 
ii)    To carry out regular monitoring & evaluation of database of children. 
iii)  To coordinate with district level authorities to determine legal status of children in timelines and 
addressing delays. 
iv)  To ensure data updation on CARINGS by state and district level authorities regarding stakeholders 
as well as children's profile. 
Further, continuous guidance has been provided to the concerned stakeholders to resolve procedural 
issues by conducting weekly interactive sessions with experts, monitoring pendencies through the 
CARINGS portal, and issuing alerts to decision-makers to expedite processes. These actions are aimed 
at bringing more children into the adoption pool, thereby facilitating quicker referrals and ultimately 
reducing the waiting period for PAPs. 

57 
 
HAMA being a personal law is being implemented by MoLJ and JJ Act is being implemented by 
MWCD. 
(ii).       To fast-track the adoption of children with special needs, CARA has invited and received inputs 
from States and UTs to assess the challenges in placing such children in family-based care.  
Further, with the objective of raising awareness on the subject, addressing the reservations of PAPs 
regarding the adoption of children with special needs, simplifying procedures, fast-tracking the 
identification and classification of such children, ensuring timely medical interventions, and providing 
counselling at the pre-adoption, adoption, and post-adoption stages, the theme for Adoption Awareness 
Month 2025 has been declared as 'Promoting Non-Institutionalised Rehabilitation of Children with 
Special Needs (Divyang Children)'.  
The objective of this year long campaign is to enhance awareness among PAPs to encourage them to 
adopt children with special needs. 
(iii).    Post-adoption support services, as per existing protocols, include maintaining a database of 
special educators, mental health professionals, counsellors, and other experts at the district level. The 
services of these professionals are utilized during both pre-adoption and post-adoption stages, 
particularly in cases of disruption or dissolution, and during root searches initiated by adoptees. 
However, it has been observed that the current database is inadequate to meet the growing counselling 
needs.  
To address the challenge of providing effective mental health counselling, CARA conducts weekly 
virtual training sessions for States and UTs. Since FY 2023–24, a dedicated session on 'Mental Health 
Counselling in Pre and Post Adoption Processes' has been included for stakeholders. 
Currently, there is no provision for legal assistance in the adoption process, as adoption orders are

(iv).     There is no red tapism in adoption procedure followed by CARA.

Recommendation/Observation by the Committee 
 
The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry wherein it is stated that, as on 13.10.2025, 6,263 
adolescent girls have been mobilized across 27 districts in 19 States under the Special Pilot for skilling 
of adolescent girls in convergence with MSDE. Further, the Committee also notes that training is

far is relatively limited when compared to the total number mobilized i.e. 6263. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry should closely monitor implementation, address any bottlenecks in 
training delivery, and ensure that the remaining mobilized girls are enrolled and trained 
expeditiously.

Recommendation 
The Committee recommends that additional steps should be taken for provision of nutritious food, 
breakfast, adequate accommodation facility to women and children in relief camps in Manipur. The 
Committee also recommends that Ministry should allocate additional funds for provision of the same as 
well as to facilitate women and children staying in relief camps in Manipur till the situation becomes 
normal.       
(Para 3.4.52 ibid) 
 
Reply 
Ministry of Women and Child Development is implementing a Centrally Sponsored Scheme 
namely ‘Mission Vatsalya’, through the State/ UT Governments on pre-defined cost sharing basis to 
deliver various services for children in difficult circumstances, which include both institutional care and 
non-institutional care services. The scheme provides services to the Children in Need of Care and 
Protection (CNCP) as well as Children in Conflict with Law (CCL) for their rehabilitation and social re-
integration into the mainstream of the society. The Child Care Institutions (CCIs) established under the 
Mission Vatsalya scheme support, inter-alia, age-appropriate education, access to vocational training, 
recreation, health care, counselling etc. Support under non-institutional care is provided by way of 
sponsorship, foster care and after care to children in need of care and protection. Under Non-
Institutional Care, Rs.4000/- per child is provided. In Manipur, 78 number of CCIs were approved for 
the State. 

62 
 
 
Child Welfare Committees under Sections 27-30 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of 
Children) Act, 2015, are empowered to take decisions with regard to the children in need of care and 
protection, keeping their best interest in mind. They are also mandated to monitor the functioning of the 
CCIs. The JJ Act, 2015 (Section 109) provides for the National Commission for Protection of Child 
Rights at national level and State Commission for Protection of Child Rights at State level respectively 
to monitor the implementation of the Act. Mission Shakti and Mission Poshan 2.0 provides support for 
women and children. Mission Vatsalya envisage State and district level committees for field level 
implementation of the schemes.   
 
In view of above there may not be requirement to establish a dedicated special committee with a 
targeted and separate program/policy/scheme for these internally displaced women and children. 
 
Recommendation/Observation by the Committee 
The Committee notes the support being provided to women and children in Manipur 
through existing schemes such as Mission Vatsalya, Mission Shakti and Mission Poshan 2.0. The 
Committee takes note of the institutional and non-institutional care mechanisms available under 
Mission Vatsalya, the approval of 78 Child Care Institutions in the State, and the statutory role of 
Child Welfare Committees and Commissions for Protection of Child Rights in safeguarding the 
interests of children in need of care and protection. 
While acknowledging the framework of schemes and institutional arrangements already 
in place, the Committee observes that the situation in Manipur is of an extraordinary and 
humanitarian nature, involving large numbers of internally displaced women and children 
residing in relief camps for an extended period. The Committee is of the view that reliance solely 
on existing schemes may not be adequate to address the immediate and specific needs particularly 
with regard to provision of nutritious food, breakfast, safe accommodation, health care and 
psycho-social support. Further, the Committee notes that the issue of additional fund allocation to 
relief camps has to be taken care of and, therefore, reiterates that temporary and targeted 
financial support, even within the ambit of existing schemes, is essential to ensure that women and 
children in relief camps are not deprived of the basic facilities. 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry, should undertake a focused assessment of 
the conditions in relief camps in Manipur and consider earmarking additional funds or 
flexibilities under existing schemes to meet emergent needs. Further, the Ministry should ensure 
close monitoring of service delivery on the ground so that women and children continue to receive 
adequate nutrition, shelter and care.   
The Committee recommends the Ministry also coordinate with other Ministries to 
evaluate what measures they may have undertaken to alleviate the issues faced by the Women 
and Children of Manipur.  
 
Recommendation 
Given the slow progress of the convergence between the Bal Vatikas and Anganwadis, the Committee 
reinforces its recommendation made in Report 363 that a national-level mission under the supervision 
of the PM be set up to operationalize and accelerate the same.      
(Para 3.4.63 ibid) 
Reply 
The Ministry acknowledges the Committee’s observation regarding the need to accelerate convergence 
between Bal Vatikas and Anganwadi Centres for effective implementation of ECCE under the NEP, 
2020. 
The Ministry is committed to ensuring seamless geographic and operational convergence 
between the two platforms to avoid duplication and ensure uniformity in the delivery of ECCE services. 
In this regard, MWCD is working in close coordination with the Department of School Education & 
Literacy (DoSEL), Ministry of Education (MoE), through joint consultations and meetings. A Joint 
Task Force, chaired by Secretary (SE&L) and comprising senior officers, has been constituted to 
develop a detailed plan, including financial aspects, for integrating Early Childhood Education with the 
school education system.  This Task Force has been constituted vide Order dated 27.09.2021 which was 
subsequently reconstituted via orders dated 23.02.2022, 19.07.2022, and 07.12.2023. An ECCE Task 

63 
 
Force has also been constituted by MWCD vide Order dated 10.03.2022 (re-constituted vide Order 
dated 19.05.2022) to come up with an action-oriented approach. Further, a Joint Advisory has also been 
issued by MWCD and DoSEL on 2nd April 2025 to strengthen collaboration between Anganwadis and 
Bal Vatikas. 
The co-location of AWCs within school premises is being promoted to enhance accessibility 
and ensure a smooth transition from pre-primary to primary education. The Guidelines on Co-location 
of Anganwadi Centres (AWCs) within Government Primary Schools were released on 03.09.2025 by 
the Hon’ble Minister of Education and the Hon’ble Minister of Women and Child Development, and 
have been circulated to all States/UTs with a request to ensure their effective implementation. 
 
Recommendation/Observation by the Committee 
 
The Committee notes the Ministry’s acknowledgement of the issue and appreciates the 
constitution of multiple Task Forces, joint consultations with the Ministry of Education, issuance 
of a Joint Advisory in April 2025, and release of Guidelines on co-location of Anganwadi Centres 
within Government Primary Schools in September 2025.  
However, the Committee observes that the existence of Task Forces and advisories over a 
prolonged period has not yet translated into the desired pace of on-ground convergence. 
Therefore, the Committee is of the view that repeated constitution and reconstitution of 
committees since 2021 indicates delays in decision-making and implementation, which may affect 
uniform delivery of ECCE services across States and UTs. Accordingly, the Committee 
recommends that a dedicated national mission with clear targets, timelines, and accountability 
mechanisms should be planned which would significantly strengthen coordination between 
stakeholders, ensure uniform adoption of guidelines by States/UTs, and accelerate co-location and 
operational integration of Bal Vatikas and Anganwadi Centres. Further, the Ministry should 
consider upgrading the existing coordination mechanism into a mission-mode framework at the 
national level to ensure timely and effective realization of ECCE objectives envisioned under 
NEP, 2020. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee notes that the critical period for fighting malnutrition and stimulating brain 
development is in the first 1,000 days of life, including the time spent in the womb. The Committee notes 
that the current system has institutional care only for children between 3-6 years in Anganwadis for a 
few hours per day. Children between 6 months and 3 years are only provided take-home rations. To 
comprehensively tackle malnutrition, and to enable female labour force participation, the Committee 
endorses the Law Commission’s suggestion that “every child under six should have an unconditional 
right to crèche and day-care…provided by the State.” Accordingly –    
i. All Anganwadis may be converted into full day-care centres (crèches) open for at least 10 
hours for children aged between six months to three years to help all working women and their 
children. As currently provided under the Palna scheme, morning snack, hot cooked meal for lunch, 
and evening snack may be provided to children  
ii.         An additional Anganwadi worker may be hired to care for the children between 6 months and 3 
years in the day care facilities. AWHs may also be considered for the same and redesignated as AWWs. 
          (Para 3.4.64 ibid) 
Reply 
The Ministry of women and Child Development has introduced Palna Scheme under the Samarthya 
Vertical of Umbrella Mission Shakti for all States and UTs w.e.f. 01 April 2022, to provide day care 
facilities and protection to children. 
Anganwadi centres are the world's largest childcare institutions dedicated to providing essential 
care and support to children ensuring delivery of care facilities till the last mile. In a first of its kind 
approach, Ministry has extended the services of childcare through Palna/Anganwadi cum Crèches 
(AWCCs). This will ensure whole day childcare support ensuring their well-being in a safe and secure 
environment. Anganwadi cum Crèche initiative aims to increase ‘women work force participation’ in 
the economy The objective of Palna Scheme is to provide quality crèche facility in safe and secure 
environment for children (from ages 6 months – 6 years), nutritional support, health and cognitive 

64 
 
development of children, growth monitoring &immunization. Crèche facilities under Palna are provided 
to all mothers, irrespective of their employment status. 
The scheme is designed to function in convergence with Anganwadi Services under Saksham 
Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0, thereby ensuring comprehensive early childhood care and nutrition. Each 
Anganwadi-cum-Creche Centre provides evening snacks to enrolled children as part of the Palna 
component. Additionally, morning snacks and hot cooked meal for lunch are provided through the 
Anganwadi platform, ensuring that the children receive supplementary nutrition, health check-ups, 
immunization and growth monitoring in an integrated manner. 
The Palna Scheme provides day-care services for up to 7.5 hours per day, six days a week. As 
per the Standard Operating Procedures and guidelines under Mission Shakti, States and Union 
Territories have the flexibility to determine the operational timings of crèches based on local needs. The 
guidelines mention that “The crèche timings need to be flexible depending on the local requirements. 
Crèches shall be open for 26 days in a month and for seven and half (7-1/2) hours per day as per the 
work schedule of majority of the mothers in the area” and the same can be accessed at 
https://wcd.gov.in/offerings/palna. Each crèches caters up to 25 Children, and offers nutritional support, 
health and cognitive development of children, growth monitoring & immunization. The government has 
made provisions for 2 additional staff per AWCC (one Creche Worker and one Creche Helper), in 
addition to the already existing Anganwadi Worker and Anganwadi Helper. This will also provide 
employment opportunities to women. The State Government is responsible for hiring these honorarium 
workers and helpers. 
 
Recommendation/Observation by the Committee 
 
The Committee examined the reply of the Ministry and appreciates the introduction of 
the Palna Scheme under Mission Shakti and efforts undertaken to extend whole-day childcare 
services for children aged six months to six years, with the objective of improving early childhood 
care, nutrition and enhancing women’s workforce participation. The Committee also notes 
positively the convergence with Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0, provision of supplementary 
nutrition, and the deployment of additional crèche staff at AWCCs. 
However, the Committee is of the view that the current provision of 7.5 hours of day-care 
may not adequately meet the needs of working women, particularly those engaged in full-time, 
informal, or shift-based employment, who often require longer and more predictable childcare 
support. The Committee is of the view that converting Anganwadis into full day-care centres with 
extended operational hours of at least 10 hours would significantly enhance accessibility and 
utility of these facilities for mothers of children between six months and three years. 
The Committee notes that while the Palna Scheme provides additional crèche workers 
and helpers, its coverage remains limited and is subject to State-level implementation and 
resource availability. In this context, the Committee emphasizes the need for a clear roadmap to 
progressively expand AWCCs to all Anganwadi Centres, particularly in urban poor, tribal, and 
high-migration areas. 
 
MISSION SHAKTI 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee also notes that Rs. 2.00 crores were allocated both at BE and RE 2023-24 under Nari 
Adalat (NA) while the Actual utilization is Rs 0.424 crores which is 21.2 % of BE and RE 2023-24. 
Similarly, Rs. 2.00 crores were allocated at BE 2024-25  which was reduced to Rs. 0.79 crores at RE 
stage under Nari Adalat (NA) while the Actual utilization is Rs 0.09 crores as on 31st December, 2024 
which is 4.5 % of BE and 11.39% of RE 2024-25. The Committee expresses its concerns over under-
utilization of funds under Nari Adalat scheme which aims at empowering women and ensuring justice 
and, therefore recommends the Ministry to ensure optimum utilization of funds allocated under this 
scheme during 2025-26. 
          (Para 3.6.7 ibid) 
Reply 
Nari Adalat is an initiative, aimed at empowering women and ensuring justice, offers services such as 
alternate dispute resolution, grievance redressal, counselling, evidence-based decision-making, pressure 

65 
 
group tactics, negotiation, mediation, and reconciliation. Addressing a broad spectrum of gender-based 
issues, the initiative focuses on themes like domestic violence, dowry-related disputes, child custody, 
and workplace gender disparities, intending to raise awareness, provide support, and advocate for 
women's rights. 
 Besides Nari Adalat, there are 3 other components under Sambal vertical of Mission Shakti i.e. 
OSC, WHL and BBBP. For implementation of the Sambal vertical of the Mission Shakti, 100% 
financial assistance are provided to States/ UTs. Funds are released to States and UTs on the basis of 
Utilization Certificate of earlier grant and subject to compliance of guidelines of Department of 
Expenditure prescribed for Single Nodal agency (SNA) or SNA SPARSH of the Public Financial 
Management System (PFMS). The primary reasons for under-utilization of funds in Nari Adalat scheme 
are: 
1. Delay in transition to Single Nodal Agency (SNA) in State/UTs and further from SNA to SNA 
– SPARSH module on the Public Financial Management System. 
2. Delay in submission of Utilization Certificate and Statement of Expenditure.  
3. At present 2 States/UT have piloted the scheme.  More States/UTs have sent the proposals for 
operationalization of Nari Adalat in respective States/UTs and the utilization of funds allocated under 
this scheme would be increased accordingly. 
 
Recommendation/Observation by the Committee 
 
The Committee has examined the reply of the Ministry regarding the under-utilization of 
funds under the Nari Adalat scheme vis-à-vis the objectives and scope of the scheme, which aims 
at empowering women through alternate dispute resolution, grievance redressal and counselling 
on a range of gender-based issues. Further, the Committee notes that the under-utilization of 
funds is primarily due to procedural delays relating to transition to the Single Nodal Agency 
(SNA) and SNA–SPARSH modules, delayed submission of Utilization Certificates and Statements 
of Expenditure, and the fact that the scheme is presently being piloted by  only two States/UTs. 
While the Committee acknowledges these implementation challenges, it observes that 
procedural and administrative bottlenecks have resulted in persistently low utilization of funds 
over consecutive years, thereby limiting the outreach and impact of an otherwise important 
initiative. The Committee is of the view that such systemic delays should be addressed in a timely 
manner, particularly given that the scheme is fully funded by the Centre and intended to provide 
accessible justice mechanisms for women at the grassroots level. 
Further, the Committee recommends facilitating faster on boarding of States/UTs, 
providing handholding support for transition to SNA–SPARSH, and streamlining the process for 
submission of Utilization Certificates. 
 
SAMBAL DIVISION 
ONE STOP CENTRE 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee appreciates the objectives of One Stop Centre (OSC) Scheme which aims at supporting 
women affected by violence and those in distress. However, the Committee notes that staffs at OSCs are 
not properly trained. They are being hired on contractual basis by State Governments and their salaries 
are very less. Further, they are not being paid salaries on regular basis. Moreover, OSCs are not 
manned as per the population density of respective area/locality. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry should take efforts that OSCs should be manned as per population 
density of respective areas/locality. Further, the Ministry should consider enhancing the salaries of 
personnel deployed at OSCs and sensitize the State Governments to disburse their salary on regular 
basis. Moreover, the Ministry should ensure proper training of personnel deployed at OSCs for effective 
implementation of the scheme.          
(Para 3.6.10 ibid) 
Reply 
There are 4 components under Sambal vertical of Mission Shakti i.e. OSC, WHL, BBBP and Nari 
Adalat. For implementation of the Sambal vertical of the Mission Shakti, 100% financial assistance are 
provided to States/UTs. Funds are released to States and UTs on the basis of Utilization Certificate of 

66 
 
earlier grant and subject to compliance of guidelines of Department of Expenditure prescribed for 
Single Nodal agency (SNA) or SNA SPARSH of the Public Financial Management System (PFMS). 
 
With regard to proper training of personnel deployed at OSCs for effective implementation of 
the scheme, it is submitted that the Ministry has taken keen action in standardizing capacity building 
sessions for the functionaries of One Stop Centres. This involves engaging expert resource persons from 
NIMHANS, UNFPA, NIPCCD/SPNIWCD, NALSA, and National Informatics Centre for facilitating 
technical sessions on psycho-social counselling, gender-based violence case management, gender 
sensitization and dashboard operations. This includes three regional training programs in Guwahati, 
Indore, and Bangalore, and two National Workshops in New Delhi between January 2024 to July 2024. 
Recently Ministry has organised two national workshops at Vigyan Bhawan, New Delhi for training of 
personnel deployed at OSC, namely, National Workshop on Mission Shakti Dashboard on 19th May, 
2025 and National Workshop for Master Trainer for One Stop Centre on 27th May, 2025. 
 
Recommendation/Observation by the Committee 
The Committee notes with appreciation the steps taken by the Ministry to standardize 
and strengthen capacity building of OSC personnel through regional and national training 
programmes, with the involvement of reputed institutions and expert resource persons which 
reflects a positive effort towards improving the quality of service delivery at OSCs. However, the 
Committee observes that several key concerns raised earlier have not been addressed adequately, 
particularly regarding inadequate staffing levels in relation to population density, low 
remuneration of contractual staff, and irregular disbursement of salaries by State Governments. 
The Committee therefore is of the view that training alone may not yield desired outcomes unless 
personnel are adequately compensated, retained, and deployed in sufficient numbers to handle 
the caseload effectively. 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry strengthen monitoring mechanisms and 
engage more closely with States/UTs to ensure that administrative and human resource issues do 
not impede the effective functioning of OSCs and the realization of the scheme’s objectives. 
 
Recommendation 
The Committee observes that One Stop Centers (OSCs) and Women Helplines need sufficient 
integration with law enforcement. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should take 
the following initiatives: 
(i) AI-Integrated Women’s Helpline: Deploy AI-powered analytics to identify high-risk cases and 
escalate responses to authorities in real time.  
(ii) Expand Mobile One Stop Centers (mOSCs): Introduce mobile OSCs to reach underserved 
areas and provide immediate support for survivors.  
(iii) Integrate Gender Sensitization in Police Training: Make it mandatory for police and judiciary 
officials to undergo regular gender sensitization training. 
(iv) Create Community-Led Safety Networks: Establish women-led neighbourhood watch groups 
trained in self-defence and crisis response.  
The Committee was informed that of the 888 approved OSCs, 802 are currently operational and that 
462 OSCs are integrated with Women Helpline. The Committee recommends the fast-tracking of the 
operationalisation of the remaining OSCs and their integration with WHLs.    
(Para 3.6.11 ibid) 
Reply 
I. With regard to the recommendation of the Committee regarding Deployment of AI-powered 
analytics to identify high-risk cases and escalating responses to authorities in real time, it is submitted 
that the technology solution provider for Women Helpline, C-DAC, has developed application for Call 
operator to digitize the related workflow, and integrate it with the ERSS – 112 nationwide single 
emergency number. Through this, the process of data logging and maintenance has been digitized. 
Further dashboards have been developed at Supervisor, State and National level for monitoring the 
scheme and provide support in evidence and data-based decision making. AI solutions will be explored. 
II. Ministry has made provision for hiring a dedicated vehicle/transport for the OSCs   for the 
purpose of rescuing women in emergency cases and underserved areas.  
III.   Time to time training programmes are being organised for OSC staffs.   

67 
 
IV. Nari Adalats have been set up at the Gram Panchayat level, and all cases of   serious nature 
registered under Nari Adalat must be promptly reported or referred to the respective District One Stop 
Centre (OSC). A detailed Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) outlining the necessary protocols has 
been developed, and the state has been appropriately advised to ensure compliance. 
V. As of now, a total of 960 OSCs have been approved, out of which 820 are operational. 
Regarding integration of the OSCs with the Women Helpline (WHL), it is submitted that 565 OSCs 
have been integrated. Furthermore, as reported by CDAC the required hardware has been delivered to 
675 locations and 602 connectivity to the OSCs has been completed across various States/UTs. 
 
Recommendation/Observation by the Committee 
 
The Committee appreciates the steps taken towards digitization of helpline workflows, 
integration with ERSS–112, development of monitoring dashboards, provision of vehicles for 
emergency response, and the increase in the number of approved and operational OSCs. 
However, the issues such as deployment of AI-powered analytics and mandatory gender 
sensitization training for police and judiciary are not clearly addressed. Further, the Committee 
is of the view that despite progress, a significant number of OSCs remain non-operational and 
many are yet to be fully integrated with Women Helplines and connectivity systems and therefore 
reiterates the need for time-bound operationalisation of all approved OSCs and complete 
integration with WHLs. It further urges the Ministry to adopt advanced technological solutions, 
strengthen coordination with law enforcement agencies, and expedite implementation to ensure 
prompt, effective and survivor-centric support for women in distress.

Recommendation 
The Committee observes that Nari Adalat scheme which aims at empowering women and ensuring 
justice, offers services such as alternate dispute resolution, grievance redressal, counselling, evidence-
based decision-making, pressure group tactics, negotiation, mediation, and reconciliation etc., is very 
slow and its implementation is not up to the mark. Further, this scheme is not operational in every 
district of the country. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry to review the 
implementation of Nari Adalat scheme and also to ensure that each and every district of the country 
should have a Nari Adalat accessible to women. The Committee also recommends that this scheme 
should 106 have support system where counsellors, psychiatrists are attached to it, so that, the 
disadvantage which the women actually face is also addressed.     
(Para 3.6.17 ibid) 
Reply 
Nari Adalat is a component of “Sambal” which is a new component of Mission Shakti of the Ministry 
of Women and Child Development. Nari Adalat scheme provides women with an alternate grievance 
redressal mechanism for resolving cases of harassment, violence and curtailment of rights or 
entitlements at the Gram Panchayat level. The scheme aims to tackle socio-economic and cultural 
challenges faced by women in the area and provides dispute resolution through mediation and referral 
to appropriate institutions such as One Stop Centre, Police Station, District Legal Service Authority and 
Women Help Desk. 
Nari Adalat is being implemented at the Gram Panchayat level. The implementation of the Nari 
Adalat is being done on pilot basis from 2023-24 in selected few States/UTs. The participation of the 
states/UTs is decided in consultation with them. 
The State of Assam and UT of Jammu & Kashmir were selected by the Ministry to implement 
the new component of Nari Adalat on pilot basis. Nari Adalat initiative is being run in 50 Gram 
Panchayats each in the State of Assam and UT of Jammu & Kashmir.  
It is also being piloted and implemented soon in 10 Gram Panchayats each in the state of Bihar, 
Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh and 5 Gram Panchayats of Andaman and Nicobar Islands.  
Further, it is also being piloted in 10 Gram Panchayats of 17 States and 5 Gram Panchayats of 2 
UTs.The Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for Nari Adalat has been reiterated and shared with all 
states and Union Territories. 
 

68 
 
Recommendation/Observation by the Committee 
 
The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry on the implementation of the Nari Adalat 
scheme under Mission Shakti and appreciates the intent of piloting the scheme and the issuance of 
Standard Operating Procedures to States/UTs. The Committee however, observes that the scale 
and pace of implementation remain inadequate in relation to the scheme’s stated objectives. 
Further, the reply does not clearly address the issue of attachment of professional support 
systems such as counsellors and mental health experts, in order to make it accessible to women in 
every district. The Committee therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation that the Ministry 
should undertake a comprehensive review of the pilot, set clear timelines for phased expansion to 
all districts, and ensure that Nari Adalats are strengthened with counselling and psychological 
support services to effectively address the complex challenges faced by women seeking justice. 
 
******* 

69 
 
CHAPTER IV  
Recommendations in respect of which replies of the Government are still awaited  
NIL 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
******* 

70

1. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry wherein it is stated that, as on 13.10.2025, 6,263 
adolescent girls have been mobilized across 27 districts in 19 States under the Special Pilot for skilling 
of adolescent girls in convergence with MSDE. Further, the Committee also notes that training is 
currently underway for 468 adolescent girls, while training has been completed for 368 adolescent girls. 
While appreciating the initial efforts made by the Ministry towards operationalizing the pilot 
programme, the Committee observes that the number of girls who have actually completed training so

recommends that the Ministry should closely monitor implementation, address any bottlenecks in 
training delivery, and ensure that the remaining mobilized girls are enrolled and trained

The Committee also reiterates its earlier recommendation that the Ministry should

(Para 3.4.50 ibid)

While acknowledging the framework of schemes and institutional arrangements already

residing in relief camps for an extended period. The Committee is of the view that reliance solely

The Committee recommends the Ministry also coordinate with other Ministries to
