1.5. The Secretary informed the Committee that after critically reviewing the Family Welfare Programme in the
Eighth Plan and their outcome, some path breaking changes have been introduced and new programmes in the Ninth
Plan have also been initiated. During the year 1998-99, some of the programmes were operationalised by the
Department.
1.6. The Secretary stated that apprehensions were expressed in many quarters that giving up of contraceptive targets
would result in a sharp decline in the performance of the population programme. Contrary to such negative
predictions, after the initial slump, the overall performance, under all the family planning methods for the period
April-January, in both 1997-98 and 1998-99, has been registering considerable improvement, i.e. 4% in Sterilisation;
1.3% in IUD insertions, 8.3% in condom use and 3.8% in use of oral pills. There is thus 5.7% increase in all family
planning methods as compared to last year. The Committee presumes that this increase represents the
reproductive age group of couples only. Otherwise this increase has no relevance. Another encouraging factor
observed is that improvement has been taking place in both sterilisation and spacing methods, the Secretary claimed.
1.7. Five major States, i.e. Assam, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Bihar have also shown an
improvement of 24.2%, 25%, 31%, 11% and 1.6%, respectively in sterilisation over last year. In IUD, Assam, Bihar
and Uttar Pradesh have shown an improvement of 48.2%, 11.8% and 7.5%, respectively. Similar improvements were
noticed in most of the States in condom use, the Secretary added.
1.8. The Committee observes that U.P. has the highest birth rate, i.e. 33.5 among the States closely followed by

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/87repfw.htm[01-07-2016 15:10:52]
Bihar, M.P., Rajasthan. So far as the death rate is concerned, M.P. tops the list with death rate of 11.0. Bihar,
Orissa and U.P. are the other States having above average rates. IMR is the highest in Orissa, closely followed
by M.P. Assam, U.P. and Rajasthan are the other three States having higher IMR. The Committee finds that no
noticeable improvement has taken place during the last three years in respect of all the aforesaid States.
Greater focussing of all the Family Welfare measures in these States is required if the current high population
growth rate of the country is to be effectively checked.
II. NINTH PLAN
2.1. The goal to be achieved by 2002 A.D. (end of Ninth Five Year Plan) are:-
1. Reduction of Total Fertility Rate to 2.6-2.9 from the existing 3.5;
2. Reduction of birth rate to 23-24 per thousand population and infant mortality rate to 50-56 against the
current rate of 72 (1996); and
3. Increasing the couple protection rate to 51-60% against the current figure of 45.4% (March, 1997).
2.2. Underlining the Ninth Plan strategy, the Secretary stated that it seeks to achieve population stabilisation through a
three-pronged effort, easy availability of and education on contraceptive choices and improvement in the health status
of women and children.
2.3. The Committee notes that for the Ninth Plan, an outlay of Rs.16,750.36 crore of Domestic Budgetary Support
(DBS) and Rs.5296.58 crore of External Assistance (EAP) for implementing the Family Welfare Programme was
proposed to the Planning Commission. Out of DBS of Rs.16,750.36 crore, Rs.10,270 crore was planned as the
requirement of the ongoing activities of the Department and Reproductive and Child Health Programme. Another
minimum of Rs.2000 crore was required for strengthening some of the key programmes. Thus, to achieve the targets
set on the domestic front, Rs.12,270 crore is the minimum requirement of DBS during IX Plan. Against this, the
Planning Commission has indicated a DBS of Rs.12000.00 crore. The corresponding EAP allocation of Rs.3717.00
crore is also far less than the amount projected.
III. BUDGET ALLOCATION
3.1. The Committee notes that the allocation to the Department has been substantially increased from Rs.2510.51
crore in B.E. 1998-99 to Rs.2940.60 crore in the current year. Out of Rs.2940.60 crore, Rs.2920.00 crore, form the
plan component and Rs.20.60 crore is the non-plan component.
3.2. Commenting on the allocation made to the Department, the Secretary, while deposing before the Committee
stated that underfunding has always been a major problem in the family welfare sector. Family Welfare Programme
being a 100 percent centrally funded programme, one result of underfunding has been the Department’s inability to
pay arrears claimed by the State Governments. Due to chronic resource crunch it has been impossible for the
Department to launch many new programmes. The Department has been able to bridge only certain glaring gaps in the
funding of the existing programmes.
3.3. Considering the severity of the problem of arrears and damage it was causing to the Family Welfare Programme,
the entire additionality in 1998-99 has been utilised to address to this most pressing problem. In normal circumstances,
the sizeable increase in the allocation for 1999-2000 would have solved about 75% of the problem of arrears for future
years. However, as per estimates, requirement on account of arrears would be around Rs.1360 crore in 1999-2000,
against which a provision of Rs.1291 crore has been made. Thus, though the size of arrears has been reduced to a
considerable amount due to the Department’s consistent efforts, yet the States’ requiremnt was likely to remain unmet
by another Rs.200 crore which was mainly on account of recommendations of the Fifth Pay Commission, it was
clarified.
3.4. The Committee notes the steps taken by the Department in this regard. The Committee strongly feels that
the Non-settlement of arrear claims is adversely affecting the Family Welfare Programme. Settlement of arrear
claims would result in better implementation of the programme. The Committee is, therefore, of the opinion

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/87repfw.htm[01-07-2016 15:10:52]
that this issue should be sorted out without delay and the Planning Commission may be approached for one
time grant.
IV. RURAL FAMILY WELFARE SERVICES
4.1. Under the head `Rural Family Welfare Services’, the allocation has been raised from Rs.605 crore on 1998-
99 to Rs.875 crore in 1999-2000. Out of this, a provision of Rs.350 crores has been proposed for
continuation/maintenance of 5435 Rural Family Welfare Centres which have been merged with the Primary
Health Centres (PHCs) after 1980. An allocation of Rs.525 crores has been proposed for 97,557 Rural Sub-
Centres funded under the national Family Welfare Programme.
4.2. To a question, as to in what manner, the additional allocation was proposed to be utilised, the Department
submitted that the whole provision was for maintenance of RFW Centres and Sub-Centres which were earlier
being inadequately provided. As per the Audited Statements of Expenditure received from the State AG
Offices, the requirement for Rural Family Welfare Services in the existing pay scales work out to Rs.980 crore,
against which a provision of only Rs.875 crore has been made. The requirement will further hike once the
States implement the recommendations of the Fifth Pay Commission, the Committee was informed.
4.3. The Committee is of the strong opinion that the Rural Family Welfare Centres and Sub-Centres are
meant for the effective implementation of the Family Welfare Programme in rural areas where need is
the most. However, the Committee is given to understand that even in the existing centres/sub-centres
required facilities are not available. If such centres are not properly maintained for want of funds, it will
result in a severe set back for the programme as more than half of the population of our country lives in
rural areas. The Committee, therefore, desires that funds as required for these centres may be provided
at the RE stage.
4.4. To a question as to how many rural sub-centres were opened during the year, the Department stated that
389 sub-centres were opened during 1997-98 and 201 centres had been opened during the period 1
st April, 1998
to 31st January, 1999. In view of the fact that the shortfall in the number of rural sub-centres which was 7,727
as per 1991 census, would reach the figure of 22,987 by the end of Ninth Plan, the Committee feels that
opening of these few centres is not going to make much of a difference. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its
recommendation made last year that the Department should urge upon the States to open fixed number of
centres each year and to set apart some provision in their Budget for the purpose.
4.5. To another question about the States which have identified opening of sub-centres as a priority within the
seven items identified under the Basic Minimum Services Programme (BMS), being funded out of the
Additional Central Assistance being made available to the States/UTs by the Planning Commission, the
Department informed that the States of Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and Maharashtra have identified
opening of sub-centres as priority within the seven BMS items. Concerned State Secretaries have been
requested to make adequate provision for opening of sub-centres under BMS, it was added.
4.6. Considering the severity of the problem, the Committee feels that the Department should persuade
all the states to give priority to opening of rural sub-centres alongwith required facilities among the seven
items under BMS and to allot reasonable share of funds therefor.
V. URBAN FAMILY WELFARE SERVICES
5.1. For Urban Family Welfare Services, the allocation has been reduced from Rs.64 crore last year to Rs.58
crore this year. Asked to explain the reasons for this reduction, the Department submitted that in the current
year, Rs.58 crore was the actual requirement for the various centres functioning under the programme in the
district and sub-district levels which was worked out on the basis of Audited Statements of Expenditure

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/87repfw.htm[01-07-2016 15:10:52]
received from the State AG Offices
5.2. In order to improve out-reach service delivery system in urban slums, Urban Revamping Scheme has been
introduced which envisages reorganisation of existing Urban Family Welfare Centres. There are 1083 Urban
Family Welfare Centres and 871 Health Posts currently in operation, the Committee was informed.
5.3. EFC has given approval on 11th March, 1999 to a proposal under IPP-VIII for systematic provision of
Urban Family Welfare Services in urban areas of West Bengal, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh which is now
being submitted for Cabinet approval. For 25 larger cities in other States, city-wise project proposals are under
preparation for their funding under World Bank assisted RCH project which was expected to be finalised by
July, 1999. Thus, re-organisation under both these programmes will be done in the second half of 1999-2000,
the Department informed.
5.4. The Committee observes that slums are proliferating at a rapid pace in the urban areas of the
country. The Committee is, therefore, of the view that Cabinet approval for re-organisation be obtained
at the earliest and hopes that the Department will be able to stick to their target date for
operationalisation of these programmes.
VI. TRAINING OF AUXILIARY NURSE MIDWIVES/LADY HEALTH VISITORS
6.1. An allocation of Rs.39.40 crore has been provided during the current year. The amount allocated under the
scheme is towards the maintenance of the existing ANM Training Schools on the basis of approved pattern of
assistance. There are at present 408 ANM (Female Health Workers) Training Schools with an admission
capacity of 16000. The Committee notes that against 1,59,777 sanctioned posts of ANMs, there are 1,34,112
ANMs only. Against the required posts of 22,962 LHVs, only 19,071 LHVs are in position.
6.2. When Committee sought to know the names of the states where the maximum number of posts were
vacant, the Department stated that maximum number of posts were vacant in the states of Bihar (2500), Uttar
Pradesh (1016), Karnataka (1006) and Andhra Pradesh (561) in respect of ANMs and in the states of Uttar
Pradesh (473), Tamil Nadu (463), Madhya Pradesh (337), Bihar (335), Karnataka (289), Assam (247) and
Gujarat (200) in respect of LHVs. The Committee believes that this problem persists in other States too.
6.3. The Committee notes with dismay that inspite of having the required number of trained personnel, a
very large number of posts are lying vacant in different States. ANMs and LHVs are the key
functionaries of the Primary Health Centres/Rural Family Welfare Centres/Health Posts and keeping
such important posts vacant for a long time is adversely affecting the quality of services provided at the
field level. The Committee feels that the matter needs urgent attention, if required, at the political level,
particularly because in some of these States, Family Welfare measures have failed to achieve the desired
results.
VII. VILLAGE HEALTH GUIDE SCHEME
7.1. Like previous year, an allocation of Rs.10 crores has been made for the scheme this year too. When the
Committee sought to know what decision was contemplated by the Department on the Expert Committee
report, which recommended for closing the scheme, it was stated that a note for the Cabinet on the report was
sent to Ministry of Finance on 3rd February, 1999 and Ministry of Law and Justice, Planning Commission and
Department of Health on 26th January for their comments. Comments from all except the Ministry of Law and
Justice have been received. After receiving the comments from all, the revised Cabinet Note incorporating the
comments will be put up before the Cabinet for a final decision in the matter, the Department informed.
7.2. The Committee feels that the Department should approach the Ministry of Law and Justice to give

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/87repfw.htm[01-07-2016 15:10:52]
their comments in this regard at the earliest so that an early decision in the matter may be arrived at.
VIII. NO-SCALPEL VASECTOMY PROJECT
1. The Committee notes that to promote male participation in the Family Welfare Programme, a UNFPA No-
Scalpel Vasectomy Project is being implemented in the country under which 1500 medical personnel are to
be trained. A total of 214 doctors have been trained so far and 23,829 acceptors have undergone No-
Scalpel Vasectomy Operation. The Committee was also given to understand that No-Scalpel Vasectomy is
one of the most effective contraceptive methods for males with practically no side effects/complications.
2. The Department further submitted that NSV training was held in the States of A.P., Orissa, Maharashtra,
Haryana, U.P., T.N., West Bengal, Kerala, Sikkim, H.P. and Rajasthan and the feedback was good. In A.P.,
especially in Karim Nagar District, there has been a reversal of trend from female sterilisation to male
sterilisation.
3. The Committee notes that neither the time-limit within which the target for training of 1,500 medical
personnel has been indicated nor the period until which the UNFPA project will be financed has
been given. So far only 214 medical personnel have been trained against a target of 1500. The
Committee is of the view that if desired results are to be obtained, the training programme should be
completed at the earliest.
IX INFORMATION, EDUCATION AND COMMUNICATION
9.1. The Information, Education and Communication (IEC) component of National Family Welfare Programme is
mainly to have an effective communication strategy to create an awareness among the masses about the means and
measures of the Programme, educate them about the perils of overpopulation and motivate and persuade them to adopt
small family norm, using all possible channels of media.
9.2. The allocation for Information, Education and Communication (IEC), has been marginally increased from
Rs.29.70 crores last year to Rs.32.95 crore this year. This is in addition to the provision of Rs.88.80 crore made
available under RCH for IEC activities.
9.3. To a specific query as to whether there exists any mechanism to assess the impact of IEC activities on the various
Family Welfare Programmes being implemented in the country, the Department stated that the ongoing Second
National Family Health Survey will throw a great deal of light on impact of IEC activities, on quality, reach and
utilisation of Family Welfare Services and the resultant impact. A system of annual District Rapid Household survey
has also been initiated which will also monitor the effectiveness of IEC campaign. Besides that, evaluation of special
programmes and schemes like PPI, Mahila Swasthya Sangh etc. are also being taken up by the Department
occasionally. The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Department in this regard.
9.4. The Committee also notes that in order to improve the awareness of the general public towards RCH and
population issues, as one of the IEC activity, the Department plans to have 5-10 big hoardings in 13 towns and the
messages in the hoardings will be replaced quarterly. The Committee feels that such a measure will be too
insignificant in view of the vastness of our country. The Committee is of the view that instead of a centralised
initiative, this strategy can be worked out in States particularly where Family Welfare measures are not
reaching the public at large due to one reason or the other, with active coordination between State
Governments and Family Welfare functionaries-both Government and NGOs.
9.5. On the IEC activities, the Secretary stated that during 1998-99, the Department tried to reinvigorate the IEC
campaign by professionalising a large part of the national and State-level IEC campaign through audio/visual media,
while local specific IEC activities were left to the district set up. Private professional agencies were used under the
World Bank funded RCH programme, for telecasting and broadcasting spots and inter-active panel discussions on
various RCH issues.
9.6. Another effort in this direction was to involve the community in IEC activities by launching a programme for

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/87repfw.htm[01-07-2016 15:10:52]
empowering the Zilla Saksharshtra Samitis (ZSSs), the mass literacy programme, for mounting local campaign on
RCH issues. Funds to the tune of 4-5 lakhs each, have been released to 111 districts through a Joint Supervisory
Committee with the Department of Education. The Committee welcomes the new initiative.
IV. DISTRIBUTION OF CONTRACEPTIVES
COMMERCIAL DISTRIBUTION
10.1. The allocation for commercial distribution of contraceptives has been steeply increased from Rs.80 crore last
year to Rs.140 crore this year. Asked how this steep increase is proposed to be utilised, the Department submitted that
the additional allocation is for strengthening of social marketing in rural areas through NGOs.
FREE DISTRIBUTION
10.2. The allocation for `Free Distribution of Conventional Contraceptives’ has been increased from Rs.92 crore last
year to Rs.107.50 crore this year. To a specific query as to the manner of utilisation of funds and about the areas of
coverage, the Department stated that under this scheme, conventional contraceptives are supplied through all
PHCs/ANMs in the country since a long time and hence no area is left uncovered. The marginal enhancement in the
allocation is because of more requirement projected by the States and also due to the increase in the cost of
contraceptives and better packaging specifications for condoms.
10.3. The Committee notes that budget allocation on both free and commercial distribution of contraceptives has not
been fully utilised during the period 1996-99 as the expenditure is dependent on the demand for the items made by the
State Governments. The Committee is constrained to note that the contraception coverage as on 31
st March,
1998 for condoms was only 10.1% of the eligible males and that for oral pills it was only 3.8% of the eligible
females. The Committee feels that for stable population, this needs to be increased many times in the next few
months. The Committee emphasises that priority should be accorded to the identification of uncovered areas
particularly in States lagging behind and subsequent distribution of contraceptives in active coordination with
local community and Panchayati Raj Institutions.
10.4. The Committee was given to understand that free distribution of contraceptives has already reached a
saturation point and it is not preferred by the Department due to lot of wastage involved. The Committee,
therefore, fails to understand the reasons for increase in the allocation for free distribution of contraceptives in
1999-2000.
XI. NATIONAL POPULATION POLICY
11.1. The Draft National Population Policy prepared by the Swaminathan Committee was presented to the Parliament
in June, 1994. However, the policy has not yet been finalised. Asked about the latest position, the Department stated
that the draft has been suitably modified which was considered by the Cabinet in its meeting held on 3
rd March, 1999.
A Group of Ministers has been formed by the Cabinet to first look at the draft. The Committee hopes that an early
decision on the draft will be taken.
XII. AREA PROJECTS
12.1. To improve health and family welfare delivery system in certain identified backward districts of the country so
as to hasten their development at par with nation’s average, Area Projects have been taken up with partial foreign
assistance from external agencies.
12.2. Details regarding allocation of funds and expenditure incurred during 1997-98 and 1998-99 are as follows:-
(Rs.in crores)
1. 1998-99
(Anticipated)

BE RE Actuals BE RE Actuals
150.00 107.00 43.70 120.00 60.00 50.00
Allocation for 1999-2000 stands at Rs.100 crore.
12.3. Asked to explain the reasons for this variation and the backward districts identified under this programme, the
Department stated that despite its efforts, most States were slow in implementation of Area Projects. Low expenditure
was due to low absorption capacity of the States. The Committee would like to be apprised about these States.
12.4. The demographically backward districts being covered under the programme are Nalbari, Dhubri, Karimganj,
Darrang and Barpeta of Assam, Mandya, Bellary, Hassan, Mysore and Shimoga of Karnataka, Pali, Barmer, Jalore,
Jaisalmer, Bhilwara and Sawai Madhopur of Rajasthan, Dhule, Gadchirol, Chandrapur, Bhiwandi and Ulhasnagar of
Maharashtra, Malappuram of Kerala, Dharampuri and Qaid-E-Milleth of Tamilnadu and Badrak and Keonjhar of
Orissa, the Department informed.
12.5. The Committee, is of the opinion, that there is no point in implementing the programme and for
sanctioning more projects, if the states are not in a position to implement the same effectively. There is a need
for frequent interaction between representatives of State Governments and Centre to identify the bottlenecks
coming in the way of effective implementation of `Area Projects’ Programme and take remedial measures. The
Committee also desires that a survey be conducted in these backward districts to know the impact of the
programme in improving the health and family delivery system.
XIII. INNNOVATIONS IN FAMILY PLANNING SERVICES PROJECT FOR U.P.
13.1. To bring down total fertility rate in U.P. from 5.4 to 4.0 and to increase the Couple Protection Rate from 35% to
50%, an agreement was signed with USAID for a 10 year project which was initiated in 1992-93. A provision of
Rs.70.00 crores has been made for this project this year against an allocation of Rs.60.00 crores made last year.
13.2. To a specific query as to whether any mid-term review of the project has been made, the Department stated that
a team from the USAID undertook a mid-term assessment of the project over the period July-August, 1997. The Mid-
term assessment report has commended the progress made so far. The report also makes observations about the need
to improve contraceptive logistics, partnership with NGOs, and expanding the Social and Commercial marketing of
contraceptives.
13.3. The Committee hopes that timely action will be taken on the observations made by the USAID team.
XIV. REPRODUCTIVE AND CHILD HEALTH PROGRAMME
14.1. For improving the effectiveness of Family Welfare Programme, the programme for mother and child care was
reorganized in 1997 in the form of Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) Programme. The programme aims to meet
the unmet needs of Family Welfare Programme by improving health status of women and children, especially the poor
and undeserved, by reducing Infant, Child and Maternal mortality and morbidity through:-
a. Sustaining and strengthening the ongoing Child Survival and Safe Motherhood Programme to ensure the
essential services as per package of services;
b. Improve the performance of the Family Welfare system in implementing policy change;
c. Strengthen the quality and effectiveness of the services under essential package of Reproductive and Child
Health Services; and
d. Improve project implementation through the application of performance-based criteria for continued
funding.
14.2. The Department stated that the allocation for the project in BE 1998-99 was Rs.758 crore which was decreased
to Rs.603 crore at RE stage. It has been raised to Rs.676.80 crore in BE 1999-2000. On being asked, how the
provision will be utilised, the Secretary stated that even though RCH was launched in October, 1997 it could be

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/87repfw.htm[01-07-2016 15:10:52]
started in full pace only from April, 1998. The key strategy of the programme is to weld the vertical services into a
unified programme, covering the family welfare sector and also to establish linkages with other allied sectors so as to
achieve proper inter-sectoral coordination for bringing about a sustained improvement in primary health care, the
Committee was informed.
14.3. Further elaborating on the programme, the Secretary stated that MMR in the country is 437 per 100,000 live
births which is unacceptably high and the main thrust of the programme is, therefore, towards expanding the scope
and improving the quality and availability of services in the area of women’s health. Under the programme, a number
of programmes and schemes have been formulated and operationalised for tackling the specific causes for high
maternal mortality and morbidity in the country. The outlines of the various RCH schemes were circulated among the
States, seeking specific proposals. A number of proposals in every State have already been sanctioned. Particular
mention must be made of such schemes as Referral transportation through panchayat level institutions; facilitating
round the clock delivery services by providing additional inputs and facilities to the rural hospitals; for engaging
doctors on a contractual basis in PHCs for conducting MTPs, the services of private anaesthesiasts in emergency
obstetric care, etc.
14.4. The Secretary further stated that the low state of institutional delivery (less than 30 per cent according to the
NFHS survey 1992) has been one of the major causes for high maternal mortality. So developing and equipping PHCs
for handling deliveries on a larger scale and the FRUs for handling complicated deliveries is a major task under the
RCH. Apart from training and contractual appointments, Government is also providing drug and equipment support to
both the FRUs, primary health centres and the sub-centre on a wide scale.
14.5. No doubt, the goals set to be achieved are laudable but the Committee feels apprehensive about the
achievement level if the programme is not monitored properly. The Committee is, therefore, of the opinion that
a Monitoring Committee consisting of the Central and State Government officials be set up for better
implementation of the programme.
XV. PULSE POLIO
15.1. Briefing the Committee about Pulse Polio campaign, the Secretary stated that in 1998-99, in order to
achieve the WHO mandated global goal of reaching polio eradication by 2000 A.D., the Government has
intensified the Pulse Polio Immunisation Programme. Even though more than 100 per cent was reported
coverage every year, it was found that about 8% of children were still left out. Therefore, the Government made
special efforts by supplementing the booth immunisation with house to house search and also through
surveillance efforts. The Cabinet has also approved a proposal for launching additional rounds covering the
whole States of U.P., Bihar, M.P. and Rajasthan as the performance of these States had come down
considerably, the Department informed.
15.2. The Committee hopes that by these measures the Department will be able to achieve zero incidence
of poliomyelitis by the end of the millennium.
XVI. NEW INITIATIVES
16.1. Elaborating on the new initiatives taken the Secretary stated that the Department has launched a scheme for
setting up drug storage centres on a regional basis in all major States and to improve the logistics of supply from the
storage point to the health institutions. The proposal which is being jointly funded by the World Bank, European
Commission and UNFPA is currently under circulation for consideration in the EFC. The Committee hopes the EFC
will clear the project at the earliest.
16.2. Among the other new initiatives taken is the launching of Urban Measles Campaign. A special drive for
elimination of Neo Natal Tetanus has been also launched in Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh. The Government proposes
to intensify these campaigns in the coming year. The Committee hopes these initiatives will yield the desired
results.

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA

XVII. COLD CHAIN EQUIPMENTS
17.1. A large cold chain system has been established under the immunisation programme since its inception which
consists of a series of transportation and storage facilities for carrying vaccines from the manufacturers to the
beneficiaries. The equipments being used for storage, distribution and transportation of the vaccines are walk-in-
Coolers (WIC), Walk-in-Freezers (WIF), Ice-lined refrigerators, Deep Freezers, Cold Boxes, Vaccine carriers and day
carriers and Refrigerated vans and Vaccine delivery vans.
17.2. The Department submitted that new equipments are to be provided to PHCs and CHCs which have not been
provided so far. In addition, equipments which have broken down or require frequent repair need to be replaced.
Further, additional population to the extent it has grown since 1985 will need additional storage facilities for vaccines.
A sum of Rs.50 crores has been provided for procurement and replacement of Cold Chain Equipments this year.
17.3. The Committee feels that priority may be given for the replacement of existing equipments and thereafter
new equipments may be provided.
XVIII. GENERAL
18.1. As per the Audit Reports made available to the Committee, financial irregularities during the period 1995-98
have been noticed as detailed below:-
96. Rs.5033.35 lakhs
97. Rs.2299.61 lakhs
98. Rs.4255.23 lakhs
18.2. Main items in which irregularities have been noticed for all the three years are:-
i. expenditure in excess of the prescribed central pattern of assistance on pay and allowances of the staff
engaged on Family Welfare Programmes, maintenance of sterilisation wards, compensation scheme,
purchase of drugs etc.
ii. misutilisation of `Miscellaneous Purpose Funds’ meant for utilising for vital activities concerning Family
Welfare Programme.
iii. Expenditure on defunct training schools.
iv. Infructuous expenditure on payment of honorarium under the Village Health Guide Scheme etc.
18.3. Taking a serious view of the matter, the Committee notes that such a situation prevailing for continuous
three years is the real indicator of the status of Family Welfare Programme in our country. The Committee
apprehends that financial irregularities as pointed out in the Audit Reports may be in respect of States not
performing well. If that be so, the matter needs to be seriously looked into. The Committee recommends that
the Department should approach the concerned States without delay and take all possible corrective measures.
XIX. Committed Liability
19.1. While examining the Demands for Grants 1997-98 of the Departments under its purview, the Committee noted
that the committed liability of the Plan Schemes has not been reflected in the budgetary allocations.
19.2. The Committee, in this, connection considered the report of the Tenth Finance Commission. The Tenth Finance
Commission have observed in this regard as under:-
"Although the Tenth Finance Commission have gone by their terms of reference in deciding
the cut off date for transfer of committed liability on account of plan scheme, the
incremental liabilities that would arise in 1997-98 on account of 8
th Plan scheme completed
in the next two financial years would have to be provided for. The Commission are,

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/87repfw.htm[01-07-2016 15:10:52]
therefore, of the view that the Planning Commission may consider providing for the
maintenance of such scheme till 1999-2000 in the Plan itself as was done for the schemes of
the two Annual Plans of 1990-91 and 1991-92".
19.3. The Committee also sought clarifications from the then Secretary (Expenditure). He informed the Committee
that even though communications were sent to various Ministries, the Ministries could not identify the committed
expenditure on time. Accordingly a lumpsum amount has been provided under Demand No. 31. The Secretary also
assured that if required, more funds for this purpose will be provided at the RE stage. He also stated that the
Departments may approach the Department of Expenditure for their share.
19.4. The Committee, accordingly, directed the Department to approach the Ministry of Finance in this regard.
However, while considering the Demands for Grants 1998-1999, the Committee noticed that no progress in this regard
seemed to have taken place. The Committee, therefore, reiterated its stand. In spite of the Departments initiating some
exercise, the matter could not be sorted out. The Committee, therefore, heard the Secretary (Expenditure) on 27
th
March, 1999.
19.5. The Secretary, while deposing before the Committee, submitted that at the end of the 8th Five Year Plan the
Planning Commission issued very detailed guidelines to carry forward the committed expenditure from plan to the non
plan side. The Ministry of Finance (Budget Division) also issued a letter to all the Financial Advisors of the
Department requesting them to indicate the amount to be included from plan to non plan.
19.6. The Secretary submitted that as on 10th February, 1997, 24 Ministries/Departments responded indicating a figure
of Rs.450.28 crore. However, some Ministries/Departments like Education, Culture, Women and Child Development
did not respond. Accordingly a lumpsum provision of Rs.500 crores in the Ministry of Finance Budget was
provided for this purpose. As a result of this exercise, a sum of Rs.150 crores was indeed transferred from plan
to non plan for the various Ministries as committed expenditure during the year, on the basis of scrutiny with
reference to the Planning Commission’s guidelines. The rest of the amount was surrendered as the proposals
were not found acceptable.
19.7. The Secretary agreed in principle that whatever is the committed expenditure, it should be transferred
from plan to non plan. Otherwise the plan has no meaning.
19.8. The Secretary assured that the proposals pertaining to UGC (Rs.27 crores) and Department of Education
(Rs. 80 crores) which were under consideration would be cleared. Moreover, the Tenth Finance Commission
Report has given a breathing time till 1999-2000 for this transition.
19.9. The Committee would like to impress that the real picture should be projected before Parliament.
19.10. The Secretary also apprised the Committee that another Sub Committee has been appointed by the
NDC, consisting of representatives from seven states and Ministry of Finance. This Sub-Committee will look
into the structural distortions which have entered into the finances of the states on account of 5
th Pay
Commission and to suggest a suitable package linked to fiscal reforms.
19.11. The Committee observes that a similar problem exists in the case of Central Ministries also. The
Committee, therefore, desires that a similar exercise be carried out in the case of Central Ministries also.

REPORT
INTRODUCTION
1.1. The National Health Policy  of  1983 visualised the importance of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy
and its role in the national health care system.    People of our Country have faith in the traditional systems especially
when the services provided are cheaper and available in  very  small  place  and rural areas.  Moreover, the remedies are
free from side-effects.  India has  a  large resource  of ISM&H practitioners of Homoepathy whose services need to be
fully utilised in the national health care delivery  system.    For this  purpose,  a  new  Department  of  Indian Systems of
Medicine and  Homoeopathy (ISM&H) has been set up to promote and develop the  Indian systems of Medicine
(Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, Homoeopathy and drugless Therapies like  Yoga  and  Naturopathy). 
II BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
2.1. The total allocation, both Plan and Non-Plan  taken  together, provided to  the Department for the year 1998-99 was
Rs.  85.60 crores  in BE which was enhanced to 89.12 crores at RE stage.    The  Committee  has  observed  that  the 
increase at the RE stage in 1998-99 was made only in Non-Plan head i.e.  from Rs.  36.60  crores  to  40.12 crores. 
2.2. On a specific query regarding amount sought by the Department for 1999-2000, the Committee was informed that
an  amount of Rs.  106.88 crores (Rs.   63.45  crores Plan  + Rs.  43.43 crores Non-Plan) was sought and the approved
amount was Rs.  100.96 crores (Rs.  59.13 crores Plan  +  Rs.    41.83 crores  Non Plan).  Thus there is an increase of
Rs. 15.36 crores in 1999-2000 as compared to the allocation made in BE 1998-99. 
2.3 The Committee notes that Plan allocation of Rs. 260 crores for the Department for Ninth Plan is at a considerably
enhanced level when compared to Eighth Plan allocation of Rs. 104.44 crores.  However, the fact remains that it is
much below the projected requirements of the Department.    The Department of ISM&H’s share of Plan allocation has
remained about 3.4% of the total health sector allocation.  If various systems under ISM&H have to develop properly,
there is a need for substantial higher allocation of funds for the Department.   Reduction  of  amount particularly  under 
plan head could severely affect the activities of the Department aimed at development of the ISM&H. The Committee
therefore recommends that Plan allocation made for the  year 1999-2000 should be increased at RE stage. 
 
III. AYURVEDA
3.1. The allocation  for  Ayurveda under Plan in BE 1998-99 was Rs. 10.54 crores which was enhanced to Rs. 13.16
crores at RE stage and again reduced to Rs. 12.09 crores in 1999-2000.    Explaining  the  reason for the uneven
increase/decrease in the plan allocation for Ayurveda,  the  Department  submitted  that  it  was  mainly due  to  
payment of arrears of salary and allowances  caused by implementation of Vth Pay Commission recommendations 
to      Ayurvedic Physicians  and  personnel.    The Department also submitted  that this additional liability was not
required to be   paid  during  1999-2000, hence the less provision. 
3.2 The Committee has noticed that there is a growing demand of Ayurveda treatment in the Western countries.  Some
private parties are reported to have shown interest in starting Ayurveda Health Care Centres so as to attract foreign
tourists.  The Committee is of the view that the Department should draw an action plan in this regard which will
popularise the Ayurvedic System of treatment in and outside India in due course  which in turn will attract more tourists.
3.3 Committee’s attention has also been drawn to a lot of misleading advertisements regarding some Ayurvedic
medicines which are not scientifically tested.   On a specific query as to what preventive action has been taken in this
regard, the Secretary informed that all the State Govts. have been requested to take stringent action in this regard. 
Action was also being taken for bringing about necessary amendments in the Magic Remedies Objectionable
Advertisements Act.  However, the Secretary admitted that there was a need for strengthening the drug control
administration at the state level.  The Committee is of the view that there is a need for building up a mechanism for
taking preventive action so that public at large is not misled. 
3.4 The Committee is aware that there are a number of persons who are doing some good work in the Ayurvedic system
of treatment.  However, due support for their achievements seems to be lacking.  The Committee strongly feels that the

88rep
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/88rep.html[01-07-2016 15:10:53]
Department should make all concerted efforts to give due recognition and provide financial support to deserving
practitioners.
IV. UNANI
4.1   Under  the allocation for the Unani System, Plan provision was reduced from Rs.  8.55 crores in BE 1998-99 to
Rs.  6.98 crores in the RE.  However,  an allocation  of Rs.  8.55 crores  has been made  in  BE  1999-2000. 
4.2. The Committee was informed that additional funds were allocated in 1998-99 for construction of buildings for
Regional  Research Institute of Unani Medicine at Srinagar and Karimganj and also for strengthening of RRIUM,
Hyderabad.  However, as these projects could not be started, amount of allocation had to be reduced at RE stage in
1998-99.  The Committee finds that approval of the appropriate authority is awaited for RRIUM, Srinagar.  For
RRIUM, Hyderabad and Karimganj, estimates are being obtained from the concerned authorities.  The Committee
hopes that necessary formalities will be completed at the earliest and the projects will not be delayed further. 
4.3. The Committee has been informed  that in view of the change in the  objective and the funding pattern, fresh
approval of EFC has become necessary for National Institute of Unani Medicine, Bangalore.  The Committee would like
to impress upon the Department to expedite the procedural requirements so that construction work of the main building
of  NIUM, Bangalore is started without any further delay.
V. HOMOEOPATHY
5.1. For Homoeopathy, the  plan provision was Rs. 6.77 crores in BE 1998-99 which was increased to Rs. 7.02 crores at
RE stage.  In BE of 1999-2000 it has been reduced to the level of Rs. 6.27 crores.  When the Department was asked to
explain the reason for these variations, it was informed that in the RE 1998-99, a provision of Rs. 7.02 crores was made
primarily to meet the arrears on amount of salary and allowances  to Homoeopathy physicians/personnel.   Since this
additional  liability is not to be paid during 1999-2000,  less provision has been made. 
5.2. The Committee notes that the increase of bed capacity for in-patient department of National Institute of
Homoeopathy, Calcutta has been linked up with the introduction of post graduate course in homoepathy which  is going
to commence from Feb, 1999. Last year, the Committee had suggested that research on detoxication  of arsenic
poisoning being conducted by NIH, Calcutta should be intensified as this problem had severely affected West Bengal. 
The Committee is happy to note that NIH has submitted a project costing Rs. 14.04 lakhs under the Department’s extra
mural research scheme and an amount of Rs. 6 lakhs has already been sanctioned during 1998-99 for this research.  The
Committee hopes that the research will be completed within the stipulated time.
VI. YOGA AND NATUROPATHY
6.1. For Yoga and Naturopathy the BE for 1998-99 on the plan side was Rs. 3.95 crores, which was reduced to Rs. 3.63
crores at the RE stage.  However, it has been increased substantially to Rs. 6.20 crores in  BE 1999-2000.  When asked
to justify the same, the Department explained that enhanced allocation is on account of construction of building  for
Morarji Desai National Institute of Yoga (MDNIY).  During 1999-2000, an amount of Rs. 325.00 lakhs has been
earmarked to accelerate the construction work. 
6.2. The Committee, however, notes  that in the year 1998-99, the provision of Rs. 170.00 lakh for the purpose could not
be utilised resulting in no expenditure upto to Feb, 1999.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that effective action
should be taken for completion of construction work of the building of the Institute. 
6.3. The Committee has been given to understand that the Institute propose to undertake experimental study on the
effect of yoga in alcohol intake and the research project in this regard has been submitted for seeking grant in aid from
W.H.O.  The Committee desires that the project should be cleared as early as possible. 
6.4. Last year the Committee recommended that Yoga be taught in schools right from the primary level.  The
Committee finds that the response of the Department of Education is awaited. The Committee recommends that the
Department should pursue the matter with the Department of Education. 
6.5. The Committee was informed last year that comprehensive project report for the establishment of the National
Institute of Naturopathy, Pune will be placed before EFC.  However the Committee is pained to note that the approval
of the EFC is yet to be obtained.  The Committee in this connection has also noted that an expenditure of Rs. 36.50
lakhs could be made  against provision of Rs. 75 lakhs.  The Committee feels that this is not a happy situation and there
is a need to expedite the matter to avoid under-utilisation of the provision made for the year 1999-2000.

General 
6.6. The Committee has been given to understand that certain positive achievements have been made in the treatment of 
Cancer by some ISM&H practitioners specially in Homoeopathy and Ayurveda.  The Committee feels that the
department should provide due patronage to the deserving cases. 
VII. MEDICAL EDUCATION 
7.1. At present, there are 311 undergraduate and 47 postgraduate ISMH colleges  in the country.  In order to improve the
standard of education in these institutions, the Department has  adopted multi pronged strategy:- 
i) To set up model ISM&H Educational Institutes under the Department with the modern facilities and to maintain very
high standard of Education;
ii) To provide financial assistance to improve UG & PG ISM&H colleges run by State Govts./NGOs/Semi Govt.
organisations; and 
 
iii) To establish statutory regulatory bodies to regulate the education by laying down the minimum standards of
education and curriculum and register the practitioner of these systems.
7.2. Last year, the Committee was informed that views of the State Govts. have been sought by the Central Council of
Indian Medicine on norms for establishing a new Ayurveda  college/prescribing the minimum standard for the existing
colleges.  However, the Committee is constrained to note that the views of the State Govts. are yet to be received. 
Position with regard to Homoeopathy education is more worrying as no action seems to be initiated by the Central
Council of Homoeopathy so far.  The Committee would like to reiterate its earlier recommendation that speedy action is
called for checking the growth of sub-standard colleges and also for having the minimum standard of education in the
existing colleges. 
7.3. Regarding para- medical education in pharmacy and Nursing, the Department informed the Committee that they
have proposed to introduce a scheme as an add-on component to the existing schemes of improving and strengthening
of the existing UG colleges of ISMH for  financial assistance for setting up of pharmacy/nursing education.  Pharmacy
Council of India and Nursing Council of India were approached for making suitable modifications/amendments in their
Acts for facilitating introduction of pharmacy and nursing education in Ayurveda, Homoeopathy, Unani and Siddha
systems.  Though the response from the Nursing Council was encouraging, the Pharmacy Council has shown their
inability.  Setting up of a separate Pharmacy Council is therefore under-examination, the Committee was informed.  The
Committee hopes that these issues would be decided without further delay. 
7.4. So far as  teaching of yoga and naturopathy is concerned, the Department informed that the task of regulating
education in Yoga and Naturopathy has not yet been entrusted to the Central Council for Research in Yoga and
Naturopathy.  Setting up of a regulatory body for education in Yoga and Naturopathy was under active examination of
the Department.  The Committee therefore, recommends that a separate regulatory body be formed at the earliest so that
research activities in yoga and Naturopathy are fostered. 
7.5. Regarding need to check huge amounts of donation/capitation fee being taken by some colleges under ISM&H, the
Committee was informed that a fee structure to be charged by private colleges as per guidelines of Supreme Court
Orders is being finalised actively and the schemes submitted by the respective Councils on fee-structures in Private
Professional ISM&H colleges have been returned to the Councils for taking opinion from the State Governments.  The
Committee recommends that the Department should pursue the matter with State Govts. so as to finalise this issue at the
earliest. 
7.6 The Committee was informed that 30 institutions have been identified to impart training under RCH programme of
Department of Family Welfare to ISM&H physicians and Para- Medics and Director ISM&H of State Governments and
other personnel.  During the year 1997-98, 2310 professionals have been trained and during 1998-99, 1450 professionals
have been trained upto February, 1999.    The Committee appreciates the initiative taken by the Department.
VIII. POOR QUALITY OF DRUGS 
8.1. In view of the Committee it is necessary to prescribe standards for ensuring efficacy of ISM&H drugs  and also for
checking their  genuineness and purity in the market  as there is general skepticism about the quality of ISM&H drugs. 
The Committee was informed that the Department was giving higher priority for standardization of drugs.  It has been
resolved that the standardisation work on drug may be completed during the Ninth Plan period.  On a specific query as
to what progress has been made so far, the Department informed as under :-

(i) The Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia Committee has approved 78 monographs on single drugs titled as  Ayurvedic
Pharmacopoeia of India (Part I, Volume II) which is expected to be published during 1999-2000. 
A further 100 monographs have been approved for inclusion in Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (Part I, Volume III) 
(ii) 32 laboratories/institutions are engaged for developing Pharmacopoeial standards of ISM drugs and out of the  387
single drugs allocated to them, data on 100 drugs has been generated.
(iii) Drug standardisation work on 915 homoeopathic single drugs have been finalised.  Standards on 710 homoeopathic
drugs have already been published.
8.2. The Committee has also noted that at present two drug testing laboratories are providing the technical back up to
these Pharmacopoeial Committees and it is proposed to strengthen these laboratories.  There is also a need for setting up
of Regional Drug Testing Laboratories.  In order to accelerate the work of  evolving of standards, 31 Research
Institutions’ laboratories have been provided financial assistance for working on the standards for 10 drugs per year. 
8.2. The Committee hopes that the Department would be able to complete the standardisation work of drugs by Ninth
Plan period and recommend that for this purpose, sufficient funds should be provided to the Department. 
VIII. NON-AVAILABILITY OF HERBS AND MEDICINAL PLANTS 
9.1 80 % of ISMH drugs are based on medicinal plants.  However, due to over exploitation, unscrupulous collection and
denuding of forests, which are the source of medicinal plants, supplies have been dwindling.  The Department informed
the Committee that it has initiated various steps to enhance the supplies of medicinal plants. These are conservation and
preservation of medicinal plants through in situ and ex-situ cultivation, developing tissue culture, storage in gene banks,
developing large-scale gardens of medicinal plants in coordination with concerned Ministries/Departments. A special
scheme to provide assistance to research organizations for development of agro-techniques has also been introduced.  26
such organizations are participating in the scheme and 97 species of plants have been allotted to them. A component of
R&D  has also been included under the scheme to achieve better result. The  Department further informed that setting
up of a National Board for Medicinal plants is under consideration and a budget provision of Rs. 1.00 Crores  has been
provided for the purpose. The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the department and hopes that desired results
would be achieved in this regard.
X INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY RIGHTS
10.1. The Department informed the Committee that a major area of concern is the keen interest being taken by foreign
countries in the development of herbal products and intellectual  property rights. Some of the well known medicinal
plants of India has been patented abroad and heritage of Ayurveda needs to be protected. There is also a lot of
traditional folklore which also needs to be protected. In order to put a check on these attempts, a patent Cell has been set
up in the Department. 
10.2. The Department  vide its ATR on 70th Report of the Committee submitted that to make Patent Cell more viable, a
detailed proposal has been submitted to the Finance Division for creation of posts under various groups. 
10.3 The Committee is constrained to note that that the Patent Cell is still functioning  with inadequate manpower and
various posts are lying vacant. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the vacant posts should be filled up
without further delay. The Committee would also like that the Patent Cell should work in close coordination with other
concerned Departments/ Agencies.
XI. Committed Liability
11.1. While examining the Demands for Grants 1997-98 of the Departments under its purview, the Committee noted
that the committed liability of the Plan Schemes has not been reflected in the budgetary allocations. 
11.2. The Committee, in this, connection considered the report of the Tenth Finance Commission.  The Tenth Finance
Commission have observed in this regard as under:- 
“Although  the Tenth Finance Commission have gone by their terms of reference in deciding the cut off date for transfer
of committed liability on account of plan scheme, the  incremental liabilities that would arise in 1997-98 on account of
8th Plan scheme completed in the next two financial years would have to be provided for.  The Commission are,
therefore, of the view that the Planning Commission may consider providing for the maintenance of such scheme till
1999-2000 in the Plan itself as was done for the schemes of the two Annual Plans of 1990-91 and 1991-92”. 
11.3. The Committee also sought clarifications from the then Secretary (Expenditure).  He informed the Committee that

even though communications were sent to various Ministries, the Ministries could not identify the committed
expenditure on time.  Accordingly a lumpsum amount has been provided under Demand No. 31.  The Secretary also
assured that if required, more funds for this purpose will be provided at the RE stage.  He also stated that the
Departments may approach the Department of Expenditure for their share. 
11.4. The Committee, accordingly, directed the Department to approach the Ministry of Finance in this regard. 
However, while considering the Demands for Grants 1998-1999, the Committee noticed  that no progress in this regard
seemed to have taken place. The Committee, therefore, reiterated its stand.  In spite of the Departments initiating some
exercise, the matter could not be sorted out.  The Committee, therefore, heard the Secretary (Expenditure) on 27th
March, 1999. 
11.5. The Secretary, while deposing before the Committee, submitted that at the end of the 8th Five Year Plan the
Planning Commission issued very detailed guidelines to carry forward the committed expenditure from plan to the non
plan side.  The Ministry of Finance (Budget Division) also issued a letter to all the Financial Advisors of the Department
requesting them to indicate the amount to be  included from plan to non plan. 
11.6. The Secretary submitted that as on 10th February, 1997, 24 Ministries/Departments responded indicating a figure
of Rs.450.28 crore. However, some   Ministries/Departments like  Education, Culture, Women and Child Development
did not respond.  Accordingly a lumpsum provision of Rs.500 crores in the Ministry of Finance Budget  was provided
for this purpose. As a result of this exercise, a sum of Rs.150 crores was indeed transferred from plan to non plan for the
various Ministries as committed expenditure during the year, on the basis of scrutiny with reference to the Planning
Commission’s guidelines.   The rest of the amount was surrendered as the proposals were not found acceptable. 
11.7. The Secretary agreed in principle that whatever is the committed expenditure,  it should be transferred from plan
to non plan.  Otherwise the plan has no meaning. 
11.8. The Secretary assured that the proposals pertaining to UGC (Rs.27 crores) and Department of Education (Rs. 80
crores) which were under consideration would be cleared.  Moreover, the Tenth Finance Commission Report has given
a breathing time till 1999-2000 for this transition.   The Committee  would like to impress that the real picture should be

11.10. The Committee observes that a similar problem exists in the case of Central Ministries also.  The Committee,
therefore, desires that a similar exercise be carried out in the case of Central Ministries also.

PREFACE
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this
Hundred  Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants (Demand No.42) of the Department of Health,  Ministry
of Health and Family Welfare for the year 2000-2001.
 
2.         The Committee considered the various documents and relevant papers received from the Department of Health
and also heard the Secretary and other Officials of that Department  on the said Demands for Grants in its meeting held
on 28
th   March, 2000.
 
3.         The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same in its meeting held on 15th  April, 2000.
 
NEW DELHI;
 April  15, 2000
 Chairman
Chaitra 26,   1922 (Saka)
 
S.B. CHAVAN
 Department-related ParliamentaryStanding Committee
on
 Human Resource Development
 
 
REPORT
I           INTRODUCTION    
1.1              The main objectives of the Department of Health are:-
 
(i)         to undertake national programmes of health and to intensify measures for the prevention, control and
eradication of communicable diseases;
(ii)        to promote education, research and training in various medical disciplines, to reorient the medical
colleges in the delivery of health services in rural areas;
(iii)       to prevent adulteration of food as well as drugs;
(iv)       to provide primary health care at the doorsteps of the people and to train the required number of
personnel for this purpose;
(v)        to take steps for better implementation of Health Care Programmes for tribal and other weaker sections
of the Society; and
(vi)       to collaborate with  member countries of United Nations and International Agencies like WHO,
UNICEF in matters relating to health promotion.
1.2       The Department of Health incurs expenditure either directly or through various institutions and establishments
run by it and by way of grants given to autonomous and voluntary organisations.  Grants to States and Union Territory
Administrations are mainly for Centrally Sponsored Health Schemes being implemented through the State Governments
and Union Territory Administrations.  They include national programmes for prevention, control and eradication of
diseases.
1.3       The Department finances, wholly or substantially, the following autonomous institutions engaged in patient care
and/ or research:
 
(i)         All India Institute of Medical Sciences and Dr. Rajendra Prasad Centre for Ophthalmic Sciences,  New
Delhi;
(ii)        Post-Graduate Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh; 
(iii)       All India Institute of Speech and Hearing Sciences, Mysore; and
            (iv)       Indian Council of Medical Research, New Delhi.

89th Report On Committee On HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/89threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:11:09]
 
1.4       The Centrally-Sponsored Health Schemes are financed by the Central Government on either 100 percent or 50
per cent basis. The following Schemes are financed by the Central Government on 100 per cent basis:
 
(i)         National Scheme for Prevention of Visual Impairment and Blindness including Trachoma;
(ii)        National Leprosy Eradication Programme;
(iii)       National Guinea-worm Eradication Programme;
(iv)       National AIDS Control Programme.
The Schemes on which the expenditure is shared between the Central Government and State Government on 50:50 basis
are:-
(i)         National Malaria Eradication Programme (Rural and Urban);
(ii)        National Sexually Transmitted Diseases Control Programme;
(iii)       National T.B. Control Programme; and
(iv)
              Kala-Azar Control Programme.
 
II.        BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.1       A Budgetary provision of Rs. 2167.86 crores has been made for the Department of Health for 2000-2001.  Rs.
1277.86 crores is the Plan component and Rs. 890.00 crores have been provided under Non-Plan.
2.2       On a specific query as to the projected requirements of the Department for 2000-2001, the Department submitted
that as against the original projected demand of Rs. 1350 crores, the amount finally approved is Rs. 1300 crores
(including a component of Rs. 22.14 crores  under Capital Works). The requirements originally proposed for Annual
Plan 2000-2001  were keeping in view the Ninth  Plan priorities and likely  expenditure.   The major programmes/
institutions where outlays have been reduced following reduction by the Planning Commission are Malaria, TB, AIDS,
Cancer and the National Institute of Biologicals (NIB).
2.3       The Committee has been given to understand that there has been no substantial increase in the allocation for
health sector.   The Committee notes that out of the total investment of 6% of GDP for the health sector, 1.3% is
contributed by the State sector, i.e. the State Governments and the Central Government.   However, due to the
constraint-ridden financial position of majority of the States, there has not been any major addition to the Plan outlay of
the State Governments.   The Committee is of the opinion that  in view of the weak financial position of majority of the
States the  Central Government has no other alternative but to bear the main responsibility in this regard.
2.4       The Committee, at the same time, is also distressed to note that the Department has not been able to utilise the
funds allocated to it for the past few years.   The Committee finds that allocations made are invariably being reduced at
the RE stage and even this reduced allocation is not fully utilised.   Provision of Rs. 2361.69 crores was made in 1998-
99 which was reduced to Rs. 2067.56 crores.   Actual  expenditure is  only Rs. 1901.69 crores.   Similarly, provision of
Rs. 2449.23 crores in BE 1999-2000 has been reduced to Rs. 2231.88 crores at the RE stage.   Details of actual
expenditure  when made available would again indicate under-utilisation of allocations.   The Committee finds that
maximum saving is due to surrender of funds under EAC component of various National Health Programmes in 1997-
98 and 1998-99.   The Committee takes a serious view of this.
2.5       In fact, it is an irony that on one hand we have funds constraint and on the other whatever allocation is made,
despite funds constraint, is not fully utilised.   The Committee is of the considered view that this is one of the reasons for
non-effective and improper implementation of most of the schemes in our country.  Last year, the Committee had
extensively dwelt on this issue and had observed that the Department of Health, being the nodal agency, has to take
remedial steps.  The Committee would like to be apprised about the measures  taken by the Department. The Committee
would also like to know about the utilization of fund under EAC component of various National Health   Programes
during 1999-2000. 
2.6       The Committee has been informed that foreign direct investment  (FDI) upto 10%  is allowed in health sector.  
FDI policy has been further liberalised thereby putting almost all items/activities except a small negative list under the
automatic route.   Further, a special Subject Group to look into the policy framework for private investment in
Education, Health and Rural Development has been recently re-constituted by the Prime Minister.   The Committee

89th Report On Committee On HRD

hopes that these initiatives would result in greater and meaningful cooperation and participation between the private and
public sector.
2.7       Performance Budget should clearly reflect both the financial provision and corresponding physical achievements
of different schemes/programmes during the financial year.  The Committee, however, observes that Performance
Budgets of almost all the Departments are prepared in such a manner that one does not get a clear  idea in this regard. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the department should take corrective steps in this regard, if the
Performance Budgeting is to have any meaning.
III.      CENTRAL GOVERNMENT HEALTH SCHEME(CGHS)
3.1       Rs. 10  crores have been provided under Plan for CGHS for  2000-2001 against an allocation of Rs. 9 crores in
BE 1999-2000 reduced to Rs. 8 crores at the RE stage.  To a question as to  in what manner  this enhancement in budget
allocation is proposed to be utilized, the Department replied that the allocation is proposed to be utilized for the new
schemes based on the proposals contained in the Ninth Plan which included extension of CGHS to new cities and also
opening of dispensaries/polyclinics/ Labs. etc. in the existing CGHS cities.
3.2       The Committee observes  that during the Ninth Plan, it was targetted  to extend the CGHS  network  by covering

districts i.e. Bharatpur in Rajasthan and Sivaganga in Tamil Nadu in 1998-99 to assess the prevalence of blindness.

16.4     The Committee notes that under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, a Drug Inspector is required to inspect not less
than twice a year, all establishments licensed for sale/manufacture of drugs within the area assigned to him.  He is also
required to investigate complaints, take samples, initiate prosecution etc.   It was found that substantial time of the Drug
Inspectors and Supervisory Staff was being spent on routine renewal of licenses.  Therefore, a proposal has been
approved by the Drug Technical Advisory Board to increase  the initial licence period from 2 years to 5 years.   State
Drugs Controllers are also being requested to focus on proper intelligence gathering and random checking.
16.5     The Committee feels that increasing the initial period of licence cannot  be the alternative for the appointment of
more Drug Inspectors.  Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that specific steps should be taken by the
Department in coordination with the State Governments to strengthen the enforcement machinery for quality control of
drugs.
XVII.   NATIONAL ILLNESS ASSISTANCE FUND
17.1     National Illness Assistance Fund was set up on 17.1.97.  The Ministry is making a contribution to the corpus of
National Illness Assistance Fund every year for running its activities.  14 States and 6 UTs have set up the Fund so far.  
  The Committee notes that allocation of Rs.5.00 crores was made in 1999-2000 for setting up National Illness
Assistance Fund which was reduced to Rs.50 lakhs at the RE stage. Same allocation has been made for 2000-2001.
17.2     The Committee was informed that during 1999-2000, a provision of Rs.5 crores was made for National Illness
Assistance Fund. It was anticipated that 5 UTs  (without Legislatures) to whom allocation of Rs.50 lakhs each were
made during 1998-99, would utilize the fund and propose further allocation. The Medical Superintendents of six Central
Government Hospital/Institutes were also sanctioned an advance of Rs. 10 lakhs each as per directions of the then
Health Minister (Prime Minister).   However, inspite of repeated reminders, the utilization of funds by UTs (without
Legislatures) and Medical Superintendent of Hospital/Institute did not pick up to the desired level.  On a review of the
position, it was decided to reduce this provision from Rs.5 crores to Rs.50 lakhs for 1999-2000 at the revised estimate
stage.  A similar allocation has been proposed in BE for 2000-2001.
17.3     Drastic  reduction in the allocation at the RE stage is not the solution. The Committee is of the view that the
Department should pursue the matter with the concerned State Govts. Under the National Illness Assistance Fund, 
Central assistance is based on 50% of the State contribution.  The Committee feels that this is the major constraint in the
operation of this Fund.   State Govts., due to lack of resources, are not in a position to contribute their share of Funds.
XVIII.  COMMITTED LIABILITY
18.1     The issue of Committed Liability has been engaging the attention of the Committee since 1997-98.  At the end

89th Report On Committee On HRD

of the Eight Five Year Plan, the Planning Commission had issued very detailed guidelines to carry forward the
Committed Expenditure from Plan to the non-plan side.  A lump sum provision of Rs. 500 crores in the Ministry of
Finance Budget for 1997-98 was provided for this purpose.  As a result of this exercise, however, only a sum of Rs.150
crores was transferred from plan to non-plan for the various Ministries as committed expenditure during 1997-98.  Rest
of the amount was surrendered as the proposals were not found acceptable.  The Secretary (Expenditure) while deposing
before the Committee on 27
th March, 1999 had informed that the Tenth Finance Commission had given a breathing time
till 1999-2000 for this transition.
18.2     The Department has  informed that the matter was taken up with the Ministry of Finance who have desired that
the matter may be discussed in the pre-budget meeting.  
18.3     The Committee notes with serious concern that while grants for Plan Schemes are getting reduced, non-plan
allocation and expenditure are steadily increasing.  What is happening is that the committed expenditure which should
appropriately be charged to the Pool, is being passed on to the respective departments which is totally against the
guidelines of Tenth Finance Commission/Planning Commission.  If the committed expenditure is charged to the Pool, it
will not have any burden on the specific schemes of the Department. Secretary, (Expenditure), who appeared before the
Committee last year was in full agreement  with the stand taken by the Committee.  The Committee is, however,
constrained to observe that in spite of Committee’s repeated efforts/directives to assist the Departments, no progress has
been made in the matter.  It seems that breathing time till 1999-2000 given by the Tenth Finance Commission has not
been availed of by any Department.  There is total lack of initiative on the part of the Departments.  The Committee
again  emphasises that the department should get this matter resolved without any further delay.  The way the
Department including Ministry of Finance is trying to escape their responsibility is against the expressed wishes of the
Finance Commission and the recommendations made by the Committee.  This tendency, the Committee is constrained
to observe, is not in consonance with the principles which are well-established.  The Committee again reiterates that the
Department should pursue the matter and report to the Committee about the outcome thereof.
 
XIX.    GENERAL
19.1     The Committee had desired to know about the progress made on the recommendations made in its 78
th Report
on the ATR  on the functioning of CGHS relating to the following two matters:-
“(a)      The practice of reimbursement of only the package deal rates to the CGHS beneficiaries would defeat the
very purpose of the Government allowing CGHS beneficiaries to take treatment from private hospitals
recognised under CGHS.         
(b)        steps be taken for amending section 2(I)(o) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, and also to approach a
larger Bench of the Supreme Court which upheld `service’ rendered at a Government Hospital is outside
the purview of the expression `service’ under the Act.”
19.2     The Department has replied that the medical expenditure  to the Central Government employees/pensioners who
take treatment in private recognised hospitals under CGHS is being reimbursed at the rates fixed by the Government.  
The balance expenditure has to be borne by the beneficiaries themselves.  The Department have again  drawn the
attention of the Committee to  the judgement dated 26.2.98 of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of State of Punjab
versus Ram Lubhaya Bagga,  wherein it was decided by the Supreme Court that the Government has a right to fix the
rates of medical treatment  taken in private recognised hospitals keeping in view the limited resources available with
them and it does not violate Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution of India.  It has been further informed that the
beneficiaries who take treatment in Government hospitals like G.B.  Pant Hospital, AIIMS , Dr. RML Hospital,
Safdarjang Hospital and Lady Hardinge Medical College and Hospital are reimbursed full medical expenditure, except
the inadmissible items like TV Charges, telephone charges and diet charges, etc.
19.3     As regards the application of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 to the services rendered by the doctors of
Government hospitals/CGHS dispensaries, the Department of Consumer Affairs has intimated as under:-
“…… The intention of the Health Ministry is to provide an alternative forum for redressal of grievances of
patients who receive  free treatment at Government hospitals.   As you are aware, Civil Courts are already for
seeking redressal of such grievances but this procedure entails delay.   We are of the view that instead of the
Consumer Protection Act, it would be better that the Ministry of Health, being the administrative Ministry

having control over Government hospitals, may consider establishing an effective alternate redressal machinery
perhaps at individual hospitals so that grievances/genuine problem of patients are sorted out at that level without
either parties going to Court.   We feel  that this would be in the overall interest of public.   You may perhaps
like to examine this proposal.”
Accordingly, instructions have been given to the Additional Directors/Joint Directors/Deputy Directors of CGHS to the
effect that CMO In charge for holdings  periodical meetings to review/settle public grievance cases arising out of the
functioning of the dispensary.   The Additional Directors/Joint Directors/Deputy Directors of the concerned city are to
hold periodical meetings to review/settle public grievance cases.
19.4     The Committee is not convinced by the stand taken by the Department and  reiterates its earlier recommendation
regarding reimbursement of the expenses incurred by the CGHS beneficiaries on the treatment taken in recognised 
private hospitals.  The Committee finds that notwithstanding the fact that certain modifications have been made in the
procedure for referral to recognised hospitals and reimbursement of expenditure of medical treatment, patients are still
facing considerable difficulties.  The Committee is of the view that the Department should enter into arrangements with
the recognized private hospitals whereunder on the production of CGHS card, the hospital should provide treatment and
the bill (restricted to package rates) should be raised directly to the parent department/office/CGHS directorate as the
case may be.  The Committee feels that the Hospitals would have no objection if their bills are settled within a
reasonable period of time.  The Committee also feels that there should be periodical review at least once in three years
of the approved package rates, keeping in view the increase in the cost of medicines and other facilities.
19.5     The Committee  is of the view that  the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 should be made applicable to the
services rendered by doctors of Government Hospitals/CGHS Dispensaries.  Suggestion of the Department of Consumer
Affairs for establishment of an effective alternate redressal machinery is not acceptable to the Committee. The
Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation that the Department should take steps for amending the Consumer
Protection Act, 1986 and also approach a larger Bench of Supreme Court which upheld `service’ rendered at a
Government Hospital is outside the purview of the expression `service’ under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986.
19.6     The Committee notes with concern that some Departments are not furnishing the required information/papers
and Hindi version thereof sought by the Committee on time and sometimes the papers are not even properly arranged
and indexed.  This results in a lot of inconvenience to the Committee.  In such a situation the Members either get very
little time or no time at all to go through the papers and actively participate in the deliberations of the Committee. The
Committee is, therefore, constrained to observe that the communications sent to the Ministries or the Departments by
the Secretariat on behalf of the Committee should be given due attention and all efforts should be made to furnish the
requisite information/ paper and Hindi version thereof to the Committee expeditiously and within the time limit.

would like to be apprised about the measures  taken by the Department. The Committee would also like to know about
the utilization of fund under EAC component of various National Health   Programs  during 1999-2000. (Para 2.5)
