4.5.8 The Committee observe that development of Ultra Mega
Power Projects require support and coordination between the various
players involved i.e, the Central Government, State Governments,
PEC, project developers, Consultants, etc. Lack of support from any
of these players can lead to delay in the development of these
projects and as such can derail capacity addition programme and, in
turn, economic growth of the country as envisaged ~ because power
is the key driver for any growth agenda set for the country.

The Committee further observe with concern that the Ministry
of Power is facing some problems in finalisation of sites in States
such as Orisssa, Karnataka and Maharashtra. Though the Ministry
has stated that the State Electricity Boards and State Companies are
involved while the site is selected, the Committee, however, feel
that the involvement of the State Governments has just been a
formality. Central Electricity Authority (CEA) which had a major
role in selection of sites did not seem to have given a serious thought
before selecting project sites. As stated by the Government of Orissa
that the Government of India/CEA had “just intimated” to the State
Government about the identification of site. It implies that the State
Government was not involved in identification of site. Similarly, the
Government of ‘Chhattisgarh has stated that no formal consultations
with the State Government were held. Regarding the site in
Maharashtra, the statement of the Ministry that it was just one of
the probable sites and not the final one, raises questions as to the
manner in which the Central Government has gone about the
selection of sites for the UMPPs. The Committee feel that since the
State Governments have better knowledge of the feasibility of
making a particular land and other resources available for the
development of power projects - also considering the environmental
and other aspects - the State Governments should be involved in
the development process of UMPPs right from the conceptual stage.
This, in turn, will ensure that the projects are not unnecessarily
held up due to land and other related disputes. Further, the sites
should be formally announced only when the finality in this regard
has been reached - after the due consultation process - with the
respective State Government.

The Committee understand that in view of the local issues
involved in the setting up of UMPP at Tadri, the Central Government

is considering certain alternative sites for the purpose which is in

67


line with what the Committee also felt after their visit at the
Proposed site for UMPP at Tadri. The Committee recommend that
the Ministry of Power takes an urgent action in the matter so that
the UMPPs can be established both in Maharashtra and Karnataka
at the earliest, at the alternative sites.

4.5.9 The Committee observe that water requirement of Sasan
UMPP at Madhya Pradesh will be met from the Govindballabh Pant
Sagar (Rihand Reservoir). As stated by the Ministry of Power, water
used for drinking and irrigation will not be diverted in this case,

The Committee further observe that there was some dispute
between the Governments of Chhattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh
regarding the use of water, required for Sasan UMPP in Madhya
Pradesh. The Government of Chhattisgarh had objected to the use
of water of Rihand reservoir for Sasan project. Thereafter, the Central
Water Commission had conducted Inter-State Meetings in which it
was decided that “the water requirement of 0.109 million acre feet
of UMPP could be met from the share of Rihand water of Madhya
Pradesh by curtailing their future requirement of 0.216 million acre
feet earmarked for medium irrigation projects.”

The Committee, therefore, desire that such disputes should be
resolved in advance so that the project developer may not have to
face any difficulty in availability of water at a later stage. If need
be, the concerned States should enter into a written agreement on
the use of water for UMPPs, to avoid any controversy in future,
which should be then made available to the developer.

4.5.10 The Committee observe that the ‘Host States’ have
demanded a major share from the power allocated from UMPPs in
the States. The Ministry while on its part has assured that major
allocation of power is made to the host State only, the Committee,
however, note that there is no particular formula for allocation of
power and it is done on the basis of consensus arrived at in
consultation with the State Governments. The Committee feel that it
leaves a lot of scope for bias. The Committee recommend that a
formula be devised by the Ministry according to which the host
State should get a reasonable share of the power generated from
UMPP located therein. This formula be devised by taking into
consideration various factors like power shortages in the State, status
of infrastructure for evacuation of power, etc. The Committee strongly
feel that the allocation on the basis of a formula should be
completely objective leaving no scope for any grievance from the

68


States. The Committee further want that the involvement of the State
Governments should be maintained by the Centre in the whole
process of development of UMPPs.

4.5.11 The Committee are concerned to note that the project at
Chhattisgarh is being held up because of the demand of 12% free
power made by the Government of Chhattisgarh. The Committee
understand that there is no policy regarding giving free power to
the Host States from the thermal projects as is the case with the
hydro projects. The Committee desire that this point should be
impressed upon all the Host States and Chhattisgarh in particular.
The delay on account of demand of the Chhattisgarh Government is
disheartening. The Committee desire that the matter be taken up
with the State Government and the issue be resolved at the earliest.
The Committee note that any demand for free power by State would
have to be borne by the electricity consumers by way of increased
tariff. This may even make the project economically unviable and
uncompetitive leading to dropping of the project. The Committee
desire that these facts should be clearly brought to the notice of the
States which are demanding free power from UMPPs.

4.5.12 The Committee observe that projects at Karnataka and
Maharashtra have been held up due to some objections from the
local people of the area. The people of Tadri in Karnataka are against
the development of Ultra Mega Project there because of this being
an ecologically sensitive area and also in view of the fact that this
area already has four hydroelectric power plants and one nuclear
plant. The local people also have a fear of losing their livelihood.
Now the Government of Karanataka has constituted an Expert
Committee on 28.05.2006 consisting of MP, MLAs and other
stakeholders, PFC and Government of Karnataka KPCL, etc. to
examine various issues involved. In one of the meetings of the
Committee, it is learnt that CEA/PFC/Government of Karnataka had
proposed that a study be carried out to assess impact of the power
plant on the environment by a reputed consultant. However no
decision in this regard has so far been taken. The Committee desire
that the Expert Committee expedite the process so that clear picture
in regard to the development of project emerges. The Committee
feel that engaging a consultant to carry out a study, as proposed by
CEA/PFC/Government of Karnataka should also be considered by
the Expert Committee. In case if it comes out that the development
of power project will have an adverse effect on the environment, an
alternative site be finalised at the earliest. Similarly in case of
Maharashtra where the local people have raised certain environmental

69


issues relating to the growing of Alphanso mangoes, the Committee
desire that the consultant appointed for carrying out environment
studies should submit its report at the earliest. Considering the
importance of these projects, the Committee strongly recommend
that these projects should not be unduly held up and finalised at
the earliest in the larger interest of the country.

The Committee also desire that before announcing any site for
UMPP, it should be ensured that there is a broad consensus amongst
the various stakeholders for a particular site. The cases of generation
of opposition after the announcement of sites as that of Tadri in
Karnataka and Girye in Maharashtra should not be allowed to
happen. The Committee desire that all the local issues should be
decided in advance by State Governments, before offering a site to
set up UMPP.

INTRODUCTION

I, the Chairman, Standing Committee on Energy having been
authorized by the Committee to present the Report on their behalf,
present this 23rd Report (Fourteenth Lok Sabha) on the action taken
by the Government on the recommendations contained in the
20th Report of the Standing Committee on Energy on Demands for

2. The 20th Report of the Standing Committee on Energy was
presented to Lok Sabha on 27th April 2007. Replies of the Government
to all the recommendations contained in the Report were received on
20th August, 2007.

3. The Standing Committee on Energy considered and adopted
this Report at their sitting held on 22nd November, 2007.

4, An Analysis on the Action Taken by the Government on the
recommendation contained in the 20th Report of the Committee is
given at Annexure-II.

5. For facility of reference and convenience, the observations and
recommendations of the Committee have been printed in bold letters
in the body of the Report.

New DELHI; GURUDAS KAMAT,
November 22, 2007 Chairman,

Agrahayana 1, 1929 (Saka) Standing Committee on Energy.

(v)


CHAPTER I
REPORT

This Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the
Government on the recommendations contained in the Twentieth Report
(14th Lok Sabha) of the Standing Committee on Energy on Demands
for Grants of the Ministry of Power for the year 2007-08.

2. The Twentieth Report was presented to Lok Sabha on 27.04.2007
and was laid on the Table of Rajya Sabha on the same day. It contained
20 Recommendations /Observations.

3. Action taken notes in respect of all the observations/
recommendations contained in the Report have been received from
the Government. These have been categorized as follows:-

(i) Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted
by the Government:

SL. Nos. 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 17, 19 and 20

(ii) Recommendations/Observations which the Committee do
not desire to pursue in view of the Government's replies:

SL No. Nil

(iii) Recommendations/Observations in respect of which the
replies of the Government have not been accepted by the
Committee and which require reiteration:

Sl. Nos. 2, 4, 7, 13, 15, 16 and 18

(iv) Recommendations/Observations in respect of which the final
replies of the Government are still awaited:

Sl. No. 14

4. The Committee desire that utmost importance should be given
to the implementation of recommendations accepted by the
Government. In cases, where it is not possible for the Government
to implement the recommendations in letter and spirit for any
reasons, the matter should be reported back to the Committee in
time along with reasons for their non-implementation.



5. The Committee will now deal with action taken by the
Government on some of their recommendations:

A. Reducing peak power shortages
Recommendation (51. No. 2, Para 2.2.29)

6. The Committee were concerned to note that peak shortages had
increased from 11.8% in 2001-02 to 13.9% in 2006-07. The Committee
felt that apart from capacity addition and generation of more power,
there was a need to consider other solutions also like having different
time zones for the country and by Staggering the office timings and
school timings by about 1-2 hours so that peak hour/rush hour were
also staggered. However, the Committee desired that these suggestions
should be considered at the appropriate level and the Committee might
be informed of the action taken in the matter.

7. The Ministry in its reply has stated:

“Though there exists a time difference between Assam-Arunanchal
and Kutch-Saurashtra of about 1!/, to 2 hours observing a single
IST schedule for the whole country may not appear to be
reasonable, however, there is a great advantage in adopting a single
time reference throughout the country. For one thing, there is no
requirement of adjustment of watches while Passing from one State
to other State etc. It also facilitates the communication between
two places especially when the literacy level in the country is
about 65% as per 2001 census.

The peak energy demand is observed during winter from 06.00
hrs. to 10.00 hrs. in the morning and 17.00 hrs. to 21.00 hrs. in the
evening. During summer, it is from 5.00 hrs. to 09.00 hrs. in the
morning and 18.00 hrs. to 22.00 hrs. in the evening. The shifting
office timing and staggering of commercial and industrial load
beyond peak hours alone would facilitate the reduction in peak
load demand. Shifting of working schedule within peak load hours
would entail marginal benefit to the power sector.

Instead of adopting different Time zones in India, people in various
parts of the country should change their life style by adjusting
their timings of their own regions. This is an easier way to address
the problem rather than to have different time zones in different
parts of India.


The issue of shifting time zones may affect not only power sector
but also other departments like Railways, Transport & Aviation,
IMD and Communication etc.

Secretary, Deptt. of Science & Technology (DST) had earlier
constituted a Committee with the representatives from Nuclear
Power Corporation (NPC), Indian Meteorological Department
(IMD), Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), National Physical
Laboratory (NPL) & Ministry of Power to consider various issues
involved in this matter and its main views were as follows:

“On behalf of NPL, it was pointed out that the country spans
about 30 degrees longitude corresponding to two hours of local
time difference of extreme Eastern and Western ends. This has
given rise to an impression that in the Far-Eastern States, there are
about 41/, hours available between sunrise and the starting of the
offices and it is felt that this results in wastage of valuable daylight
time and may be reducing the efficiency of the workers by the
time they reach their work places. NPL has scientifically
demonstrated that there will be no drastic improvement by
incorporating two time zones. There may be an-hour saving in
daylight in places like Imphal, the same amount would be lost in
Delhi and western parts of the country. According to NPL, balance
of advantage for the purpose of saving daylight may be in
advancing the clocks throughout the country by one hour in
summer as this may -result in saving of one hour daylight in the
morning between sunrise and office time. Perhaps more pragmatic
way may be that the Eastern States resort to a time schedule of
8.00 a.m to 4.30 p.m. where as the western parts follow a time
schedule of 9.00 a.m to 5.30.p.m.

Central Electricity Authority was also of the view that instead of
going in for two standard times for India, the proposal for different
working hours could be considered in different zones of India.

On the current reckoning of consumption of electricity, the Tata
Energy Research Institute is also of the view that the benefit arising
out of the introduction of different time zones is small. Therefore,
before a decision can be taken to have different time zones in the
country, a consensus would have to be built among State
Governments and within various Ministries in the Government
and also among the major interest groups like industry, education
and the users of facilities like telecom, airlines, railways etc.”



8. The Committee have considered the reply of the Ministry in
regard to having different time zones in the country in the light of
submissions made by the Ministry as also in the light of the views
expressed by the expert bodies like NPL, TERI and CEA on the
issue,

9. The Committee tend to agree that adopting different time zones
in India may affect many departments like Railways, Transport &
Aviation, IMD and Communication, etc. and may have some practical
problems in view of low literacy level in the country and involves
many difficulties in arriving at a consensus to this effect between
various players like State Governments and various Ministries, etc.
While there is going to be no drastic improvement on account of
this. However, at the same point of time, the Committee feel greatly
concerned over the increase in peak power shortages in the country
from 11.8% in 2001-02 to 13.9% in 2006-07. The idea behind the
suggestion to have different time zones is to make full use of natural
light, which is available in abundance in our country so that peaking
shortages can be met. The Committee, therefore, find views of the
NPL that the Eastern and Western States in the country to follow
different time schedules and also view of the CEA to follow different
working hours across different zones in the country more pragmatic.
The Committee would like the Ministry to consider these and other
suggestions to check the peak shortages with a sense of urgency
and come up with a solution to the problem before the Committee
within next six months.

B. Encouraging private sector participation in capacity addition
Recommendation (SI. No. 4, Para 2.2.31)

10. The Committee in their Twentieth Report on Demands for
Grants (2007-08) had observed that out of the target of 7121 MW set
for the private sector during the 10th Plan, the likely achievement was
only 1930 MW which cannot be termed as satisfactory at all. Despite
allowing and facilitating the entry of private sector in the power sector
as per promise of the Electricity Act, 2003, its participation remained
very poor. Therefore, the Committee desired that a detailed study
should be made by the Government to know the reasons for poor
participation, the difficulties faced by the private sector and the steps
proposed to be taken to resolve those difficulties. The Committee
further desired to be apprised of the details in this regard.

11. The Ministry in its reply has stated:—
“As far as the participation of the private sector in the hydel

power is concerned, the original target of 1170 MW hydro capacity
addition in private sector in 10th Five Year (2002-07) Plan period


was subsequently revised to 700 MW during mid term appraisal
held in July-August, 2005. As per information available, the two
projects dropped were namely Maheshwar HEP(400 MW) of
M/s. Shree Maheshwar Hydel Power Corp. Ltd., M.P., due to
backing out of the foreign promoters .and Dhamwari Sunda HEP
(70 MW) of M/s. Dhamwari Power Co. Ltd., H.P,, due to non-
achievement of financial closure. The revised target of 700 MW
fixed during mid term appraisal was completely achieved with
the commissioning of Vishnuprayag HEP - 400 MW and Baspa
HEP - 300 MW.

As regards the participation of the private sector in the thermal
capacity addition, the Tenth Plan original target of 5951 MW was
revised to 4199 MW during the mid term appraisal held in
July-August, 2005. As against this revised target of 4199 MW,
projects having capacity totalling 1970.60 MW including two
projects, namely, 119.8 MW Karuppur CCPP, T.N. and 52.8 MW
Valantharavai CCPP, T.N., which were not included in the original
targets, were commissioned during the Tenth Plan period as per
detail given in Annexure-1. Twelve projects totalling 4767.60 MW
were dropped/slipped from the Tenth Plan target. Detail of these
projects including reasons for slippage/dropping is given at
Annexure-2.

The slow pace of private investment has been due to a number of
constraints. The foremost problem has been the inability of
Independent Power Producers( IPPs) to achieve financial closure
(inspite of progressing well on the other inputs/clearances), due
to the poor financial health of the state utilities who did not have
the financial capabilities to support more private projects in terms
of ability to open revolving letter of credit and escrow accounts
for regular payment of power. The other reasons for the private
projects not achieving financial closure, have been inordinate delay
in finalisation of PPA and the high cost of power perceived by the
buying utilities. In addition, some projects could not be
synchronized due to non-availability of gas and delay in supplies
by BHEL.

Government of India has been assisting wherever required, to
resolve issues coming in the way of implementation of IPPs,
including setting up of an Inter-Institutional Group (IIG) comprising
of senior representatives from the Financial Institutions and Ministry
of Power to facilitate early financial closure of power projects.
9 projects totalling 5535 MW have achieved financial closure during
this period and are presently under construction.”

data furnished by the Ministry, it is also apparent that contrary to
what has been stated the inability to achieve financial closure is not
only the foremost problem for Independent Power Producers (IPPs).
In fact out of 12 cases of slippages in the 10th Plan cited by the
Ministry only in two cases has this been a factor. Obviously, there
are many other factors, which are leading to such poor achievements
by the private sector in capacity addition. The Committee find reply
of the Ministry, thus, incomplete because while reasons for poor
participation of private sector in power sector have been put before
them, other than resolving the financial closure issue coming in the
way of implementation of IPPs, the steps taken to address other
issues have not been reported to them.

14, The Committee would, therefore, not only want the Ministry
of Power to address all the other issues involved in poor participation
of private sector in power sector and report back to them but also
to ensure that those constraints do not come in the way of private
investment in the power sector during the XIth Plan, by constant
monitoring. There is a need to make a detailed study of the two
factors for delay, which appear to be interlinked. The supply from
gas based power projects is likely to be costlier and supply of gas
has also to be ensured for the gas based projects. The Government
should make a specific study as to at what level of price the gas
based electricity is acceptable to the consumers. While agreeing to
these projects the Government should also see that the private players
have firm availability of gas with them.

17. The Ministry in its reply has stated:

“In order to resolve the issue of placing of bulk orders 8-10 units

unit through NTPC, Hon’ble Prime Minister had referred the matter
to Chairman, NMCC to give suitable recommendation/suggestion,
the Chairman, NMCC in his report dated 15.06.2007 submitted to
PMO, Ministry of Power and to Ministry of Heavy Industry, has

placement of a specific number of units on a negotiated basis on
BHEL, the Indian manufacturer, who is in the state of readiness to
start the work. Secondly, he is not in favour of setting up of
manufacturing unit by NTPC due to various reasons enumerated
in the report. A meeting on this issue under the chairmanship of
Minister of Power was held on 21.06.2007 in which it was
emphasized that the BHEL should prepare themselves to cater to
the requirement of power manufacturing equipments as envisaged
in the 11th plan and further. Ministry of Power is however in
favour of ICB with mandatory condition of setting up of
manufacturing base in India because of transparency satisfying the
condition of Mega power guidelines and assurance of regulator’s
consent.


So far as NTPC is concerned, International Competitive Bidding
(ICB) procedure is generally followed in respect of Main Plant
Equipment and other major packages of its Projects in view of the
following:—

— Obtaining the best competitive price in a transparent manner.

— Mega Power Project Benefits - In the case of interstate
thermal projects of capacity 1000 MW or more, mega benefits
such as Custom Duty & Excise Duty Exemptions/Refunds
are available for contracts awarded through ICB route.

However for 210/500 MW Main Plant Equipments BHEL has been
the lowest evaluated techno-economically responsive bidder. As has
been the experience in 10th Plan there are serious bottlenecks in
the power capacity addition in terms of delay in supplies,
inadequate deployment of construction machinery, non-availability
of skilled manpower at site and delay in placement of orders for
balance of plants by BHEL, inadequate project management
capability. As capacity addition envisaged in 11th Plan (78601 MW)
is more than three times actually achieved during the 10th Plan
(21094 MW) and even higher capacity targets are envisaged during
12th Plan (100000 MW), it is imperative to have more sources of
equipment supply.

Strong domestic power equipment manufacturing capability will
go a long way in creating generating capacities for meeting the
power demand of Indian economy, and there is an urgent need to
have more than one domestic manufacturer as a long-term strategy
to meet the growth of power sector. Even if action is initiated
immediately, it will take 3-4 years time for a new facility to come
into existence and roll out its first product. As such, the first plant
can be commissioned in 7 years from now i.e. in 12th Plan.

As such, in the short term, BHEL needs to change its focus to be
Project centric from existing focus on Tonnage/Turnover Centric.
They need to bring paradigm shift in their project management
method and strengthen their weak links like Project Engineering
Management (PEM), Piping Centre, Transformer Division etc. This
change needs to be demonstrated in shortest time frame and BHEL
must be put to strict scrutiny thereof by independent authority.

As regards NTPC entering into manufacturing, while NTPC may
not like to go on its own, it is open to the idea of Partnering with
suitable entity on the basis of a sound business model. This might


result in encouraging competition and achieving the overall target
of capacity addition in the long run. It has to partner with a
strategic partner who can bring the expertise in manufacturing
which in combination with NTPC’s strength in Planning,
Engineering, Project Management, Operational Expertise can be
used to develop a viable competitor.

It may be noted in this regard that NTPC has recently entered
into a Business Collaboration and Shareholders Agreement with
Transformers and Electricals Kerala Limited (TELK) and Govt. of
Kerala for synergy in the field of manufacturing and repair of
high voltage power transformers and associated equipment and
shall be acquiring 44.6 % stake in TELK.

As regards supercritical technology based plants, NTPC’s two
projects at Sipat-I (3x660 MW) and Barh (3x660 MW) awarded
through ICB are already under construction and all the units are
targeted for commissioning in 11th Plan. Further, Bidding is
presently in process for two more super critical technology based
projects namely North Karanpura STPP (3x660 MW) and Barh-II
(2x660 MW) for benefits starting in 11th Plan.”

18. The Committee are in full agreement with the views of the
Ministry that strong domestic power equipment manufacturing will
go a long way in creating generating capacities for meeting the power
demand of Indian economy. They, therefore, strongly endorse the
observation that BHEL not only changes its focus to be project centric
from existing focus on Tonnage/Turnover Centric but also strengthen
their weak links like Project Engineering Management (PEM) and
other associated factors in shortest time frame. The Committee desire
that all out efforts should also be made to encourage more firms to
take up power equipment manufacturing so that there is no
constraints on supply of these equipments.

20

33. The Ministry in its reply has stated:

“The main objective of Accelerated Power Development and
Reforms Programme (APDRP) was reduction of AT&C losses from
the level of around 40% to around 15% in five years to begin with
in the urban areas and high density/consumption areas. Further,
it was also targeted to reduce commercial and cash loss of the
utilities. Under Investment Component Government provided
Additional Central Assistance for strengthening and upgradation
of Sub-transmission and Distribution Network to SEBs/Utilities.
The assistance was in the form of 25% grant and 25% loan of the
project cost. Special category States were provided 90% grant and
10% loan. However, the loan portion was discontinued w.e.f. April
2005 on the recommendation of 12th Finance Commission. Under
Incentive Component SEBs/Utilities were incentivised for cash loss
reduction to motivate them towards reduction of their losses.
Funds are released for actual cash loss reduction, for every
Rs. 2 of cash loss. reduction Rs. 1 is given as grant.

Right from the beginning, it was made clear’to the States that the
programme was reform oriented and not budget and expenditure
oriented. The off take by the States was obviously slow as they
had to agree to various conditionalities for becoming eligible for
APDRP assistance (signing of MOA), standardize their technical
specification, streamline their bidding process and switch over to
turnkey contracting. Only a few States like Andhra Pradesh, Goa,
Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Uttaranchal
took early initiatives and most of their districts headquarter towns
have been covered under the programme. These States have shown
significant improvement in reduction of AT&C loss and commercial
loss as well. At the town level, wherever they were able to complete
the projects even up to 75-80%, visible improvements have been
seen in most of such cases. Other States were late in signing the
Memorandum of Agreements and in submission of schemes.
Further unrealistic DPRs, heavy quantum of work, increase in price


of material, poor availability of contractors etc. also resulted in
delay in implementation of the scheme. The States of North-Eastern
Region and Jammu & Kashmir were especially late starters. Due
to these constraints APDRP projects of only Rs. 17033.58 crore
could be sanctioned by the Ministry.

The implementation of the sanctioned Projects was also delayed
due to delays in transfer of funds by State Government to the
distribution companies. Under the Additional Central Assistance,
funds mandatorily pass through the State Government and on
account of delay in release to the implementing distribution
companies funds were not available in time for the Project
execution, In many instances, it took even more than a year to
release funds to the implementing agency after release by the
Central Government.

Under the Incentive Component, out of the proposals received from
various States, nine States namely, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat,
Haryana, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, West
Bengal and Punjab were found eligible, as per the guidelines of
the programme, for release of incentive under the programme,

2007-08.”

the Ministry regarding poor achievement in implementation of

Committee would, therefore, like the Ministry to work more
purposefully so that the target of restricting these losses to 15% is
achieved sooner than later.

Government are not further released by the State Governments to
the implementing agencies for quite a long time. The Committee
feel that Ministry ought to take immediate steps to ensure that the
funds so released are not held up by the respective State

to the implementing agencies. The Committee feel that it would be
better if certain guidelines are fixed to this effect.

36. Unless and until such a system is put in place the success of

right earnest so that APDRP does not get mired in red tapism and

The Committee note that a target of 41110 MW was fixed for 10th

end of 10th Plan only 21180 MW has been achieved. The performance
of the Ministry regarding capacity addition in the 10th Plan is thus
abysmally disheartening. The actual achievement has been only 51.5%
of targeted capacity addition. It is a matter of great concern in a fast
growing economy like India where generation of power has to grow
almost in direct proportion to the growth of Gross Domestic Product
(GDP). The Committee find many a reasons responsible for this
scenario. Delay in the award of works/ order placement, delay in
supplies by BHEL, delay in supply of Aux. Boiler, delay in placement
of order for material handling plant, etc., are the reasons which show
slackness on the part of executing agencies and should have been
tackled through proper monitoring. Starting from the planning stage,
the Committee feel that the targets for the plan period are seemingly
unrealistic. Since gestation period for development of Power Project
varies from 4 years to almost 7-8 years, many projects spill over into
two plans. The Committee fail to understand as to how the proposed
capacity addition of 68,869 MW for the 11th Plan would be achieved
- especially when the 10th Plan target of 41110 MW could not be
achieved. The Committee, therefore, desire that the annual and plan
targets for capacity addition should be fixed realistically.

26

Commission. However, it is Proposed to add a capacity of 78577 MW
during the 11th Plan period. Out of this capacity, a capacity of 47595

order for the remaining capacity of 29402 MW by December, 2007 so
as to achieve the target as planned. Further a capacity of 1580 MW
has already been commissioned in 11th Plan till 21.06.2007.

Recommendation (Serial No. 5, Paragraph No.2.2.32)

Committee note that 53% of capacity addition target has slipped
to 11th Plan. Out of this, major slippage has been due to delay in
Supercritical technology and supply of equipment & materials by BHEL.
Since BHEL is the sole supplier of equipment, it seemed to be
overburdened with work. Extremely worried by the situation as
obtaining presently in regard to the equipment supply for the Power
Plants, the Committee strongly recommend that to ensure that the
capacity addition does not suffer during the 11th Plan due to delay on
the part of BHEL, the government should go for international
competitive bidding for procuring equipment from other suppliers as
well.

The Committee further desire that the proposal of the Government
to enhance equipment manufacturing capacity in India, under the
flagship of NTPC and other players, should be vigorously pursued to
its logical conclusion in a fixed time frame and the Committee be
apprised of the same. Similarly, the proposal of NTPC for looking at
the possibility of entering into some on-going equipment manufacturing
business should also be pursued simultaneously. The Committee also
strongly endorse that in order to avoid delays in the setting up of
higher capacity power projects which are caused mainly due to non-
availability of advance environment clearances for the same, the

27



Government should invariably try and secure clearances in advance.
The Government should also make all out efforts to get Super Critical
alternate technologies available worldwide for the setting up of Power
Plant as a number of NTPC projects have been held up due to non-
availability of this technology.

Reply of the Government

In order to resolve the issue of placing of bulk orders 8-10 units
of Supercritical technology on BHEL and a separate manufacturing
unit through NTPC, Hon’ble Prime Minister had referred the matter
to Chairman, NMCC to give suitable recommendation/suggestion, the
Chairman, NMCC in his report dated 15.06.2007 submitted to PMO,
Ministry of Power and to Ministry of Heavy Industry, has suggested
that Ministry of Power should consider favourably placement of a
specific number of units on a negotiated basis on BHEL, the Indian
manufacturer, who is in the state of readiness to start the work.
Secondly, he is not in favour of setting up of manufacturing unit by
NTPC due to various reasons enumerated in the report. A meeting on
this issue under the Chairmanship of Minister of Power was held on
21.06.2007 in which it was emphasized that the BHEL should prepare
themselves to cater to the requirement of power manufacturing
equipments as envisaged in the 11th plan and further. Ministry of
Power is however in favour of ICB with mandatory condition of setting
up of manufacturing base in India because of transparency satisfying
the condition of Mega power guidelines and assurance of regulator’s
consent.

So far as NTPC is concerned, International Competitive Bidding
(ICB) procedure is generally followed in respect of Main Plant
Equipment and other major packages of its projects in view of the
following:

— Obtaining the best competitive price in a transparent manner.

— Mega Power Project Benefits—In the case of interstate
thermal projects of capacity 1000 MW or more, mega benefits
such as Custom Duty & Excise Duty Exemptions/ Refunds
are available for contracts awarded through ICB route.

However for 210/500 MW Main Plant Equipments BHEL has been
the lowest evaluated techno-economically responsive bidder. As has
been the experience in 10th Plan there are serious bottlenecks in the
power capacity addition in terms of delay in supplies, inadequate
deployment of construction machinery, non-availability of skilled

28


manpower at site and delay in placement of orders for balance of
plants by BHEL, inadequate project management capability. As capacity
addition envisaged in 11th Plan (78601 MW) is more than three times
actually achieved during the 10th Plan (21094 MW) and even higher
capacity targets are envisaged during 12th Plan (100000 MW), it is
imperative to have more sources of equipment supply.

Strong domestic power equipment manufacturing capability will
go a long way in creating generating capacities for meeting the power
demand of Indian economy, and there is an urgent need to have more
than one domestic manufacturer as a long-term strategy to meet the
growth of power sector.Even if action is initiated immediately, it will
take 3-4 years time for a new facility to come into existence and roll
out its first product. As such, the first plant can be commissioned in
7 years from now ie. in 12th Plan.

As such, in the short term, BHEL needs to change its focus to be
Project centric from existing focus on Tonnage/Turnover Centric. They
need to bring paradigm shift in their project management method and
strengthen their weak links like Project Engineering Management (PEM),
Piping Centre, Transformer Division etc. This change needs to be
demonstrated in shortest time frame and BHEL must be put to strict

As regards NTPC entering into manufacturing, while NTPC may
not like to go on its own, it is open to the idea of partnering with
suitable entity on the basis of a sound business model. This might

partner who can bring the expertise in manufacturing which in

The Committee note with concern that no exemption in Excise

Recommendation (SI. No. 9, Para No. 2.4.8)

The Committee feel that the hydro power generation has not been
given the desired impetus. The percentage of hydro share in aggregate
capacity during the 9th & 10th Plan has been only 25% & 26%
respectively whereas the ideal ratio between thermal & hydro should
be 60:40. Considering the shortage of coal and gas and also combined
with the fact that India has an estimated unutilized hydro-power
potential of 1,50,000 MW, the Committee strongly desire that more
emphasis should be given to hydro power generation. The Committee,
therefore, recommend that Government should work out a strategy
for exploiting the hydro power and increasing the share of hydro
power generation to an ideal 40% during the 11th Plan.

The Committee note that the tariff policy notified in January 2006
requires that all distribution utilities shall procure power only through
competitive bidding. But there are uncertainties and risks associated
with construction of hydro projects like geological surprises,
resettlement and rehabilitation problems inaccessibility of sites, law
and order problems etc. This renders tariff based bidding as a difficult
Proposition for hydroelectric projects. The Committee are happy to
note that to address this complex issue, the Central Government has
prepared a policy, which is yet to be firmed up after having a re-look
at the same and taking into consideration the concerns expressed by
the States in regard thereto. The Committee expect the Government to
come up with this policy within a definite time fame so that the road
blocks or irritants in the way of exploiting huge unexploited hydro-
power potential in the country could be removed on due priority.
Since delay in getting environment clearance is a major reason for
delay in hydro power projects, the Committee feel that there is a need
to reassess the remap the forest area in the country so as to ensure
that the environment clearances are secured early. The Committee desire
that the Ministry of Power should take up this matter with the Ministry
of Environment and Forests. The Committee further desire that a Joint
Coordination Committee—consisting of the representatives of the

34


Ministry of Power and the Ministry of Environment and Forests be
formed to address and resolve the issues involved in power generation.
The Committee desire that this matter should also be brought to the
notice of PMO for necessary action.

Reply of the Government
Capacity Addition Target for Hydro Projects during 11th Plan:

In Ith Plan (2007-12) 16553 MW is proposed to be added through
hydro Projects. In addition, hydro projects with total capacity of
2745 MW have also been identified on which additional efforts would
be needed to realize benefit during 11th plan.

To realize the planned benefits during 11th Plan, advance action
on the identified hydroelectric schemes has been initiated in the early
part of the 10th Plan itself as pre-DPR activities are normally time
consuming and relatively longer period is required for obtaining various
clearances,

50,000 MW Hydroelectric Initiatives:

For speedy development of hydro power potential this Ministry
had launched 50,000 H.E. Initiatives. Under the programme, Preliminary
Feasibility Reports (PFRs) of 162 hydro-electric projects (47,930 MW)
were prepared in the year 2003-04. As a follow up of preparation of
PFRs, it was decided to take up implementation/preparation of DPRs
for attractive schemes selected from PFR schemes thereby providing a
shelf of projects for execution in the near future. Out of 162 schemes
(47930 MW) for which PFRs have been prepared, at first instance,
based on their preliminary techno-economic analysis, 77 schemes
(33951 MW) whose first year tariff works out below Rs. 2.50/kWh
have been taken up for detailed survey & investigation and preparation
of DPR/ implementation.

Constitution of Task Force:

Pursuant to the decision taken in the Conference of Chief Ministers
on the Power Sector on 28th May, 2007 where Hon’ble Prime Minister
was also present, it was decided to constitute a Task Force for Hydro
Power Development. Since the bulk of the undeveloped hydro potential
is along the Himalayas ie. in hill States of Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal
Pradesh, Uttarakhand and North-East more particularly Sikkim and
Arunachal Pradesh, this Ministry has proposed for constitution of Task
Force for accelerated development of hydro potential in the country

35


especially in the above said States. The Task Force would be headed
by the Hon’ble Minister of Power with representation from the above
said States and concerned Ministries/Departments of Government of
India. In addition to ensuring coordinated and balanced hydropower
development, the Task Force will also look into the issues of
rehabilitation & resettlement of project-affected persons. The Secretary,
Ministry of Environment & Forests (MoEF) has also been proposed to
be nominated as a Member in the Task Force. The issues relating to
environment/forest clearance will also be looked into by the said Task
Force.

Recommendation (51, No. 11, Para No. 2.6.5)

The Committee note that 10th Plan outlay for NEEPCO was
Rs. 4224 crore out of which only Rs. 832.62 crore are likely to be
utilized. The Committee are, however, unhappy to note that even at
BE stage annually, funds were not allocated as per 10th Plan outlay.
At RE stage these were further reduced drastically every year and
actual utilization turned out to be much less. The Committee are
concerned to note that NEEPCO have totally failed to achieve the
prescribed financial and physical targets of 10th Plan. The Committee
feel that this is a clear case of poor planning. Where the Ministry of
Power, Government of India does not appear to have taken any
corrective steps. Considering the immense importance of NEEPCO and
the objective behind its establishment—exploiting the power potential
of North Eastern Region which would lead to development of North
Eastern Region, the under utilization of funds is a serious matter. The
Committee desire that the reasons for gross under-utilization of funds
by NEEPCO during the 10th Plan be analyzed in details and the
corrective steps taken accordingly. The Committee desire that 11th Plan
targets, both physical and financial, should be based on more realistic
assessment keeping in mind the various factors which have led to
gross under-utilisation of 10th Plan outlay.

57


The Committee also find that most of the reasons cited by the
Ministry of Power, for under-utilisation of funds are such which could
have been easily known if any serious examination of those projects
would have been done. But this is perhaps lacking even when review
meetings are held for the projects in hand. The Committee desire that
every review meeting should identify various reasons for delays and
also take immediate steps to remove those reasons. This should be a
standard practice for all the review meetings.

Reply of the Government

Reasons of Underutilisation of 10th Plan Outlay/Failure to achieve
the financial & physical achievements during the 10th Plan:—

The 10th Plan outlay in respect of NEEPCO was Rs. 4224.18 cr.
out of which Rs. 747.40 cr. has been utilized during the period
(2002-2007). The Project-wise analysis of underutilization of funds
during 10th Plan is elaborated hereunder.

1. Tuirial H.E. Project (60 MW), Mizoram: Out of total outlay
of Rs. 255 cr. during 10th plan, only an amount of
Rs. 119.14 cr. was utilized during 10th plan period. Adverse
law & order situation due to frequent bandhs, kidnapping
sand extortion threats were major concerns which hampered
timely implementation of the project. Further, all project
activities came to a total stop wef. 09-06-04 because of
agitation called by Tuirial Crop Compensation Claimants’
Association (TCCA) demanding payment against crop
compensation.

Other attributable reasons for underutilization of funds include:

(i) Delay in Review of Feasibility: One year delay had
occurred in the preparation and submission of the Review
of Feasibility by the review consultant primarily due to
adverse law and order situation and non-availability of
principal access roads.

(ii) Lack of Principal Access Road: Access road to the Project
was of very poor condition and NEEPCO had to
imperatively engage itself a substantial period of time in
developing these infrastructural works resulting in delayed
starting of the main works.

(iii), Change in Technical Parameters of the Project: Review
report submitted by the consultant, M/s Electro Watt

ensure overall safety of the structures. Despite precaution

numbers of Adit due to topographical constraints, the
progress of HRT works are badly affected leading to
underutilization of fund.

Reducing cost of generation of power
Past and Current activities:

The cost of generation of power depends primarily on the fuel
related costs. Reducing cost of power generation must, therefore, focus
on reducing costs associated with fuel. The cost of fuel input in a
power station is dependent on the unit heat rate, the station heat rate
(which considers the coal yard losses in a coal fired unit), the auxiliary
power and the specific secondary oil consumption (for coal fired units
only).

Recommendation (SI.No. 2, Para 2.2.29)

The Committee are concerned to note that peak shortages have
increased from 11.8% in 2001-02 to 13.9% in 2006-07. The Committee
feel that apart from capacity addition and generation of more power,
there is a need to consider other solutions also like having different
time zones for the country and by staggering the office timings and
school timings by about 1-2 hours so that peak hour/rush hour are
also staggered. The Committee desire that these suggestions should be
considered at the appropriate level and the Committee may be informed
of the action taken in the matter.

Reply of the Government

Though there exists a time difference between Assam-Arunanchal
and Kuch-Saurashtra of about 1-1/2 to 2 hours observing a single IST
schedule for the whole country may not appear to be reasonable,
however, there is a great advantage in adopting a single time reference
throughout the country. For one thing, there is no requirement of
adjustment of watches while passing from one State to other State etc.
It also facilitates the communication between two places especially
when the literacy level in the country is about 65% as per 2001 census.

The peak energy demand is observed during winter from
06.00 hrs to 10.00 hrs in the morning and 17.00 hrs to 21.00 hrs in the
evening. During summer, it is from 5.00 hrs to 09.00 hrs in the morning
and 18.00 hrs to 22.00 hrs in the evening. The shifting office timing
and staggering of commercial and industrial load beyond peak hours
alone would facilitate the reduction in peak load demand. Shifting of
working schedule within peak load hours would entail marginal benefit
to the power sector.

Instead of adopting different Time zones in India, people in various
parts of the country should change their life style by adjusting their
timings of their own regions. This is an easier way to address the
problem rather than to have different time zones in different parts of
India.

82


The issue of shifting time zones may affect not only power sector
but also other departments like Railways, Transport & Aviation, IMD
and Communication etc.

Secretary, Deptt. of Science & Technology (DST) had earlier
constituted a Committee with the representatives from NPC, IMD, BIS,
NPL & MOP to consider various issues involved in this matter and its
main views were as follows:

“On behalf of NPL, it was pointed out that the country spans
about 30 degrees longitude corresponding to two hours of local
time difference of extreme Eastern and Western ends. This has
given rise to an impression that in the Far-Eastern States, there are
about 4!/ 2 hours available between sunrise and the starting of the
offices and it is felt that this results in wastage of valuable daylight
time and may be reducing the efficiency of the workers by the
time they reach their work places. NPL has scientifically
demonstrated that there will be no drastic improvement by
incorporating two time zones. There may be an-hour saving in
daylight in places like Imphal, the same amount would be lost in
Delhi and western parts of the country. According to NPL, balance
of advantage for the purpose of saving daylight may be in
advancing the clocks throughout the country by one hour in
summer as this may result in saving of one hour daylight in the
morning between sunrise and office time. Perhaps more pragmatic
way may be that the Eastern States resort to a time schedule of
8.00 a.m to 4.30 p.m. where as the western parts follow a time
schedule of 9.00 a.m to 5.30. p.m.

Central Electricity Authority was also of the view that instead of
going in for two standard times for India, the proposal for different
working hours could be considered in different zones of India.

On the current reckoning of consumption of electricity, the Tata
Energy Research Institute is also of the view that the benefit arising
out of the introduction of different time zones is small. Therefore,
before a decision can be taken to have different time zones in the
country, a consensus would have to be built among State
Governments and within various Ministries in the Government
and also among the major interest groups like industry, education
and the users of facilities like telecom, airlines, railways etc.”

[Ministry of Power’s U.O No. 14/8/2007-EC Dated 18.07.2007]

Recommendation (SI. No. 4, Para No. 2.2.31)

The Committee observe that out of the target of 7121 MW set for
the private sector during the 10th Plan, the likely achievement is only
1930 MW which cannot be termed as satisfactory at all. Despite
allowing and facilitating the entry of private sector in the power sector
as per promise of the Electricity Act, 2003, its participation remains

by the Government to know the reasons for poor participation, the
difficulties faced by the private sector and the steps proposed to be

Reply of the Government

As far as the participation of the private sector in the hydel power
is concerned, the original target of 1170 MW hydro capacity addition
in private sector in 10th Five Year (2002-07) Plan period was
subsequently revised to 700 MW during mid term appraisal held in
July-August, 2005. As per information available, the two projects
dropped were namely Maheshwar HEP(400 MW) of M/s Shree
Maheshwar Hydel Power Corp. Ltd., M.P., due to backing out of the
foreign promoters .and Dhamwari Sunda HEP(70 MW) of
M/s Dhamwari Power Co. Ltd., H.P., due to non-achievement of
financial closure. The revised target of 700 MW fixed during mid term
appraisal was completely achieved with the commissioning of
Vishnuprayag HEP—400 MW and Baspa HEP-300 MW.

As regards the participation of the private sector in the thermal
capacity addition, the Tenth Plan original target of 5951 MW was
revised to 4199 MW during the mid term appraisal held in July-August,
2005. As against this revised target of 4199 MW, projects having capacity
totaling 1970.60 MW including two projects, namely, 119.8 MW
Karuppur CCPP, T.N. and 52.8 MW Valantharavai CCPP, T.N., which
were not included in the original targets, were commissioned during
the Tenth Plan period as per detail given in Annexure-1. Twelve
projects totaling 4767.60 MW were dropped/slipped from the Tenth
Plan target. Detail of these projects including reasons for slippage/
dropping is given at Annexure-2.

The slow pace of private investment has been due to a number of
constraints. The foremost problem has been the inability of Independent
Power Producers (IPPs) to achieve financial closure (inspite of
progressing well on the other inputs/clearances), due to the poor

84


financial health of the state utilities who did not have the financial
capabilities to support more private projects in terms of ability to
open revolving letter of credit and escrow accounts for regular payment
of power. The other reasons for the private projects not achieving
financial closure, have been inordinate delay in finalisation of PPA
and the high cost of power perceived by the buying utilities. In
addition, some projects could not ‘be synchronized due to non-
availability of gas and delay in supplies by BHEL.

Government of India has been assisting wherever required, to
resolve issues coming in the way of implementation of IPPs, including
setting up of an Inter-Institutional Group (IIG) comprising of senior
representatives from the Financial Institutions and Ministry of Power
to facilitate early financial closure of power projects. 9 projects totaling
5535 MW have achieved financial closure during this period and are
presently under construction.

Recommendation (Sl. No. 7, Para No. 2.2.34)

The Committee appreciate the initiative of the Ministry of Power
regarding the development of Ultra Mega Power Projects, which the
committee feel will help in meeting the rising demand of the power
in the country to a great extent. During the course of evidence on
Demands for Grants for the year 2007-08, Members raised a number
of queries regarding the setting up of Ultra Mega Power Projects
expressing concern as to whether these projects would come up as
scheduled earlier. Also an apprehension was expressed that the targets
fixed by the Government for achieving the generation of 1,00,000 MW
by 2012 to meet the goal of electricity for all may be jeopardized, the
representative of the Ministry of Power, however, explained that they
have set upon themselves the target of 1,00,000 MW capacity addition
alongwith the transmission links and related activities by the year
2012.

The Committee, however, are greatly concerned with the present
status of development of Sasan Ultra Mega Power Project, which was
awarded to Glogleq Singapore Private Limited and Lanco Consortium.
However, Globleq Singapore was later on sold by its parent company
to Prince Stone Investments, a holding company for Lanco Consortium
Limited and Jindal Steel and Power Limited.

The Committee had categorically desired to know from the Ministry
as to how the matter concerning award of contract for Sasan Project
consequent on change of ownership of the successful bidder was
proposed to be resolved. The Ministry had informed that they were
seeking legal opinion in the matter and considering all legal opinions
they would take appropriate decision. The Committee, however, have
now been informed on 23rd April, 2007 by the Ministry that the matter
is now under consideration of Central Vigilance Commission (CVC).
The Committee feel that an urgent action is required to resolve the
issue at the earliest and desire that all possible steps be taken to
ensure that the setting up of the Project is as per schedule without
any time and cost overruns. But considering the fact that there arose
a need for Central Vigilance Commission’s involvement in the
beginning of the project itself, the Committee feel apprehensive about
the project as due diligence was not shown by the Ministry of Power
in award of the project. The Committee, therefore, desire that
responsibilities be fixed in the matter and stern action be taken against
the guilty. The Committee should be apprised of the position at the
earliest regarding the development of this project-clearly analyzing the
matter as to how far this controversy is likely to affect the time and
cost overrun of the project.

The Committee are surprised to note that while the former Power
Secretary assured the Committee in meeting held on 2.8.2006 that some
units of Mega Power Projects would come up by the end of 11th Plan,

88


the new Secretary in his evidence before the Committee on 21.3.2007
stated that it was not possible to complete Ultra Mega Power Projects
in the 11th Plan and these would spill over to 12th Plan. The
Committee note that a programme for completion of 1,00,000 MW
capacity to ensure electricity for all by 2012 was announced by the
Government with much fanfare. The Committee are concerned with
the turn of events in the case of Sasan project and feel that apart from
non achievement of the targets, it may give bad publicity to the
Government's move to set up other Ultra Mega Power Projects and
ultimately affect the goal of electricity for all. The Committee note
that having achieved only 21180 MW during 11th Plan, there is no
likelihood of achieving 1,00,000 MW generating capacity by 2012 as
had been envisaged by the Government. The Committee desire that
no effort should be spared to achieve this target if the goal of electricity
for all is to be accomplished. The Committee feel that the power
situation in the country requires daily monitoring and accountability
to ensure progress as envisaged by the Government.

Reply of the Government

Achieving equilibrium in the demand and supply of power is essential.
Excess demand in the system invariably leads to poor quality of electric
supply including scheduled and unscheduled cut offs. Therefore,
creation of adequate capacity is necessary to ensure reliable and quality
power supply in line with the accepted international practices. The
National Electricity Policy notified on 12th February, 2005, inter alia
aims at achieving the following objectives:

* Access to electricity—Available for all households in next 5
years

* Availability of Power—Demand to be fully met by 2012.
Energy and peaking shortage to be overcome and adequate
spinning reserve to be available.

¢ Supply of reliable and quality power of specified standards
in an efficient manner and at reasonable rates.

Central Electricity Authority has assessed that for elimination of
shortages and achieving the goal of power for all by 2012, capacity
addition to the tune of about 1,00,000 MW is required during X and
XI Plan. During the X Plan, a generation capacity of 21180 MW has
been added. For the XI Plan, a generation capacity of 78,577 MW is
proposed to be added. Of this capacity, a generation capacity of above
49,000 MW is under execution. Ordering in respect of rest of generation
capacity targeted in XI Plan is planned to be completed by December,
2007. With the achievement of proposed capacity addition programme
during the course of XI Plan, it is assessed by Central Electricity

89


Authority that by 2012, marginal peaking surplus and energy surplus
to the tune of 5.6% is likely to be available in the country.

The recently concluded Conference of the Chief Ministers has
resolved that a Standing Group of Power Ministers under the
Chairmanship of the Minister of Power would be set up to look into
all issues affecting the power sector. Further, the resolution adopted in
‘the Conference inter alia includes that Centre would set up a National
Power Project Monitoring Board (NPPMB) for monitoring the timely
commissioning of the unprecedented generation capacity addition target
for XI Plan as also monitoring of associated transmission Projects.
Accordingly, Standing Group and the NPPMB are being constituted.

Regarding the development of Ultra Mega Power Projects it is to
mention that the Central Electricity Authority in consultation with States
has identified 9 sites suitable for development of Ultra Mega Power
Projects based on coal with a capacity of 4000 MW each. Out of these,
5 are at coastal locations and remaining 4 are pit head sites. The
details of sites are as follows:

(a) Five coastal locations:

(ii) Krishnapatnam in A.P

(b) Four pithead locations:
(i) Sasan in M.P
(ii) Tillaiya in Jharkhand
(ii) Sundergarh (Ib Valley) in Orissa
(iv) Akaltara in Chhattisgarh

Recommendation (SI. No. 13, Para No. 2.8.7)

The Committee note that out of 10th Plan Outlay of Rs. 21,370
crore, PGCIL could spend only Rs. 18,181 crore. However, with this
lesser outlay, the physical achievements have been more than the 10th
Plan targets. The Committee while appreciating the work done by
PGCIL in the field of transmission of power would suggest that
financial targets should be properly assessed. There is a need to
encourage the participation of private sector in the power sector as a

92


whole and in transmission sector as well. With this purpose the
Government has notified guidelines for encouraging competition in
the development of transmission projects. A Committee has been set
up and 14 projects have been identified for development through the
competitive bidding route. The Committee desire that these projects
be taken up for development by the private sector at the earliest and
the participation of private sector be allowed only in conformity with
the provision of the Electricity Act, 2003. Presently, the Committee
note, most of the private investment has come through Joint Venture
route only. Considering the fact that 11th Plan target is to attract
Rs. 20,000 crore investment for creating inter-regional transfer capacity
of 11500 MW, the Ministry should identify sufficient Projects in advance,
which can be offered to the private sector. The Committee should be
informed of the action taken in the matter.

Reply of the Government

It may be mentioned that all efforts are made to assess the financial
targets properly. However, as implementation of transmission schemes
are dependent upon system requirements like generation addition and
growth in demand, change/reduction in outlay of various transmission
schemes in Xth Plan was necessitated to match with the system
requirements.

During the Xth Plan, besides cost saving achieved in various
transmission projects from approved/estimated cost at the time of
finalisation of Xth Plan, there was rescheduling of transmission projects
due to deferment/deletion of planned generation projects (Net Rs. 875
crore), change in mode of implementation of few system strengthening
schemes (Rs. 410 crore) etc. Further some new strengthening schemes
were taken up for implementation as per system requirement. Besides
there was also a reduction in telecom outlay (Rs. 1575 crore) on account
of change in business plan considering market condition.

Recommendation (SI. No. 15, Para No. 2.9.13)

The Committee strongly feel that rural electrification means not
only electrification of households and villages but also catering to the
needs of farmers and small scale industries which are the backbone of

93


the rural economy. However, this aspect seem to have been ignored
by the Government as no mention has been made about achievements
in this regard under RGGVY. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that in addition of electrification of households, electricity for agriculture
and industrial activities should also be given due importance under
RGGVY.

Reply of the Government

RGGVY, through creation of Village Electricity Infrastructure (VEI),
Rural Electricity Distribution Backbone (REDB) and Decentralized
Distributed Generation (DDG) would also facilitate the following
activities indirectly:—

* irrigation pumpsets

* small and medium industries
* khadi and village industries
* cold chains

* healthcare

* education and IT

However, funds have not been allocated for providing electricity
for agriculture and industrial activities under RGGVY. Therefore, there
can be no targets for these activities under RGGVY. If States so desire,
they can approach financial institutions for loans for augmenting the
infrastructure being created under RGGVY to adequately cater for these
activities. Ministry of Power has also requested all the States to prepare
a Rural Electrification Plan for their State which will take into

consideration among other things the demand for electricity from
agriculture and industry.

[Ministry of Power’s U.O No. 44/3/2007-RE Dated 6.07.07]

Recommendation (Sl.No. 16, Para No. 2.10.16)

APDRP was launched by the Government in 2002-2003 with the
objective of reducing Aggregate Technical & Commercial (AT&C) losses
to around 15% in five years from the then existing which were

94


around 60%. The Committee, however, observe that even after
completion of five years, AT & C losses could only be reduced to
33.5% by 2005-06. The Committee would like to know the reasons for
such slow progress in reduction in AT & C losses. The Committee
note that in a number of States, both Non-Special Category and Special
Category States, utilisation of APDRP investment is less than 50% as
on 31.12.2006. These are Chattisgarh, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa,
Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur and Meghalaya etc. Similarly, in a number
of cases, loss reduction cash incentive has also not been released to a
number of eligible States like Gujarat’ Kerala, Madhya Pradesh etc.
The Committee would like to know the reasons for less utilisation of
funds by certain States as well as reasons for the non release of loss
reduction cash incentives to some States.

Reply of the Government

The main objective of Accelerated Power Development and Reforms
Programme (APDRP) was reduction of AT&C losses from the level of
around 40% to around 15% in five years to begin with in the urban
areas and high density/consumption areas. Further, it was also targeted
to reduce commercial and cash loss of the utilities. Under Investment
Component Government provided Additional Central Assistance for
strengthening and upgradation of Sub-transmission and Distribution
Network to SEBs/Utilities. The assistance was in the form of 25%
grant and 25% loan of the project cost. Special Category States were
provided 90% grant and 10% loan. However, the loan portion was
discontinued w.e.f. April, 2005 on the recommendation of 12th Finance
Commission. Under Incentive Component SEBs/Utilities were
incentivised for cash loss reduction to motivate them towards reduction
of their losses. Funds are released for actual cash loss reduction, for
every Rs. 2 of cash loss reduction Rs.1 is given as grant,

Right from the beginning, it was made clear to the States that the
programme was reform oriented and not budget and expenditure
oriented. The off take by the States was obviously slow as they had
to agree to various conditionalities for becoming eligible for APDRP
assistance (signing of MOA), standardize their technical specification,
streamline their bidding process and switch over to turnkey contracting.
Only a few States like Andhra Pradesh, Goa, Gujarat, Himachal
Pradesh, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Uttaranchal took early initiatives
and most of their districts headquarter towns have been covered under
the programme. These States have shown significant improvement in
reduction of AT&C loss and commercial loss as well. At the town
level, wherever they were able to complete the projects even up to

95


75-80%, visible improvements have been seen in most of such cases.
Other States were late in signing the Memorandum of Agreements
and in submission of schemes. Further unrealistic DPRs, heavy quantum
of work, increase in price of material, poor availability of contractors
etc. also resulted in delay in implementation of the scheme. The
States of North-Eastern Region and Jammu & Kashmir were especially
late starters. Due to these constraints APDRP projects of only
Rs. 17033.58 crore could be sanctioned by the Ministry.

The implementation of the sanctioned projects was also delayed
due to delays in transfer of funds by State Government to the
distribution companies. Under the Additional Central Assistance, funds
mandatorily pass through the State Government and on account of
delay in release to the implementing distribution companies funds were
not available in time for the project execution. In many instances, it
took even more than a year to release funds to the implementing
agency after release by the Central Government.

Under the Incentive Component, out of the proposals received from
various States, nine States namely, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Haryana,
Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, West Bengal and
Punjab were found eligible, as per the guidelines of the programme,
for release of incentive under the programme. These States had
achieved cash loss reduction of Rs. 5254.60 crores and had become
eligible for incentive of Rs. 2627.30 crore. The Government has so far
released Rs. 1749.03 crore. The balance amount will be released during
the current financial year 2007-08.

[Ministry of Power’s F.No. 5/1/2007-APDRP Dated July 4, 2007]

is implemented through CPRI. However, the R&D activities of CPRI

The Committee note that some research schemes on Power were

Reply of the Government

The Standing Committee on Energy has desired that Research
Schemes should be judiciously selected by various power utilities and

The Ministry of Power had formed a Standing Committee on R&D

CHAPTER V

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH
FINAL REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT IS STILL AWAITED

Recommendation (Sl. No. 14, Para No. 2.9.12)

The Committee note that the Government of India had launched
a number of schemes/programmes for electrification of rural areas in
the country, Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana (RGGVY) has
now been introduced by the Government in April, 2005 with an
objective of providing access to electricity to all rural households over
a period of 4 years. Rural Electrification Corporation is the nodal agency
for the programme. RGGVY proposed to electrify 40,000 villages during
2006-07 with a budgetary allocation of Rs. 3,000 crore. The Committee
note that till 9-2-2007, only 18,422 villages have been electrified and
4.87 lakhs connections have been released to BPL households. One of
the reasons given by the Government is that “lead time of 4-6 months
is required for pre-award activities.” The Committee feel that this
should have been preconceived of while setting the ambitious targets.
Another reason is “delay in issue of tenders by State power utilities
and State Government departments.” The reasons cited by the
Government for their poor performance only reflect poor planning
and lack of coordination. The Committee note that CPSUs like
POWERGRID, NTPC, NHPC, DVC & NEEPCO are providing their
services in the implementation of this scheme. Hence, any difficulties
being faced by State Governments in implementation of RGGVY should
have been removed/addressed in consultation with these organizations,
which does not seems to be the case.

The Committee, therefore, recommends that firstly targets should
be realistic and secondly, various PSUs and REC—which is the nodal
agency—in implementation of RGGVY should be asked to provide all
necessary technical and training support to State Governments in their
respective areas. The Committee further recommend that first a
thorough assessment be made about the targets to be achieved during
llth Plan and the funds required for the same. Then the sufficient
funds should be made available under the RGGVY in each of the five
years of 11th Plan to achieve the set target.

Reply of the Government

As the scheme aimed to electrify all villages in four years by 2009,
the action plan for village electrification had been prepared in a manner
such that it achieves the targets within the prescribed time limit. In
98


the year 2006-07, 28,706 villages were electrified, which is almost 75%
achievement. Besides electrification of 28,706 un-electrified villages
around 6.5 lakh Below Poverty Line (BPL) Households were electrified,
which cover not only un-electrified villages but also already electrified
villages for intensive electrification. The slippage of 25% in 2006-07
was due to factors which were beyond the control of executing agencies
like delay in approval by Ministry of Finance for enlarging the shelf
of projects from 125 to 235 projects for release of funds. Projects were
in abeyance for 2-3 months in the last quarter of the year. In the year
2006-07 funds were released only to 125 projects with an awarded cost
of Rs. 6032 crores covering 46,280 villages out of which 9819 villages
were already electrified in 2005-06. It was only after December, 2006
when the Ministry of Power took up the matter with Ministry of
Finance for increasing the shelf of projects that Ministry of Finance
increased the shelf to 235 projects covering 68,763 un-electrified villages
in February, 2007. Only one month was given for release of funds to
235 projects.

Till date only 235 projects are eligible for funds and accordingly
the implementing agencies can not go ahead with awarding of further
projects. As a result, till the CCEA Note is approved, the coverage of
un-electrified villages cannot be increased. It may also be noted that
project cycle is of 18 months from date of award. In view of this, it
will be extremely challenging to achieve the target of electrification of
40,000 villages. At present, for the year 2007-08 Ministry is left with
only 30,000 un-electrified villages for electrification which is not a
sufficient shelf of villages for achieving the target of 40,000 villages.

Secondly, as recommended by the Standing Committee, the Ministry
of Power has now written to REC, the Nodal Agency for
implementation of the scheme, to provide all necessary technical and
training support to State Governments in their respective areas.

Year-wise targets to be achieved within the prescribed time limit,
by 2009 have been assessed. It has been decided to electrify all un-
electrified villages included in the projects currently under
implementation in 2007-08 and 2008-09 subject to timely release of
adequate funds. The matter will be reviewed after obtaining fresh
CCEA approval to the programme.

INTRODUCTION

I, the Chairman, Standing Committee on Energy having been
authorized by the Committee to present the Report on their behalf,
present this 24th Report (Fourteenth Lok Sabha) on the action taken
by the Government on the recommendations contained in the 19th
Report of the Standing Committee on Energy on Demands for Grants
(2007-2008) of the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy.

2. The 19th Report of the Standing Committee on Energy was
presented to Lok Sabha on 27th April, 2007. Replies of the Government
to all the recommendations contained in the Report were received on
16th October, 2007.

3. The Standing Committee on Energy considered and adopted
this Report at their sitting held on 29th November, 2007.

4, An Analysis on the Action Taken by the Government on the
recommendation contained in the 19th Report of the Committee is
given at Annexure-II.

5. For facility of reference and convenience, the observations and
recommendations of the Committee have been printed in bold letters
in the body of the Report.
